--- Page 9 ---
<meta>Following the title page, this text provides the Foreword (Avant-Propos) to the 1886 edition. It establishes Dr. Bernheim's core argument: that the effects previously attributed to "animal magnetism" are actually the result of psychological suggestion.</meta>

## FOREWORD

The first part of this book was already published in 1884. I have reworked it, adding new facts and new considerations, and responding to the criticisms addressed to me. The second part, which is entirely new, focuses on *suggestive therapeutics* <note>The medical use of psychological suggestion to treat illness.</note>.

I entitle this book: *On Suggestion*. The word magnetism <note>Bernheim is distancing himself from "animal magnetism," the belief in a physical magnetic fluid flowing between the doctor and patient.</note>, born from an erroneous interpretation of phenomena, no longer has a reason to exist. It is suggestion that dominates most manifestations of hypnosis; the so-called physical phenomena are, in my view, nothing but psychic phenomena. It is the idea conceived by the practitioner <note>original: "opérateur"</note> which—once grasped by the subject and accepted by their brain—realizes the phenomenon, thanks to a heightened suggestibility <term>suggestibility: the quality of being inclined to accept and act on the suggestions of others</term> produced by the specific mental concentration of the hypnotic state. *Suggestion is the key to Braidism* <note>Named after James Braid, the surgeon who moved hypnosis away from "magnetism" toward a more scientific, psychological understanding.</note>.

This doctrine has led us to follow Mr. Liébeault in his method of suggestive therapeutics.

It is to Mr. Liébeault, a doctor of medicine in Nancy, that I owe my knowledge of the method I use to induce sleep <note>In the context of 19th-century hypnosis, "sleep" often refers to the hypnotic trance state.</note> and obtain certain undeniable therapeutic effects. For more than twenty-five years, this colleague—braving the ridicule and discredit attached to the practices of what is called animal magnetism—has pursued his research and devoted himself selflessly to the treatment of diseases through sleep.

<summary>In this foreword, Bernheim defines hypnosis as a psychological state of "suggestibility" rather than a physical magnetic force, crediting Dr. Liébeault for the clinical methods used in his practice.</summary>
<keywords>Suggestion, Hypnosis, Braidism, Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault, Nancy School, Psychical Phenomena, Medical History, Sleep Therapy</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Bernheim expands on the historical development of the Nancy School of hypnotism, tracing the lineage from Faria and Braid to Liébeault, and describing his own transition from skeptic to believer.</meta>

II

-># FOREWORD<-

The idea of suggestion, put forward by Faria <note>Abbé Faria (1756–1819) was a monk who pioneered the study of hypnotism, arguing it was generated by the subject's mind rather than an external "magnetic fluid."</note>, was more effectively applied by Braid <note>James Braid (1795–1860), the Scottish surgeon who coined the term "hypnotism" and moved the practice away from "animal magnetism."</note>; Mr. Liébeault, perfecting the method and reducing it to its simplest expression, showed—after Braid—that the vast majority of subjects are susceptible to being influenced; and many can obtain beneficial effects through the psychic state thus induced. The first researches of the Nancy doctor are recorded in a volume entitled: *On Sleep and Analogous States, Considered Especially from the Point of View of the Mind's Action on the Body. Paris, 1866.* <note>original: "Du Sommeil et des états analogues considérés surtout au point de vue de l'action du moral sur le physique."</note>

Mr. Liébeault's claims met only with skeptics. His practices seemed so marked by strangeness, if not to say naivety, that doctors rejected them without further examination. Mr. Liébeault lived in isolation, outside the medical world, entirely devoted to his patients (almost all from the poorer classes) and to his convictions.

Five years ago, Mr. Dumont, head of physical works at the Faculty of Medicine, having followed Mr. Liébeault's consultations, was convinced of the reality of the observed phenomena; he experimented successfully at the Maréville asylum <note>A psychiatric hospital near Nancy, France.</note> and had the good fortune to make a contracture <note>A condition of shortening or hardening of muscles, tendons, or other tissue, often leading to rigid or deformed joints.</note> of the right leg—which had lasted three years—disappear in a patient with hystero-epilepsy <term>hystero-epilepsy: a 19th-century medical diagnosis involving severe convulsions thought to be triggered by psychological distress</term>, as well as attacks of hystero-epilepsy that repeated 5 or 6 times a day.

At my request, on May 10, 1882, he presented four subjects to the Medical Society of Nancy, upon whom he performed a certain number of experiments that vividly struck the members of the Society.

I have myself experimented since that time—with great skepticism, I admit, at the beginning; and after some trial and error and hesitation, I soon observed certain striking results, which impose upon me the duty not to remain silent.

In the first part of this book, I will first explain the method used to produce hypnotism and the various manifestations that can be determined in hypnotized subjects.

<summary>Bernheim traces the lineage of suggestion from Faria and Braid to Liébeault, recounting how successful clinical trials at the Maréville asylum overcame his initial skepticism. This page establishes the scientific legitimacy of the Nancy School by citing successful treatments of chronic physical ailments through hypnotism.</summary>
<keywords>Abbé Faria, James Braid, Auguste Liébeault, Nancy School, suggestion, Maréville asylum, hystero-epilepsy, clinical hypnotism, medical skepticism</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>Continuing from page II, where Bernheim discusses the pioneering work of Abbé Faria, James Braid, and Dr. Liébeault in Nancy, Bernheim concludes his preface by outlining the scope of his own research and its multidisciplinary applications.</meta>

III

-># FOREWORD<-

Next, I will provide a brief historical overview of the question; I will examine the theoretical views put forward on this subject and I will present my personal opinions on the psychological mechanism of these phenomena.

Finally, I will examine in a general manner the applications of the doctrine of suggestion to psychology, to <term>forensic medicine</term> <note>Also known as legal medicine, this field applies medical expertise to legal cases, such as determining the mental state of a defendant or the validity of a witness's testimony.</note>, and to sociology.

In the second part, I will specifically study <term>suggestive therapy</term> <note>original: "thérapeutique suggestive" — the practice of using mental suggestion to treat physical or psychological ailments, a cornerstone of the Nancy School's approach.</note>, and I will report my personal observations.

H. BERNHEIM.

June 1886.

<summary>Bernheim outlines the remaining structure of his book, promising a historical review, a theoretical analysis of psychological mechanisms, and an exploration of how suggestion impacts law, society, and medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Hippolyte Bernheim, forensic medicine, suggestive therapy, psychology, sociology, Nancy School, history of science</keywords>

### CHAPTER ONE

->Method for obtaining hypnotism by suggestion. — On the various<-

Here is how I proceed to induce <term>hypnotism: a state of focused attention and increased suggestibility, historically referred to as "nervous sleep"</term>. 
I begin by telling the patient, whom I believe would benefit from hypnotic <term>therapeutics: the branch of medicine concerned with the treatment of disease and the action of remedial agents</term>, that it is possible to cure or relieve them through sleep; that it involves no harmful or extraordinary practice; that it is a simple sleep that can be induced in anyone—a calm, beneficial sleep that restores the balance of the nervous system, etc.; if necessary, I have one or two subjects sleep in front of them to show that this sleep is not painful and is not accompanied by any experimentation; and when I have thus removed from their mind the preoccupation caused by the idea of magnetism <note>original: "magnétisme"; referring to "animal magnetism" or Mesmerism, which many patients at the time associated with occultism or "mystical" fluids</note> and the somewhat mystical fear attached to this unknown, especially when they have seen other patients—

<summary>This introductory page outlines the author's clinical protocol for inducing hypnosis, emphasizing the use of verbal reassurance to distinguish the practice from "animal magnetism."</summary>
<keywords>hypnotism, suggestion, therapeutics, nervous system, clinical method, magnetism</keywords>

# HYPNOTIZATION PROCEDURE

cured or improved following this sleep, he is confident and yields. Then I say to him: "Look at me closely and think only of sleeping. You are going to feel a heaviness in your eyelids, a fatigue in your eyes; they are blinking, they are going to water; your vision is becoming blurry; they are closing." Some subjects close their eyes and sleep immediately. With others, I repeat, I emphasize more, I add a gesture; the nature of the gesture matters little. I place two fingers of my right hand before the person’s eyes and I invite them to fixate on them, or else with both hands I pass several times from top to bottom before their eyes; or else again I invite them to fixate on mine and I try at the same time to concentrate all their attention on the idea of sleep. I say: "Your eyelids are closing, you can no longer open them. You feel a heaviness in your arms, in your legs; you no longer feel anything, your hands remain motionless, you no longer see anything; sleep is coming," and I add in a somewhat imperious tone: "Sleep." Often this word tips the scales; the eyes close; the patient sleeps.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If the subject does not close their eyes or does not keep them closed, I do not prolong the fixation of their gaze on mine or on my fingers for long: for there are some who keep their eyes indefinitely wide open and who, instead of conceiving the idea of <term>sleep: here referring to the induced hypnotic state or "provoked sleep"</term>, have only that of staring with rigidity: the <term>occlusion: the physical act of closing or shutting the eyelids</term> of the eyes then succeeds better. After two or three minutes of fixation, I keep the eyelids closed, or else I spread them slowly and gently over the <term>eyeballs: the globe of the eye within the socket</term>, closing them more and more, progressively, imitating what happens when <term>sleep</term> comes naturally; I end by keeping them closed, while continuing the <term>suggestion: the psychological process by which the practitioner guides the thoughts and sensations of the patient</term>: "Your eyelids are stuck together, you can no longer open them; the need to sleep becomes deeper and deeper; you can no longer resist." I gradually lower my voice, I repeat the <term>injunction: a firm, authoritative command or order</term>: "Sleep," and it is rare that more than four or five minutes pass without—

# HYPNOTIZATION PROCEDURE

...until sleep is obtained. This is sleep by suggestion; it is the image of sleep that I suggest, that I instill into the brain.

The "passes" <note>original: "passes" — these were sweeping hand movements used by earlier Mesmerists, believed to move "animal magnetism" through the body</note>, the fixating of the operator's eyes or fingers—which are only suited to concentrating the attention—are not absolutely necessary.

Children, once they have reached the age of reason and are able to listen and understand, generally become hypnotized very quickly and easily. I often settle for closing their eyes, holding them shut for a few moments, telling them to sleep, and then affirming that they are asleep.

Some adults fall asleep in the same way, as easily as can be, by simple <term>occlusion: the physical act of closing or shutting the eyelids</term> of the eyes. Therefore, I often proceed immediately, without passes or fixating on an object, by closing the eyelids, keeping them gently closed, asking the subject to keep them together, and suggesting the phenomena of sleep. There are those who quickly fall into a more or less deep sleep.

Others resist more; I sometimes succeed by keeping the eyes closed for a long time, imposing silence and stillness, speaking continuously and repeating the same formulas:

> "You feel a numbness, a <term>torpor: a state of physical or mental inactivity; lethargy</term>; the arms and legs are motionless; there is warmth in the eyelids; the nervous system is calming down; you no longer have any will, your eyes remain closed; sleep is coming, etc."

After a few minutes of this prolonged auditory suggestion, I remove my fingers and the eyes stay closed; I lift the subject's arms, and they remain in the air: this is <term>cataleptic: a state where the limbs remain in whatever position they are placed by the operator</term> sleep.

Others are more rebellious; preoccupied and unable to let go, they analyze themselves, overthink, and say they cannot sleep. I impose calm upon them; I speak only of torpor and numbness:

> "This is enough," I say, "to obtain a result. Suggestion can be effective, even without sleep. Stay still and do not worry."

In this state of mind, I do not seek to provoke <term>cataleptiform: appearing like or mimicking the stiff state of catalepsy</term> effects; for the subject, being simply numb but still awake, al— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("tou-"), likely "always" (toujours).</note>

<summary>The author describes various methods for inducing hypnosis, emphasizing that verbal suggestion and the closure of the eyes are more vital than traditional magnetic rituals. He notes that children and cooperative adults respond quickly, while more skeptical subjects require persistent, calming verbal formulas.</summary>

# HYPNOTIZATION PROCEDURE

...always inclined to pull themselves together, the subject easily emerges from their <term>torpor: a state of mental or physical inactivity; lethargy</term>. Sometimes then, contenting myself with a doubtful numbness, and without wishing to verify if the subject is actually influenced, I leave them to themselves, inviting them to remain in this torpor for some time. Certain subjects stay there quite long, without being able to say if they did so voluntarily or involuntarily. Usually at the second or third session, through this suggestive education of the subject, I manage to provoke a more advanced degree of non-doubtful hypnotization, with <term>suggestive catalepsy: a state where a person's limbs stay in whatever position the hypnotist places them</term>, or even with <term>somnambulism: a deep hypnotic state where the subject can follow complex commands while appearing to be in a trance</term>.

If for some, one succeeds better by proceeding with gentleness, for others, who are resistant to gentle suggestion, it is better to be blunt—to speak in a tone of authority to repress the tendency to laugh or the impulse of involuntary resistance that this maneuver may provoke.

Many people, I repeat, are affected as early as the first session; others only at the second or third. After one or two hypnotizations, the influence becomes rapid. It is often enough to look at them, to extend one’s fingers before their eyes, or to say: “Sleep,” so that, in a few seconds, even instantaneously, the eyes close and all the phenomena of sleep are present. Others only acquire the ability to fall asleep quickly after a certain number of sessions, which are generally few in number.

It sometimes happens that I put seven or eight patients to sleep in succession, each in next to no time. Then come others, refractory or more difficult to put to sleep. I only persist for a few minutes; a second or third session often brings the sleep that was not obtained at the first.

Subjects in whom hypnotic suggestibility is highly developed fall asleep as soon as they are given the idea of sleeping. One can hypnotize them by correspondence, by affirming to them, for example, that as soon as the letter is read, they will sleep; one can hypnotize them by telephone, as <note>Jules Liégeois (1833–1908) was a professor of law and a colleague of the author at the Nancy School; he was particularly interested in the legal and criminal possibilities of hypnotic suggestion.</note>Mr. Liégeois has done. Whatever the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the effectiveness of hypnotic suggestion. The previous page ended while describing how some subjects require several sessions to fall asleep quickly, concluding that once the suggestion reaches the mind, it takes effect.</meta>

# ->HYPNOTISM UNDER CHLOROFORM<-

...the way in which the suggestion reaches the understanding, it produces its effect.

Some individuals become hypnotized under chloroform even before the chloroform has been fully administered. All surgeons have seen patients fall asleep suddenly, without any agitation, after just a few breaths of the anesthetic, at a time when the chemical has certainly not yet done its work. I have observed this fact in female patients whom I was anesthetizing in the dentist's presence for tooth extractions. Therefore, taking advantage of this observation, I make sure, every time I administer chloroform, to suggest to the patient from the very first breath that they are going to fall asleep gently and quickly. In some cases, hypnotic sleep thus arrives before the sleep induced by the chloroform. If it is deep enough to result in complete <term>anesthesia: a state of controlled, temporary loss of sensation or awareness</term>—which I have witnessed—the operation can be performed without waiting. If not, I continue the inhalation of chloroform until total anesthesia is reached, which occurs more quickly with the help of suggestion; and by proceeding in this way, I prevent the period of agitation in these cases.

One should not believe that the susceptible subjects are all <term>neuropaths: a historical term for people with nervous system disorders</term>, weak-minded individuals, <term>hysterics: a Victorian-era diagnosis for emotional or physical symptoms without a clear cause</term>, or women; most of my observations relate to men whom I have chosen specifically to address this objection. Undoubtedly, susceptibility varies; the common people, docile minds, former soldiers, craftsmen, and subjects accustomed to passive obedience have seemed to me, as they did to <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904) was a French physician and a founder of the Nancy School of hypnotism, known for using suggestion to treat patients.</note> Mr. Liébeault, more suited to receiving suggestion than refined, preoccupied minds that offer a certain moral resistance, often unconsciously. The <term>insane: referred to in the original text as "aliénés"</term>, the <term>melancholic: those suffering from what we would now call clinical depression</term>, and the <term>hypochondriacs: people with excessive anxiety about their health</term> are often difficult or impossible to put to sleep; the mental will to sleep must be present; the subject must let themselves go, without mental resistance, to the instructions of the hypnotist; and I repeat, experience shows that the vast majority of people achieve this easily.

He also argues that hypnotism is not limited to the "weak-minded" or "hysterical," but is often most effective on those accustomed to discipline and obedience.</summary>

# DEGREES OF HYPNOTISM

I have put to sleep very intelligent people, belonging to the upper classes of society, who were in no way "nervous" <note>original: "nerveuses." In the 19th century, "nervousness" was often used as a medical category for those with perceived physical or mental sensitivities, rather than just everyday anxiety.</note>, at least in the sense we attach to that word. Undoubtedly, those who make it a point of honor to demonstrate that they are not hypnotizable, that they have a better-balanced brain than others, or that they are not <term>suggestible: the quality of being inclined to accept and act on the ideas or instructions of another person</term>, often cannot be put to sleep. This is because they do not know how to put themselves into the mental state necessary to realize the <term>suggestion: the psychological process by which an idea is induced or adopted by the mind</term> of sleep; they refuse to accept it consciously or unconsciously, and they create for themselves a kind of <term>counter-suggestion: an internal resistance or opposing thought that blocks an external suggestion</term>.

The degree of induced sleep varies according to the subject.
Some experience only a more or less pronounced numbness, a heaviness of the eyelids, or drowsiness; these represent the smallest number of cases. This is the *first degree of Mr. Liébeault* <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904) was a French physician and a pioneer of the Nancy School of hypnotism, which emphasized the power of suggestion over physical magnetism.</note>. This drowsiness may disappear as soon as the operator ceases to exert their influence; in some people, it persists for a few minutes, while in others, it lasts much longer—for an hour, for example. The subjects often remain inert; others perform a few movements, change position, or turn over, but continue to remain drowsy. In one of the following sessions, this sleep may pass to one of the more advanced degrees; other times, on the contrary, one cannot go beyond it. In the case of one lady, I established drowsiness lasting half an hour to an hour more than a hundred times, but nothing beyond this first-degree drowsiness.

Certain people do not experience drowsiness, strictly speaking, but they keep their eyelids closed and cannot open them; they speak, answer questions, and say that they are not sleeping. But I tell them: "You cannot open your eyes"; they make fruitless efforts to open them, for the eyelids are as if <term>cataleptized: a state where muscles become rigid and the body or limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed</term>. It seemed to me—though I cannot state it with certainty—that this form of hypnotism is more...

# DEGREES OF HYPNOTISM

...more frequent in women than in men. One of them made extraordinary efforts to separate her eyelids; she laughed and spoke volubly. I repeated to her: “Try to open them”; she applied all her willpower without succeeding until I brought the <term>charm: a 19th-century term for the hypnotic state of fascination or fixation</term> to an end by saying: “You can open them.”

I still call this a variety of the first degree.

In a second degree, the subjects keep their eyelids closed and their limbs are in a state of relaxation; they hear everything said to them and everything said around them. But they remain subject to the will of the hypnotizer <note>original: "l'endormeur," literally "the one who puts to sleep."</note>; their brain is in that state that magnetizers call *hypotaxy* <note>original: "hypotaxie," an early term for a state of light trance or increased suggestibility.</note> or *charm*.

*This degree is characterized by suggestive catalepsy.*

We designate by this word the following phenomenon: As soon as the subject is asleep and relaxed, if I raise their arm, it remains in the air; if I raise the leg, it remains in the air: the limbs passively maintain the attitude that is impressed upon them. We call this <term>catalepsy: a state where muscles remain rigid and limbs stay in whatever position they are placed</term>, *suggestive*, because, as it is easy to confirm, it is purely psychological <note>original: "psychique." In this context, it refers to the mind's influence over the body rather than supernatural phenomena.</note>, linked to the passive state of the subject who automatically maintains the given posture, just as they maintain a received idea. Indeed, one sees in the same subject or in different subjects that the phenomenon becomes more or less pronounced depending on the depth of the sleep and the psychological receptivity. At first, this cataleptic-like state is barely marked; the raised limb remains in the air for a few seconds, but then falls back with a certain hesitation. Or perhaps only the forearm remains in the air; if one tries to lift the entire upper limb—both arm and forearm—it falls; the fingers individually do not maintain the posture one gives them, but the entire hand and the forearm remain fixed.

Some subjects, if one lifts their arm quickly and releases it, let it fall back; but if one holds it in the air for a few seconds, of...

Finally, in others, catalepsy is only obtained through a verbally stated suggestion: one must say to the hypnotized subject: "your arms stay in the air, your legs stay in the air." Only then do they remain. Some maintain the new posture passively if nothing is said to them; but if they are challenged to move out of it, they "pull themselves together," so to speak, calling upon their numbed willpower and lowering their limb; often, they wake up at that moment. These cases constitute intermediate stages between the first and the second degree. Most subjects, on the contrary, are unable to modify the imposed posture despite all their efforts.

In this way, through the specific mode of the <term>cataleptiform state: a condition resembling catalepsy where the limbs can be placed in positions that the subject then maintains</term>, one follows the progressive development of suggestibility. In a very large number of people, this state is very pronounced from the outset; from the very first hypnotization, the limbs spontaneously keep the position communicated to them, without it being necessary to voice the suggestion; they remain there, sometimes fixed as long as the hypnotism persists, sometimes falling back slowly and gradually after a few minutes, a quarter of an hour, half an hour, or even longer.

Upon waking, some of the subjects who have not gone beyond the second degree imagine that they did not sleep because they remember having heard everything; they believe they were simply being compliant, but when the experiment is repeated, the suggestive catalepsy reappears. If it is not a "sleep" in the traditional sense, it is at least a special psychological state <note>original: "état psychique."</note> that diminishes the power of cerebral resistance and renders the brain docile to suggestion.

In a *third* degree, the numbness appears more pronounced, and tactile sensitivity may be dulled or extinguished; in addition to suggestive catalepsy, the subject is susceptible to <term>automatic movements: actions performed without conscious intent or control</term>. # DEGREES OF HYPNOTISM

In some, this <term>rotary automatism: the continued, repetitive rotation of the arms or hands after they have been set in motion by the hypnotist</term> follows the impulse communicated to the arms; verbal suggestion is not necessary. In this degree, one can also determine <term>suggestive contracture: the induced stiffening of a limb or muscle group through the power of suggestion</term>.

The *fourth degree* is characterized, in addition to the preceding phenomena, by the loss of connection with the outside world. The subject hears what the operator says, but does not hear what other people say or what is being said around them: their senses are in communication only with the hypnotist. However, they are capable of being put in touch with everyone.

The *fifth and sixth degrees*, characterized, according to <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904) was a French physician and a pioneer of the Nancy School of hypnotism, which argued that hypnosis was a normal phenomenon produced by suggestion.</note> Mr. Liébeault, by the forgetting upon waking of everything that occurred during sleep, constitute *somnambulism*. The *fifth degree* is *light somnambulism*: subjects still remember vaguely; they have heard things confusedly at certain moments; certain memories awaken spontaneously. Total loss of sensation, suggestive catalepsy, automatic movements, and hallucinations by suggestion—it is then that all these phenomena, which we will discuss in more detail, reach their highest level of expression.

In deep somnambulism, or the sixth degree, the memory of everything that happened during sleep is completely extinguished and cannot be awakened spontaneously.

*We will see later that these memories can always be awakened artificially.*

The subject remains asleep at the will of the operator and becomes a perfect automaton, obedient to all their orders.

### VARIETIES OF SLEEP

...variants, intermediaries between these various degrees; one observes all possible transitions, from simple torpor and uncertain sleep to the deepest <term>somnambulism: a state of deep hypnosis where the subject may perform actions or answer questions without having any memory of it upon waking</term>.

I should add that docility to suggestions and the ease of provoking various phenomena are not always in proportion to the depth of sleep. Certain subjects sleep little, answer questions, and remember everything upon waking, and yet <term>suggestive contracture: the induced stiffening of a limb through the hypnotist's command</term>, insensibility, commanded or communicated automatic movements, and therapeutic suggestions succeed well with them. This will become easy to conceive when I have spoken about <term>suggestion in the waking state: the phenomenon where a person accepts and acts upon a suggestion without being in a hypnotic sleep</term>.

Others, on the contrary, fall into a heavy, deep sleep and remember absolutely nothing upon waking. While they sleep, no matter how much one interrogates them or harangues them with questions, they remain inert. <term>Suggestive catalepsy: a trance-like state where the subject’s limbs remain fixed in any position they are placed in</term> is obtained with difficulty in these cases; they only keep their arms in the air for a short time. The suggestions, actions, illusions, and hallucinations commanded to take place after waking are not realized; it is as if they were not in rapport with the operator. And yet, it is enough to pronounce the word: "Wake up," for them to wake up spontaneously; evident proof that this connection exists. In the case of one man whose sleep was like the one I have just described—apparently inert—I obtained immediate therapeutic effects through auditory suggestion <note>original: "suggestion auditive"</note>: a return of sensation, the disappearance of pain, and an increase in muscular strength measured by the <term>dynamometer: an instrument used to measure the force of a muscle contraction</term>. This is proof that, despite his apparent inertia, he had remained in rapport with me during his sleep.

Others finally answer all questions, speak with volubility, and appear—except for the closing of their eyes—completely awake; they are not <note>or only slightly</note> susceptible to catalepsy; one cannot provoke hallucinations or illusions in them. And yet, upon waking, their amnesia is complete.

Each sleeper has, so to speak, his own individuality...

# ON WAKING

own, special way of being. I simply wish to establish for the moment that the aptitude for realizing <term>suggestive phenomena: the physical or psychological effects produced in a subject through the hypnotist's commands</term> is not always proportional to the depth of sleep.

Awakening can be spontaneous. Subjects who sleep lightly during their first session sometimes have a tendency to wake up quickly; they must be kept <note>original: "sous le charme," here referring to the hypnotic influence or rapport</note> under the spell by keeping their eyelids closed or by repeating from time to time: "Sleep." Soon, the habit of sleep is acquired by the organism; the <term>hypnotized subject: the person undergoing hypnosis</term> no longer wakes as long as the <term>hypnotist: the practitioner inducing the state</term> is by their side; some wake as soon as they no longer feel this influence. Most, left to themselves, continue to sleep for several minutes, half an hour, one or several hours; I have let one of my patients sleep for fifteen hours, and another for eighteen hours.

To obtain an immediate awakening, I proceed by **vocal suggestion**, just as I do to induce sleep. I say: "It is finished, wake up." And this word, spoken even in a low voice, is enough for subjects who have already been hypnotized several times to achieve an immediate awakening. For some, one must repeat the <term>injunction: a firm, authoritative command</term>: "Your eyes are opening, you are awake." If that is not enough, the act of blowing one or several times on the eyes triggers the awakening; I have never had to resort to other methods, such as splashing with cold water; awakening has always been as easy as could be.

Nothing is stranger at times than this awakening. Here is a subject in a deep sleep; I question him, he answers me; if he is talkative by nature, he may speak with volubility. In the middle of his conversation, I suddenly say: "Wake up." He opens his eyes and has no memory of what has happened; he does not remember having spoken to me, even though he may have been speaking a tenth of a second before waking. To make the phenomenon more striking, I sometimes wake them like this: "Count to 10; when you say 10 aloud, you

When he has finished, I ask him: "Why are you counting?" He no longer remembers having counted. I have repeated this experiment many times on very intelligent people.

In the case of certain hysterical patients <note>The term "hysteric" was a common 19th-century medical diagnosis for patients, usually women, exhibiting a wide range of psychological and physical symptoms believed to originate in the nervous system.</note>, one must proceed with caution and avoid touching painful points or provoking <term>hysterogenic zones: specific areas of the body that, when pressed or stimulated, were believed to trigger an immediate hysterical attack</term>; for then a hysterical crisis can be produced, the <term>hypnotic sleep: a trance state induced by the practitioner</term> may give way to <term>hysterical sleep: an involuntary, often cataleptic state where the patient is no longer responsive to the hypnotist</term> and the operator is no longer in rapport with the subject. In such cases, suggestion remains without influence.

Upon waking, some people continue to remain drowsy; it is sometimes sufficient to pass one's hands transversely—so as to wave the air in front of their eyes—to dissipate this numbness. Others complain of heaviness in the head, of dull <term>cephalgia: a medical term for a headache</term>, or of vertigo; to prevent these various sensations, I say to the subject before waking them: "You are going to wake up and you will be quite at your ease; you have no heaviness in the head, you feel perfectly well," and this <term>suggestive awakening: the act of using verbal commands to ensure a subject wakes up feeling refreshed</term> is obtained without any unpleasant sensation.

# PROPORTION OF HYPNOTIZABLE SUBJECTS

No doubt, one must take into account the fact that Mr. Liébeault operates primarily on common people who come to him specifically to be put to sleep and who, convinced of his <term>magnetic power: a reference to the older theory of "animal magnetism" or a physical force emanating from the doctor</term>, offer a greater <term>cerebral docility: a state of mental openness and readiness to follow instructions</term>. Perhaps the number of people influenced would be lower without these favorable and predisposing conditions; however, I have been able to confirm through my own research that refractory <note>original: "réfractaire"; meaning subjects who are resistant or non-responsive to hypnotic induction</note> subjects constitute the vast minority; and it often happens that I produce <term>hypnotism: the induction of a trance state</term> during the very first session on patients who come into my office and have no idea what <term>hypnotic sleep: a state of artificial sleep induced by suggestion</term> even is.

According to this statistic and another also covering the span of a year, collected by Mr. Liébeault and reported by Mr. Beaunis, the proportion of <term>somnambulists: subjects who reach the deepest level of hypnosis, characterized by a lack of memory upon waking</term> out of 100 subjects taken at random can be considered to be between 15 and 18.

We call "somnambulists" those hypnotizable subjects who do not retain any memory of what happened during their sleep upon waking. It appeared to me that this proportion can be notably increased if one takes care to say to the sleeping subjects: 

> "Upon waking, you will remember nothing." 

In a certain number of cases, <term>amnesia: the loss of memory for the duration of the trance</term> is thus produced by <term>suggestion: the act of influencing a subject's mind through verbal commands or ideas</term>.

It emerges from the same statistical table by Mr. Beaunis that the proportions of hypnotizable subjects are nearly the same for men and for women and that, in particular, contrary to popular opinion, the proportion is almost identical regarding somnambulism: 18.8 percent among men; 19.4 percent among women.

As for variations depending on age, here is the table drawn up by Mr. Beaunis according to the same statistics, taking proportional figures for each age; for example, for 100 children from 1 to 7 years old, how many cases of somnambulism, very deep sleep, etc., there are, and so on for each age group.

## CHAPTER II

The phenomena observed in hypnotic sleep. — Concerning sensitivity. — Spontaneous anesthesia or anesthesia through suggestion. — Hypnotism cannot replace <term>chloroform: a liquid solvent used as an early general anesthetic, known for its rapid and potent effect</term>. — Alterations of <term>motility: the capability of movement or the power of moving spontaneously</term>. — Suggestive <term>catalepsy: a state in which the limbs or body remain in any position in which they are placed</term>. — On automatic movements. — On imitation movements. — On suggestive paralysis. — On <term>somnambulism: the deepest stage of trance where the subject may move or speak but usually forgets the experience upon waking</term> with forgetfulness upon waking. — Automatic obedience. — On sensory suggestions. — On suggested hallucinations. — On the suggestion of acts, sensory illusions, and hallucinations for the time following waking. — On negative hallucinations. — On long-term hallucinations.

I am now beginning a brief study of the phenomena that manifest themselves or can be induced during hypnotic sleep. At times, the eyes close abruptly, without any preamble, and the subject falls like a dead weight; at other times, sleep arrives gradually: the eyelids become heavy, they blink, vision becomes blurred, the eyes water, they open and close alternately, and then finally close for good. The closed eyelids remain motionless in some; in others, they are agitated by a vibratory quivering throughout the entire duration of the hypnosis. The eyeballs maintain their normal position during light sleep; when the sleep is deep, they are often—though not always—turned upwards, the pupils hidden beneath the upper eyelid.

Some nervous subjects experience muscular twitches in their limbs or <term>fibrillary movements: fine, involuntary contractions of small bundles of muscle fibers</term> in the face during sleep; most are motionless or become so through suggestion. A few perform reflex movements—scratching themselves, for example—

# SENSITIVITY IN SLEEP

...move their hands, change position; others, on the contrary, remain motionless.

Sensitivity, in its various forms, is more or less modified. In light sleep, it is preserved; a tickle, a pinprick, or the touch of a painful area triggers reflexes and causes the subject to wake up.

In deep sleep, sensitivity is diminished or totally abolished; according to <term>Mr. Liébeault: Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), a French physician known as the father of the Nancy School of hypnosis, who emphasized the power of suggestion</term>, it begins to disappear at the extremities, and it is always the periphery of the body that is most anesthetized. "By pushing the examination further into the organs of sensation, one notices that it is the two closed senses, sight and taste, which become dull first, followed by smell; hearing and touch are muffled last. When the methods of hypnotists are used (staring at an object, or the operator's fingers or eyes), the eyes are the sense organs that lose their properties after all the others, because, due to the attention to which the <note>original: 'endormeurs' — literally 'sleep-bringers' or 'those who put to sleep'</note> hypnotizers condemn them, these organs are forced to stay awake until the end."

If anesthesia is complete, one can pierce the skin through and through with a pin, apply electricity, push foreign bodies into the nostrils, or expose them to ammonia fumes, and the subjects do not flinch. This total <term>anesthesia: a state of controlled, temporary loss of sensation or awareness</term> can develop spontaneously by the mere fact of hypnosis.

In other subjects, it does not exist spontaneously, but it can be developed more or less completely through suggestion. Take a hypnotized subject: I prick him with a pin, and he reacts sharply; I unstop a bottle of ammonia before his nose, and he contracts his nostrils, showing the sensation he has perceived. Then, I say to him: "You no longer feel anything; your entire body is insensitive; I am pricking you, and you do not feel it; I am placing ammonia before your nose, and you perceive absolutely nothing." In many, anesthesia occurs in this way through suggestion. Sometimes, <term>cutaneous: relating to or affecting the skin</term> anesthesia is obtained alone to a certain degree, while the mu- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; it likely intends to say 'muqueuses' or mucous membranes.</note>

# SUGGESTIVE CATALEPSY

...olfactory and ocular mucous membranes remain resistant to suggestion. <note>The word "muqueuses" (mucous membranes) began at the end of the previous page.</note>

Therefore, while hypnotic insensibility is perfect enough in a certain number of subjects to permit the most laborious surgical operations, for most it is not so. Hypnotism cannot be established as a general method for surgical <term>anesthesia: the medical practice of inducing a loss of sensation or awareness</term>; it cannot replace <term>chloroform: a common 19th-century anesthetic gas</term>. We should add that the anxious concerns haunting the minds of patients at the moment of an operation often prevent the mental concentration necessary for the hypnotic state to develop.

Alterations in <term>motility: the capacity for movement</term> are more frequent and easier to obtain than those of sensitivity. All hypnotized subjects, except those in the first degree <note>referring to the lightest stage of trance</note>, are susceptible to suggestive catalepsy.

We have seen that this phenomenon manifests with variations according to the mode and degree of suggestibility. The brain carries out the suggestion with more or less contraction or <term>contracture: a state of prolonged muscle shortening or rigidity</term>. Sometimes the catalepsy is flaccid, if I may say so; the limb, fixed in the air, falls back at the slightest pressure exerted upon it. Sometimes the catalepsy is firmer without being rigid; this is "waxy catalepsy." The limbs obey the movements imposed upon them, allowing themselves to be extended and bent as obediently as soft wax (<note>original: "flexibilitas cerea"</note> waxy flexibility); one can extend certain fingers, bend others, fold a thigh, extend the other, sit the patient up, tilt the head toward a shoulder, and impart the most bizarre attitudes to various segments of the body: they remain frozen, like a jointed mannequin, in the position communicated to them; they follow the movement given without exceeding it. Finally, sometimes the catalepsy is rigid, accompanied by a true muscle stiffening that can only be resolved by suggestion. For example, I raise an arm vertically; it remains fixed and stiffened. # SUGGESTIVE CATALEPSY

...a limb, it snaps back like a spring to its original, vertical position in the air. This is a true rigid catalepsy that I will call *tetanic catalepsy* <note>named after tetanus because of the extreme muscle tension</note>. As soon as the subject is asleep, I raise the arms and legs without saying anything; they immediately become fixed, as if tetanized in the position I gave them. This rigidity is usually much greater in the upper limbs than in the lower limbs. In some subjects, the whole body can be immobilized and tetanized in this way, so much so that one can place the head on one chair and the feet on another and put weight on the body without breaking the <term>contracture: a state of continuous, involuntary muscle contraction</term>.

Suggestion alone always succeeds in resolving this tetanic state. I say: "I can lower your arm and move it as I wish." Then the rigidity disappears and the catalepsy persists, waxy or flaccid, as in the previous degrees.

In a word, one observes in the hypnotic state all the forms that appear in the pathological <note>referring to diseased or abnormal</note> state; and if one takes the trouble to reread the various observations of spontaneous catalepsy that have been published, one will soon be convinced that many actually refer to cases of hypnotism or spontaneous somnambulism. <term>Lasègue: Ernest-Charles Lasègue (1816–1883), a French physician famous for his work on hysteria</term>, by closing the eyes of his <term>hysterics: a historical diagnostic category for patients with various sensory or motor symptoms thought to originate in the mind</term>, produced artificial cataleptic fits showing the special characteristics of spontaneous catalepsy; he did not realize that his hysterics were, in reality, hypnotized: he had induced suggestive catalepsy.

In most hypnotized subjects, I repeat, it is not necessary for the suggestion to be formulated for the limbs to remain cataleptic. The psychological state is such that every idea received by the brain is imprinted upon it, and every position given to a limb is maintained; this position imposed on the limb by the operator is accepted by the subject's brain as a guessed suggestion; the subject does not have enough cerebral initiative to spontaneously modify the muscular state created.

## CATALEPSY IN TYPHOID FEVER

I will cite two cases. In the first, it concerned a thirty-five-year-old man suffering from a mild form of typhoid fever, but complicated by <term>anxious lypemania: an obsolete term for a form of melancholic depression characterized by deep sorrow and anxiety</term>, from the 15th to the 35th day, at a time when the fever was already in the process of <term>defervescence: the period during which a fever subsides and the body temperature returns to normal</term>. The patient was immobile and insensitive to everything happening around him; he responded to questions with monosyllables, and at other times retreated into absolute mutism. His eyes were closed, with the pupils hidden under the upper eyelids. Reflexes were preserved; sensitivity was notably diminished. The patient appeared to hear questions but did not respond. He could be awakened for a moment by vigorous and repeated commands; he would open his eyes only to immediately return to his original immobility. His arms would maintain indefinitely the position in which they were placed, as in suggestive catalepsy, but without rigidity. He would remain seated indefinitely when placed in that position. This state was observed for six days; it then gave way to delirium, accompanied by agitation, stiffness, and trembling of the limbs, as well as a refusal of food, necessitated the use of an <term>esophageal tube: a feeding tube used for patients unable to swallow or refusing to eat</term>; the patient recovered.

In the second case, it concerned a fatal <term>adynamic: characterized by a profound loss of physical strength or "vital power"</term> typhoid fever in a twenty-one-year-old Italian mason, who succumbed on the 11th day. From the 8th day onward, the patient was prostrate and spoke little; however, he answered questions in a clear but slow manner. He suffered from urinary retention; <term>catheterization: the insertion of a tube to drain the bladder</term> left him inert, yet his sensitivity was preserved.

His eyes were open; he did everything he was told to do, often without answering a single word. Sometimes, if asked his name, he would utter it in a low voice. If one placed the patient’s arm in the air, he would keep it in that position for a long time, as if in a state of catalepsy, his face maintaining—like that of those who have been <term>hypnotized: individuals placed in a trance-like state of heightened suggestibility</term>—a mask of impassivity. # BRAIDISM AND MESMERISM

->suggestion: everyone realizes it as they conceive it, as they interpret it.<-

All these facts, and those which we shall still present, show that all the phenomena of so-called **animal magnetism** are nothing more than phenomena of suggestion: hypnotism places the subject’s brain in such a state that the idea suggested to this brain imposes itself with a greater or lesser force and determines the corresponding act through a sort of **cerebral automatism**. I have not observed in my hypnotized subjects a single fact that cannot be interpreted in this way, or that calls for the intervention of any sort of fluid analogous to the force of a magnet or electricity, escaping from certain organisms to react upon others. This is the doctrine of <note>James Braid (1795–1860), a Scottish surgeon who moved the study of "magnetism" away from mystical fluids toward a physiological and psychological basis, coining the term "hypnotism."</note> Braid or **braidism**, the doctrine of suggestion, which arises from observation, as opposed to the doctrine of <note>Franz Mesmer (1734–1815), the German physician whose "fluid" theory—the idea that an invisible natural force (animal magnetism) flowed between bodies—preceded modern hypnotism.</note> Mesmer or **mesmerism**, the doctrine of mesmerian or magnetic fluid.

The mesmerists offer, for example, in support of the fluid theory, the following facts: if one makes a "pass" <note>In mesmerism, a "pass" is a sweeping movement of the hands over the patient's body intended to direct the "magnetic fluid."</note> over a limb, arm, or leg, lightly touching the parts, the muscles, they say, contract and the limb can be lifted: this is a *mesmerizing pass*. If one then makes the pass above the limb without touching it, merely agitating the air over the limb, it would fall back: this is a *de-mesmerizing pass*. — One agitates the air on the side of the head; the head follows the operator’s hand and turns toward it. If the pass is made on the opposite side, the head turns that way. — Pass the hand quickly over the subject’s hand and withdraw it abruptly; if you repeat this several times, the hand may lift and become <term>cataleptic</term> <note>A state where muscles become rigid and limbs remain in whatever position they are placed.</note>. Evident proof, say the mesmerists, that the operator's hand attracts that of the patient as the magnet attracts iron!

### SOMNAMBULISM

...manifests, through a gesture or a touch interpreted by the hypnotized brain, a will that it may not actually possess. The same "passes"—whether involving touching the limb or not, and whether "mesmerizing" or "de-mesmerizing" (to use the <term>magnetizers'|Followers of Franz Mesmer who believed that an invisible "magnetic fluid" flowed from the doctor to the patient.</term> vocabulary)—can trigger the same phenomenon: the raising or lowering of the hand. The subjects' movements, provoked by a specific sensory impression, are instinctive and automatic. It is the subject’s own posture that dictates the movement naturally suggested by that posture. A muscle at rest will contract, while a contracted muscle will relax under the influence of the same maneuver. If pressure is applied to a hand or arm resting on the knee, that arm can no longer be lowered; it rises and becomes rigid. If the same pressure is applied to an arm held in the air, it triggers the most natural movement: the lowering of the limb. If the upward or downward movement of the limb is obstructed, the same pressure will provoke sideways movements.

Let us add that a subject who has been made to repeat the same experiment several times, or who has seen it performed on others, retains a memory of the muscular movements or acts corresponding to each impression. They are, so to speak, "trained," and automatically repeat—through simple **cerebro-spinal reflectivity**—the same acts they have seen performed or have performed themselves in previous sessions.

Subjects who are more deeply influenced by hypnotism enter the state known as **somnambulism**: it is then that new phenomena appear. The **automatism** is total: the human organism has become almost a machine, docile to the operator's will. I say to him: "Stand up"; he stands. One stands very quickly; another obeys only slowly—the machine is sluggish, and the command needs to be repeated with authority. I say: "Walk"; he walks. "Sit down"; he sits.

I touch him with my two hands extended, and, making the gesture of drawing him toward me, I withdraw; he follows me passively wherever I go.

I command him to dance; he dances and stops as if frozen at my command.

General and various sensory sensitivities <note>This refers to the "five senses" as well as the general sense of touch or pain.</note> can be modified, heightened, diminished, or perverted at will. I put salt in his mouth, saying that it is sugar; some receive this suggestion only imperfectly—they still perceive the salty taste more or less clearly. Others, and they are numerous, suck the salt with happiness and find it very sweet. I make them drink water or vinegar in place of wine. I make them breathe ammonia <note>Ammonia has a sharp, suffocating scent; the fact that a subject would breathe it as if it were perfume demonstrates a profound suppression of natural physical reflexes.</note> as if it were Eau de Cologne.

I induce deafness: the subject declares he can no longer hear, answers nothing, and does not react to the most deafening noises. I make him mute, or a stutterer. The strangest illusions can be suggested: a pencil in the mouth serves as a cigar, the aroma of which he inhales with delight, and he blows imaginary puffs of smoke into the air.

In the advanced stages of hypnotism, all illusions and all hallucinations are realized successively with surprising precision and promptness.

Furthermore, all commanded acts are executed: the hypnotized subject walks and dances at command, shakes his fist at the people I point out to him, searches in

<header>->ACTIVE SOMNAMBULISM<-</header>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of suggested actions from the previous page.</note> ...picks their pocket more or less skillfully, steals, or commits whatever physical assaults are ordered; one acts with a certain hesitation, while another acts resolutely.

Somnambulists <note>In 19th-century medicine, "somnambulism" referred both to natural sleepwalking and the deep state of hypnotic trance where the subject could still move and speak.</note> can write, work, play music, and converse with one another; seeing them act this way, with eyes either closed or open, as if in a waking state, one would swear they were not asleep. Though they are most often passive and inert when left to themselves, they become active and mobile under the influence of suggestion.

Take, for example, a woman in my ward: fifty-five years old, a housewife, suffering from rheumatic pains and not at all hysterical <note>The author specifies "not hysterical" because, at the time, many doctors believed only "hysterical" women could be hypnotized. He is arguing that hypnosis is a more universal phenomenon.</note>. I can easily place her into somnambulism. This somnambulism is passive if I say nothing: she sleeps with relaxed limbs, peacefully. Through verbal affirmation, I develop in her a state of anesthesia <note>Insensitivity to pain.</note>, catalepsy <note>A state where limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed.</note>, muscular contraction, or hallucinations; I draw her out of her passivity. I say to her: "Get up now, since you are cured. Do your work." There she is, rising, getting dressed, looking for a chair, climbing onto the windowsill, opening it, dipping her hands into the jug containing the herbal tea—which she believes is water for domestic use—and setting herself to conscientiously washing both sides of the windowpanes. Then, she makes her bed or sweeps the floor of the room with a broom brought to her. Once awakened, she remembers nothing and believes she has slept peacefully in a chair.

These are not exceptional cases. If one examines the most diverse subjects of varying temperaments lying in a hospital ward from this perspective, one is surprised to see the great number who can carry out these phenomena of active somnambulism. I sometimes have three or four women in a ward of twenty who work in this manner: one knits, another sews, and a third goes to find—with her eyes closed—old linens and irons, with which she presses the laundry. Some, susceptible to hallucinations, perform their work with imaginary utensils: one, for example, takes the bedsheet, folds the...

# SUGGESTION OF POST-HYPNOTIC ACTS

...sill <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "climbing onto the windowsill."</note>, then, threading an imaginary needle and putting on an imaginary thimble, she precisely executes all the movements to sew a hem, step by step, without error. All of this is accomplished through suggestion with eyes either open or closed; and the memory of everything is extinguished upon waking.

To further clarify the nature of somnambulists <note>The term used for subjects in a state of hypnotic trance who can move and speak as if awake.</note> and the complex manifestations they can achieve, I will later recount several observations that are more eloquent than any descriptions I could provide.

But beforehand, I wish to call attention to one of the most interesting phenomena of somnambulism. I am referring to the possibility of creating, in a somnambulist, suggestions of actions, sensory illusions, or hallucinations that will manifest not during sleep, but upon waking: the subject has heard what I said to them during sleep, but has retained no memory of what I said; they no longer know that I spoke to them. The suggested idea presents itself in their brain upon waking: they have forgotten its origin and believe it to be spontaneous. Facts of this kind have been observed by A. Bertrand, General Noizet, Dr. Liébeault, and Charles Richet <note>Alexandre Bertrand (1795–1831), General Noizet (1792–1885), Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), and Charles Richet (1850–1935) were all early researchers who helped transition the study of "animal magnetism" into the scientific study of hypnotism and suggestion.</note>. I have successfully repeated them a great many times with many sleepers and have convinced myself of their good faith <note>Meaning the subjects were truly under hypnosis and not merely "playing along" or pretending.</note>.

Here are some <term>suggestions of actions</term> <note>Today these are known as "post-hypnotic suggestions."</note>: I choose bizarre ones on purpose, to make the experiment more conclusive:

To one of my patients, D..., I suggested during his sleep that after waking he would rub his ailing leg and thigh, then get out of bed, go to the window, and return to bed: which he did without suspecting that the order had been given to him during sleep.

To Sch..., I suggested one day that upon waking he should put my hat on his head, bring it to me in the next room, and place it on my head. This is what he did without realizing why.

> “The way in which suggestions take root in subjects,” says <note>Henri Beaunis (1830–1921) was a French psychologist and member of the Nancy School of hypnotism</note> Mr. Beaunis, “provides valuable information on the state of the will during somnambulism. Nothing is more curious, from a psychological point of view, than to follow upon their countenances the dawn and development of the idea that has been suggested to them. This might occur, for example, in the middle of a mundane conversation that has no relation to the suggestion. Suddenly, the hypnotist, who has been forewarned and who watches his subject without appearing to do so, perceives at a given moment a sort of pause in thought, an internal shock reflected by an imperceptible sign: a look, a gesture, a crease in the face. Then the conversation resumes, but the idea returns to the charge, still weak and undecided; there is a bit of astonishment in the gaze; one feels that something unexpected occasionally crosses the mind like a flash of lightning. Soon the idea grows little by little; it takes more and more hold of the intelligence; the struggle has begun; the eyes, the gestures—everything speaks, everything reveals the internal combat. One follows the fluctuations of thought; the subject still listens to the conversation, but vaguely, mechanically; he is elsewhere. His whole being is prey to the <term>fixed idea</term> <note>a "fixed idea" or *idée fixe* refers to a suggestion that has become an irresistible compulsion</note> which is implanting itself more and more in his brain; the moment has arrived, all hesitation disappears, and the face takes on a remarkable character of resolution; the subject rises and performs the suggested act.
>

A <term>somnambulist</term> <note>In 19th-century medical terms, this refers to a person in a deep hypnotic state, not necessarily someone who walks in their sleep.</note> who is made to promise during their sleep that they will return on a certain day at a certain hour, although they have no memory of the promise upon waking, will almost certainly return on the designated day and hour. To S..., I suggested that he would come back to see me after thirteen days, at ten o'clock in the morning. Once awakened, he remembered nothing. On the thirteenth day, at ten o'clock in the morning, he was present, having traveled three kilometers from his home to the hospital. He had spent the night working at the ironworks, had gone to bed at six in the morning, and at nine o'clock woke up with the idea that he had to come to the hospital to see me. “This idea,” he told me, “he had not had on previous days; he did not know he was supposed to come find me; it only presented itself to his mind at the very moment he had to carry it out.”

Thus, a suggestion can lie dormant and unconscious in the brain where it was deposited during sleep, and only <term>hatch</term> <note>Original: "éclosion"—literally a "blooming" or "hatching," used here to describe the moment a latent idea becomes a conscious impulse.</note> on the day assigned in advance for its appearance. Further research is necessary to fully elucidate this curious psychological fact, to establish how long a hypnotic suggestion can remain latent in this way, by command, before being realized; it goes without saying that not all somnambulists are susceptible to such long-term suggestions.

I have spoken of suggestions of acts; I shall now move on to sensory-perceptual suggestions. Illusions of the senses and of physical feeling can be suggested to most somnambulists. I tell them: “Upon waking, you will feel a numbness in your foot, or a cramp in your calf, a sharp pain in a tooth, an itching on your scalp”: these various sensations invariably manifest in all or nearly all deep sleepers. One patient suffering from <term>aortic insufficiency</term> <note>A condition where the heart's aortic valve doesn't close tightly, which can lead to heart failure.</note> to whom I had suggested an itching in his hair, scratched himself violently, not understanding where he had caught all these vermin during his sleep. ->3.<-

Messrs. Binet and Féré <note>Alfred Binet (1857–1911) was a psychologist famous for developing intelligence testing; Charles Féré (1852–1907) was a psychiatrist. Both worked at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris.</note>. "This name is singularly poorly chosen," say these authors, "for it is not a matter of hallucinations at all. One can only understand the nature of this sensory disorder by comparing it to systematic paralyses of movement... For the eye as for the arm, it is a phenomenon of **inhibition** <note>In 19th-century physiology, inhibition referred to the nervous system's ability to suppress or block a particular function or reflex.</note> which produces a systematic paralysis." (*Philosophical Review, January 1885.*)

My honorable opponents seem to deserve the reproach they give me of having poorly grasped the nature and meaning of the phenomenon.

When I make a <term>hypnotizable</term> subject see, by hypnotic suggestion or by suggestion in a waking state, a person or a thing that is not before their eyes, I have created an image evoked by their brain; I have given rise to a **visual hallucination**.

If, in the same subject and by the same process, I have rendered invisible a person or a thing that is before their eyes, I have not produced a paralysis of the eye; the subject sees all objects, except for the one suggested to be invisible to them; I have erased a sensory image in their brain, I have neutralized or rendered negative the perception of this image: I call this a **negative hallucination**.

In both cases, the psychic or **psycho-sensory** <note>Pertaining to the mental processing of physical sensations.</note> phenomenon is of the same order; in both cases, I have created a person in a state of hallucination.

Moreover, in all complex hallucinations, such as we produce artificially or as they develop spontaneously, the two phenomena coexist. A <term>mentally ill person</term> <note>original: "aliéné" — a 19th-century term for someone suffering from mental alienation or insanity.</note> believes himself to be in prison; he sees his dungeon, the jailer, the chain that binds him: these are sensory perceptions created in his brain. On the other hand, he does not see the real objects before him, he does not see or hear the people surrounding him: these are real sensory perceptions that have been erased.

Will it be said that of these two orders of phenomena, the first alone constitutes a hallucination, while the second is not one? The term **negative hallucination** seems to me, by a common figure of speech <note>original: "abus de mot" — literally an "abuse of word," referring to the use of a term in a way that is technically inaccurate but widely accepted.</note> authorized in our language (examples:

<summary>The author debates Alfred Binet and Charles Féré over the terminology of "negative hallucinations," arguing that the mental erasure of a real object is psychologically identical to the mental creation of a false one.</summary>

Sensory and hallucinatory illusions, like <term>suggestions of acts</term> <note>Instructions given to a patient during hypnosis to be carried out after they have woken up, often called post-hypnotic suggestions.</note>, can be commanded long in advance. In some subjects, one can achieve suggested phenomena after an even longer period of time. Here are two examples:

On Saturday, December 22, 1883, I say to Mrs. G..., who has been mentioned several times, after having hypnotized her: "Next Tuesday in three weeks—that is, in 25 days—when I pass by your bed during the morning rounds, you will see my colleague, Mr. V. In the meantime, she is hypnotized on several occasions, and other suggestions [are given to her]...

# CHAPTER III

->Observations on various types of somnambulism. — On the <term>doubling of personality</term> <note>original: "dédoublement de la personnalité." In modern psychology, this is often referred to as "dissociative identity" or a split in the sense of self.</note> in certain somnambulists. — On spontaneous dreams with or without the persistence of a sense of reality.<-

We have seen that most people can be influenced by <term>hypnotism</term> to varying degrees; but not everyone is capable of entering a state of deep sleep or <term>somnambulism</term> <note>While we usually use this word for "sleepwalking," in 19th-century medicine, it referred to a deep state of trance where the subject can speak and act while appearing to be asleep.</note>. According to a record shared with me by **Mr. Liébeault** <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904) was a French physician and a founder of the Nancy School of hypnotism, known for treating patients through suggestion.</note>, out of 2,534 individuals he subjected to hypnotization, there were 385 somnambulists—that is, 15.19 out of 100, or approximately 1 in 6.58.

Here now, briefly, are a few examples of induced somnambulism:

**OBSERVATION I.** — **Mr. Sch...**, aged forty, a cardboard maker—whose case I will relate later from a <term>therapeutic</term> <note>Relating to the healing or treatment of disease.</note> perspective—is a small man, rather stout, of a mixed temperament, reserved, of a somewhat dull and unrefined intelligence, yet sufficiently balanced. He has no history of nervous disorders. Following a fracture of the spinal column accompanied by a <term>cerebral concussion</term>, he had suffered for a year from a certain <term>paresis</term> <note>A condition of muscular weakness or partial paralysis caused by nerve damage.</note> of the lower limbs and <term>epileptiform</term> <note>Seizures or symptoms that resemble epilepsy but may have other underlying causes.</note> attacks, from which he has now (September 1883) been cured for several months (See Observation III).

For several weeks, I was only able to hypnotize him to the "third degree"; then he reached the stage of deep sleep. Currently, I can put him to sleep in a single second by a simple command: I order him to sleep deeply, and he remains motionless in whatever position I place him. In our first sessions, he would wake up on his own; today, he continues to sleep indefinitely unless I wake him

I cannot tell you that he told me to kill this man, because he told me nothing.” — And the improvised prosecutor could not wring the truth from him, since the truth for him was my final suggestion: that he had acted of his own accord. The significance of this experiment from a psychological and <term>medico-legal</term> <note>Relating to both medicine and law; today we would call this forensic psychology.</note> point of view calls for many reflections!

Once awakened or returned to his normal state, Cl... believes he has slept peacefully in his chair and has no memory of the drama of which he was the author; the terrible emotions that assailed him, the violent scenes evoked before him, have left no imprint on his brain. One could walk him for hours in a state of <term>somnambulism</term>, eyes open; one could impose the most bizarre acts upon him, and he would carry them out resolutely; one could then lead him back to the spot where he was transformed into a somnambulist to wake him or return him to his true nature, and he would remember absolutely nothing of what happened in this automatic second life imposed by the will of another person.

Cl... is also remarkable for the ease with which one can induce <term>hallucinations</term> <note>Perceived sensations that occur without an external stimulus, such as seeing an object that isn't there.</note> or post-hypnotic acts in him. Hardly is he asleep when I suggest to him that upon his awakening—and I do not wake him until an hour later—he will see his portrait on the blackboard: he sees it and finds it to be a very good likeness. — I suggest to him that he will see a large dog in every bed!

A person stands in front of the exit door: he looks in vain for the lock and, not finding it, believes he is mistaken and goes to another door. Finally, he is allowed to leave. As soon as he is out of the room, he sees and recognizes everyone he meets on his way.

In all these personality changes that are easily obtained in many <term>somnambulists</term> <note>In 19th-century medical terms, this refers to people in a deep state of hypnotic trance who are capable of movement and speech.</note>, the subject's own character reveals itself: each plays their role with the qualities that are personal to them, with the aptitudes at their disposal.

### OBSERVATION IV.

S..., aged thirty-nine, is a former sergeant, currently a worker at the blast furnaces, who was referred to me by Mr. Liébeault <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904) was a French physician and a founder of the Nancy School of hypnotism, known for using suggestion to treat patients</note> who has put him to sleep on several occasions. Wounded at Patay by a shell fragment to the scalp, he bears a deep scar on his head; he suffered from cystitis <note>inflammation of the bladder</note> following a narrowing of the urethra, from which he is currently cured. # THE SENSE OF IDENTITY

...human to the questions addressed to him. We believe ourselves to be in a dream, returned to the time of our youth; memories deeply buried in our brain revive and become images once more. We see again those who are no longer living, we converse with them, and at the same time, the feeling of the present moment is not lost; sometimes it is distinct enough that we say to ourselves: "It is only a dream!" 

> "It seems," says **Maudsley** <note>Henry Maudsley (1835–1918) was a prominent British psychiatrist whose work focused on the relationship between mental health and the physical brain.</note>, "that through all the wanderings of dreams, there is generally at the bottom of us an obscure feeling or an instinct of our identity; for otherwise we would never be surprised to see that we are not ourselves, or that we are doing something extraordinary, nor would we have that kind of personal feeling that is within us in every personal drama where we may play a role. I believe that the **organism** maintains its identity, even though our conscious functions are most distracted; although we are asleep..., our fundamental personality feels itself with more or less strength, in every state of consciousness, in dreams or in the waking state. The resident of a madhouse who has the illusion of being the Almighty and of being able to do in an instant everything he wishes, humbly asks for a slight favor at the very moment he proclaims his omnipotence. These are the consequences of a **distracted identity**."

The hallucinations of **somnambulism** <note>In this context, somnambulism refers to the deep trance state induced by hypnosis, rather than simple sleepwalking.</note> are in reality only provoked dreams; the produced image is more or less vivid, and the consciousness of identity can persist, more or less confused, alongside the dream, without the dreamer being struck by the contradiction. **S...** feels that he is at my side, dominated by me; he is at the same time on the battlefield and repeats aloud the dream he sees, that he lives, suggested by me.

Alongside these types of somnambulism, such as I have just described—and of which I could multiply the examples indefinitely—there exists a rarer variety, in which the sleeper is assailed by dreams

**Observation V.** — Such is the case of a young hysterical <note>In 19th-century medicine, "hysteria" was a broad diagnosis for various psychological and neurological symptoms, often attributed to the nervous system.</note> girl whom I treated in my service from October 1881 to January 1882. **OBSERVATION VI.** — A thirty-seven-year-old man, suffering since 1872 from stomach pain <term>gastralgia</term>, came to consult me. He does indeed find himself there: he tells me everything he sees during the walk that I lead his imagination through.

Despite his dream, he has preserved a sense of reality; he knows who I am, he knows that he is sleeping! He is simultaneously asleep in Nancy and awake in a lumber yard in Bar-le-Duc; the contradiction does not bother him; he remains, during his spontaneous dreams, in relation with the person who put him to sleep. ### CASE STUDY VII. — Madame de X..., aged fifty-six,
is highly intelligent; she has suffered for many years from chronic gastritis with stomach dilation. I put her to sleep easily by the simple closing of the eyelids maintained for one minute. She displays a certain degree of suggestive catalepsy <term>catalepsy: a state where a person's limbs remain in whatever position they are placed by another person</term>; she keeps her arms in the air for some time, but eventually lowers them of her own accord. I can also induce rotatory automatism in her lower limbs by telling her: "You cannot stop yourself." But the movement I set in motion lasts no more than ten seconds or so; I cannot provoke in her any muscle stiffness <term>contracture: a state of prolonged, involuntary muscle contraction</term>, nor numbness <term>anesthesia: a loss of physical sensation or pain</term>, nor sensory suggestion. If I say to her, for example: "Hear the music," she hears nothing. If I say to her: "Swallow this spoonful of medicine," she replies: "You know, doctor, that doesn't work on me."

She retains a great deal of spontaneity during her sleep, discusses matters with me, informs me of all the details of her illness, or speaks to me of external and worldly affairs.

Thus she had suggested to herself during her sleep to preserve this memory; all the others were erased.
