# REALITY OF THE PHENOMENA

...the somnambulistic state, as in the waking state, <insert>retains</insert> their own special individuality. <note>This sentence fragment completes a thought from the previous page, suggesting that a person's unique personality remains intact even when they are hypnotized.</note>

In the preceding pages, I have sketched in broad strokes the curious phenomena that can be observed in <term>provoked sleep</term> <note>A 19th-century term for a hypnotic trance induced by a practitioner.</note>, phenomena that anyone who cares to take the trouble can easily verify. Undoubtedly, one may encounter subjects who knowingly simulate, or who, out of a desire to please, believe they are obliged to simulate; one may encounter doubtful cases that do not command conviction; the state of sleep is separated from the waking state by gradual nuances; sometimes the practitioner doubts if a certain subject is truly influenced; on the other hand, the subject, who remembers hearing everything, may believe he did not sleep and imagine that he was faking.

Here, as in all things, experience will teach how to discern whether the influence obtained is real. A man of great science and intelligence, whom I hypnotized for some time for a <term>nervous illness</term> <note>A general category in Victorian medicine used to describe various neurological or psychological symptoms.</note>, fell during the first session into the third degree: <term>suggestive catalepsy</term> <note>A state where the patient’s body or limbs remain fixed in whatever position the hypnotist places them, as if they were made of wax.</note>, with memory preserved upon waking. I asked him if he had slept. He thought so without being absolutely certain, having heard everything. At my request as to why he had neither opened his eyes nor lowered his raised arms, and whether he could have done so, he replied: "I do not know if I could have; I did not have the idea to do it, the will failed me." I was convinced that he had been influenced; he was so much so that at the next session and at all others since, he fell into a deep sleep, with an absolute loss of memory upon waking. I observe this fact daily.

It is not lightly, based on a single positive or negative observation, that one must pronounce a judgment. I do myself the justice of saying that I have observed coldly, without bias, and without enthusiasm. But when, after several hundred observations collected from all classes of society, at the hospital and in the city, I have seen the phenomena occur constantly, affecting a mode...

He emphasizes his own impartial, clinical approach based on hundreds of diverse cases.</summary>

# REALITY OF THE PHENOMENA

->SUGGESTION. 5<-

...preserved in a uniform manner; when I know, on the other hand, that all the people who have studied the question without bias have observed facts identical or analogous to those I have observed, must we then admit that all our subjects have conspired together to <term>mystify</term> <note>From the French "mystifier," meaning to play a hoax or deliberately deceive someone into believing something false.</note> us?

Certain minds have a horror of the <term>marvelous</term> <note>A 19th-century term for things that seem supernatural or defy the known laws of nature.</note>; they are right to feel so; but they are wrong to consider as marvelous—and to systematically deny—facts that they have not verified, simply because these facts do not agree with the <term>preconceived</term> <note>original: "à priori"</note> conceptions of their brains. 

Facts are unshakable; interpretation comes afterward: if it is lacking, let us not blame the facts, but rather the insufficiency of our knowledge in psychology and nervous physiology.

## CHAPTER IV

On circulation and respiration in hypnotized subjects. — The modifications noted by authors are due to the emotion of the subjects. — Influence of hypnotic suggestion on the functions of organic life: slowing and acceleration of the pulse, influence on <term>vaso-motor</term> <note>Related to the nerves and muscles that control the constriction and dilation of blood vessels.</note> circulation: redness, <term>blisters</term> <note>original: "vésicatoires"</note>, hemorrhages by suggestion.

One more word on circulation and respiration in hypnotized subjects.

According to <term>Braid</term> <note>James Braid (1795–1860), a Scottish surgeon who is considered the "Father of Modern Hypnotism."</note>, the pulse and respiration are at first slower than usual, but as soon as the muscles are put into activity, there occurs a tendency toward <term>cataleptiform rigidity</term> <note>A state where the limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed, as if the subject were a statue.</note> with acceleration of the pulse and rapid, oppressed breathing. According to his experiments, the acceleration of the pulse resulting from the muscular effort a subject normally makes to keep the legs and arms extended for five minutes is about 20 percent; in the state of hypnotism, it would be 100 percent. If all the senses are then excited, if one cataleptizes, at the same time as the limbs, the muscles of the head and neck, there would be a rapid decrease to 40 percent (that is to say, double what the acceleration was during the natural state); if the muscles are made to return to their <term>flaccid</term> <note>Limp or relaxed.</note> state while the subject is still in hypnotism, the pulse drops rapidly to the figure it was at before the experiment and even below it. Moreover, during cataleptiform rigidity, the pulse <unclear>w</unclear>ould be small and contracted; at the same time, a vivid <term>injection</term> <note>An increased flow of blood to a specific area, causing redness or swelling.</note> of the <term>ocular conjunctivae</term> <note>The thin, clear membranes covering the white part of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.</note> and of the entire capillary system of the neck, head, and face would occur. Braid thinks that the rigidity of cataleptized muscles opposes the free transmission of blood to the extremities and causes

### PHENOMENA DUE TO EMOTION

...thus the increase in cardiac action and <term>hyperemia</term> <note>An excess of blood in the vessels supplying an organ or other part of the body; congestion.</note> of the brain and the spinal cord.

Other authors have observed, like Braid, modifications of the cardiac and respiratory functions. Pau de Saint-Martin, in a case of <term>hypnotic lethargy</term> <note>A state of profound sleep or unconsciousness induced by hypnosis.</note> recorded in a Strasbourg thesis, notes the acceleration of the pulse and respiration, the decrease in vascular tension, and the secretion of abundant sweat.

<term>Heidenhain</term> <note>Rudolf Heidenhain (1834–1897), a German physiologist who studied the physical mechanisms of hypnosis.</note>, by means of more precise methods, arrived at the same results and further noted an increase in salivary secretion. More recently, Tamburini and Seppilli, using the graphic method and the <term>plethysmograph</term> <note>An instrument used to measure changes in volume within an organ or the whole body, often used to track blood flow.</note> of Mosso, found that at the moment of transition from waking to hypnotic sleep, respiratory movements become irregular, unequal, and more frequent; cardiac and vascular beats accelerate; and the face becomes congested.

Dr. <term>Hack Tuke</term> <note>Daniel Hack Tuke (1827–1895), a prominent English physician and expert on mental illness and the influence of the mind upon the body.</note> observed in one subject an acceleration of cardiac and respiratory movements; in another, the movements of the heart and respiration were, on the contrary, calm.

It seems to me that observers have not taken into account, in their assessment, the process used for hypnotization and the <term>moral conditions</term> <note>The psychological or emotional state of the subject.</note> in which it is obtained.

Subjects who are invited to fixate upon a bright object or the eyes of the operator make a more or less intense effort to fixate; to the muscular fatigue of the eye and the psychic concentration is added a certain <term>moral emotion</term> <note>Emotional agitation or anxiety.</note>, especially when they are submitted to the experiment for the first time; from this comes an irregular, accelerated, and sometimes gasping respiration; the pulse is agitated by emotion; this is the pulse that clinicians call the <term>medical pulse</term> <note>original: "pouls médical"; also known as "doctor's pulse," referring to a temporary rise in heart rate caused by the anxiety of being examined by a physician.</note>. The congestion of the face, the muscular tremors, and the sensation of unease experienced by some do not seem to me to stem from any other causes.

In the subjects whom I put to sleep by the **soft suggestive method**, who maintain a calm spirit, and in all those who, having already been hypnotized several times, fall asleep—

### SUGGESTED MODIFICATIONS OF THE PULSE

...with complete confidence, without emotion or agitation, none of these symptoms manifest. Under these conditions, I have observed neither acceleration nor slowing of the pulse, nor acceleration or slowing of respiratory movements; I took the pulse using a <term>sphygmograph</term> <note>An early physiological instrument used to create a visual record (a "sphygmogram") of the strength and rhythm of the pulse.</note> before and during <term>hypnotization</term>, and I found it to be identical. Nor did I observe the considerable acceleration that would be produced, according to Braid <note>James Braid (1795–1860), the Scottish surgeon considered the "father of modern hypnotism."</note>, by <term>cataleptiform rigidity</term> <note>A state associated with deep hypnosis where the limbs remain stiffly in whatever position they are placed, resembling a plastic-like immobility.</note> during the extension of the limbs; no sensible difference appeared to exist, in this regard, between the waking state and the hypnotic state.

Can suggestion modify the functions of organic life that are, under ordinary conditions, beyond the reach of the will? Mr. <term>Beaunis</term> <note>Henri-Étienne Beaunis (1830–1921), a French physiologist and psychologist who was a key figure in the Nancy School of hypnosis research.</note> has conducted several physiological experiments to resolve this question. He sought to vary the frequency of heartbeats by suggestion in <term>somnambulists</term> <note>In 19th-century clinical terms, "somnambulists" referred to highly susceptible hypnotic subjects who could perform complex tasks or experience vivid hallucinations while appearing to be in a deep, sleep-like state.</note>, recording these beats through physiological processes. For this purpose, <term>Marey's transmission sphygmograph</term> <note>A device developed by Étienne-Jules Marey that used air pressure to transmit the pulse signal to a pen, which then traced the rhythm onto a rotating recording cylinder.</note> was applied to the left radial artery; an electric clock recorded the seconds on the recording cylinder. Here are the results obtained from two somnambulists: in one, the average pulsations per minute before hypnotic sleep being 96, and during sleep 98.4; the suggestion of slowing the pulse resulted in 92.4 per minute. Then, the pulse having returned to its normal state and marking 102 per minute, the suggestion of acceleration brought it to 115.5. Upon waking, it was at 100.2. The slowing and acceleration followed the suggestion immediately. In another somnambulist, the suggestion of slowing the pulse gave a similar result.

Suggestion can also act upon the <term>vasomotor circulation</term> <note>The system of nerves and muscles that controls the contraction and expansion of blood vessels, thereby regulating blood flow and skin tone.</note>. In certain subjects, one can determine a redness on a specific point of the body. Mr. Beaunis said to a somnambulist: "After you wake up, you will have a red spot on the spot I am touching right now." Ten minutes after waking, a faint redness...

# REDNESS AND BLISTERING BY SUGGESTION

...was beginning to appear at the indicated spot, then increased little by little and, after persisting for ten minutes or a quarter of an hour, gradually disappeared. Moreover, through suggestion, it can be made to persist for a long time.

In certain subjects, one can go further; one can produce <term>vesication</term> <note>The process of forming a blister on the skin.</note> by hypnotic suggestion. Mr. Focachon, a pharmacist at Charmes, showed us this phenomenon in a <term>somnambulist</term> <note>In this context, a highly susceptible hypnotic subject.</note> whom he brought to Nancy so that we could oversee the experiment. During her sleep, at 11 o'clock in the morning, eight postage stamps were applied to her left shoulder, with the suggestion that a <term>vesicatory</term> <note>A medicinal plaster used to induce blistering, typically containing cantharides (crushed beetles).</note> was being applied. The subject was left asleep all day; she was only awakened for meals; she was never out of sight. She was put to sleep for the night with the suggestion that she would not wake up until seven o'clock in the morning. That day, at eight-fifteen, the dressing was removed; the postage stamps had not been disturbed; across an area of 4 by 5 centimeters, the <term>epidermis</term> <note>The outer layer of the skin.</note> appeared thickened and altered, of a yellowish-white color; however, the epidermis was not raised and did not form a bubble; it was thickened, slightly wrinkled, and, in a word, presented the appearance of the stage immediately preceding actual blistering. This region of the skin was surrounded by a zone of intense redness and swelling. The person returned to Charmes with Mr. Focachon; by four o'clock in the evening, four or five <term>phlyctenae</term> <note>Small blisters or skin elevations containing watery fluid.</note> had developed; fifteen days later, the blister was still in full <term>suppuration</term> <note>The process of forming or discharging pus.</note>.

Mr. Focachon succeeded in the same experiment with another person: the blistering occurred within forty-eight hours.

Mr. <term>Dumontpallier</term> <note>Victor-Alphonse-Amédée Dumontpallier (1826–1899), a prominent French physician and hypnotism researcher at the Pitié Hospital.</note>, having tried to reproduce this phenomenon, observed several times not blistering, but a notable elevation in temperature.

# CHAPTER V

**On suggestion in the waking state. — Production of the same phenomena by simple affirmation in hypnotizable subjects who are not hypnotized. — Transfer of <term>hemianesthesia</term> <note>A loss of sensation affecting one side of the body, frequently studied by 19th-century neurologists in relation to psychological triggers.</note> in a <term>hysteric</term> <note>In the medical context of the era, this referred to a patient diagnosed with hysteria, a condition then believed to cause various physical symptoms without an organic cause.</note>. — Sensory suggestions. — Hallucinations. — Suggestive modifications of the visual field.**

I now approach the study of several facts I have observed regarding suggestion in the <term>waking state</term> <note>The state of normal, everyday consciousness, as opposed to a hypnotic trance.</note>.

I have noted that many subjects who have been previously hypnotized can—without being hypnotized again, provided they have been trained by a small number of previous sessions (one, two, or three are enough for some)—present while in the waking state the aptitude to manifest these same suggestive phenomena.

Here, for example, is X..., one of my patients accustomed to hypnotization and who reaches a state of light <term>somnambulism</term> <note>A deep stage of hypnosis where the subject can move and speak but remains under the influence of the hypnotist.</note>. Without putting him to sleep, I say to him point-blank: “Close your hand; you can no longer open it.” He holds his hand closed in a <term>contracture</term> <note>A state of prolonged muscle contraction or rigidity that the subject cannot voluntarily release.</note> and makes fruitless efforts to open it. I have him extend the other arm, hand open, and I say: “You cannot close it.” He tries in vain to close it, bringing the phalanges to a state of half-flexion upon one another, and despite all his efforts, he can do no more.

I say: “Now, your closed hand opens, and your open hand closes,” and in a few seconds, the phenomenon occurs; the hands remain immobilized in this new position.

<term>Automatic movements</term> <note>Physical actions that continue repetitively without the subject's conscious control once initiated by suggestion.</note> succeed very well with him. I say: “Rotate your arms; you can no longer stop them.” He rotates them indefinitely over each other. I add: “Make every effort to [stop them]...”

I can similarly produce <term>trismus</term> <note>original: "trismus"; a spasm of the jaw muscles that causes the mouth to remain tightly closed, commonly called lockjaw.</note>, <term>torticollis</term> <note>original: "torticolis"; a condition where the neck muscles contract, causing the head to twist to one side.</note>, <term>suggestive paralysis</term> of a limb, etc.

And I obtain the effect not on docile subjects who are weak-willed or merely compliant, but on well-balanced subjects who reason well and have their own will—some even possessing a spirit of insubordination.

Modifications of sensitivity can be obtained in certain individuals by suggestion in the waking state.

Here is a remarkable fact: A young <term>hysterical</term> girl (see Part 2, observation IX) is in my care; she exhibits complete left-side sensory-sensitive <term>hemi-anesthesia</term> <note>A total loss of sensation on only one side of the body.</note>; she is, moreover, hypnotizable into a deep sleep.

In the waking state, she undergoes catalepsy or suggestive rigidity. Without putting her to sleep, without touching her, I produce in her the <term>transfer</term> <note>A phenomenon where a symptom, such as numbness or a motor defect, moves from one side of the body to the corresponding location on the other side.</note> of the hemi-anesthesia from the left to the right side.

<header>TRANSFER OF SENSITIVITY IN THE WAKING STATE</header>

I say to her: "You are going to feel again in your left arm and hand; sensitivity will return completely"; I imperiously fix her attention on this return of sensitivity. After three minutes, she feels a sharp pain in the shoulder; at this moment, the shoulder is sensitive, the forearm is not yet, and the right shoulder is insensitive; the pain radiates quickly from the center to the periphery, along the arm into the fingers, then disappears. This lasts from a few seconds to a quarter of a minute. The return of sensitivity accompanies this <term>painful radiation</term> <note>original: "irradiation douloureuse"; a sensation of pain that spreads from a central point outward along a nerve path.</note>. Sensitivity is completely restored in the left upper limb; it is abolished in the right upper limb; a <term>transfer</term> <note>original: "transfert"; in 19th-century neurology, this referred to the phenomenon where a symptom (like numbness) moves from one side of the body to the symmetrical spot on the opposite side.</note> has occurred; this transfer was not suggested; only the restoration of sensitivity on the left was suggested.

I operate in the same way—either simultaneously, if the suggestion is sufficiently imperious, or successively, if the suggestion is less imperious or less effective—for the transfer in the lower limbs: the special senses (smell, taste, vision, hearing) most often underwent the same transfer from left to right at the same time, and without any special suggestion for them.

One can immediately induce the transfer in the opposite direction once again, and so on, as many times as one wishes.

I can produce crossed sensitivity in the left upper limb and the right lower limb, for example, and *the other way around* <note>original: "vice versâ"</note>, while the other limbs remain <term>anesthetic</term> <note>original: "anesthésiques"; here meaning a total lack of physical sensation or touch.</note>.

By forcefully emphasizing the suggestion and sustaining the patient's attention on both her arms and both her legs—which is sometimes, though not always, possible—I induce the return of sensitivity without transfer; both sides are then sensitive. If, on the contrary, the suggestion is insufficient, the painful radiation and sensitivity stop halfway; the arm and the upper half of the forearm, for example, remain the only sensitive parts, while the wrist and hand remain anesthetic.

<header>TRANSFER OF CONTRACTURE IN THE WAKING STATE</header>

<term>Anesthesia</term> <note>original: "anesthésie"; a complete loss of sensation or feeling in a part of the body.</note> occurs more quickly than the restoration of sensitivity: the latter requires at least a minute, while the former is obtained instantly. I prick the left hand with a pin: the patient reacts sharply (her eyes being closed to avoid any deception); I say to her: "You no longer feel anything," and I prick her again: immediate and complete <term>analgesia</term> <note>original: "analgésie"; the specific inability to feel pain.</note>.

The transfer or the complete return of sensitivity can be achieved by another process, which is even more effective and which embodies, so to speak, functional restoration through a visible and tangible phenomenon.

I have her raise the anesthetized arm with the hand closed; the limb remains in a state of <term>catalepsy</term> <note>original: "catalepsie"; a trance-like state where the muscles become rigid and the limbs remain in whatever position they are placed.</note>. I then say: "Your hand will open, your arm will fall, and you will feel again." After half a minute to a minute, the hand opens abruptly, as if by a painful electric shock; the transfer of sensitivity has taken place. At the same time, if I have suggested it, a transfer of <term>contracture</term> <note>original: "contracture"; a condition where muscles remain in a shortened, rigid state, preventing normal movement.</note> is established; the other hand closes and the arm becomes cataleptic.

Instead of contracting the hands in flexion (curled inward), I contract them in extension (opened wide), and I suggest the closing of the hands; the same effect occurs.

I can prevent the transfer and restore sensitivity in the anesthetized limb while maintaining it in the healthy limb by the following method: I raise both arms and both legs and hold them in catalepsy, but with the hands closed; then I say: "Your hands will open, your legs will fall, and you will feel everywhere." After a few moments, the hands open, the legs fall, and sensitivity becomes general.

Finally, if while I am performing these suggestive phenomena, I say and repeat with authority: "Sensitivity is returning without pain; you have no pain"; the patient recovers her sensitivity without any painful shocks or radiations.

I should add that after a variable amount of time, the left <term>hemianesthesia</term> <note>original: "hémianesthésie"; a loss of sensation affecting only one vertical half of the body.</note> spontaneously returns.

One more word, before finishing this chapter, on a question of priority.

These phenomena of **suggestion in the waking state**, I was the first to report them in my communication to the Congress for the Advancement of Sciences, held in Rouen, in August 1883. These phenomena have since been verified by Bottey, by Dumontpallier, by Charles Richet, and by all observers.

Fourteen months after my communication, Charles Richet, in a note entitled: *On Suggestion without Hypnotism*, relating some facts, seems to claim priority for the discovery and recalls a communication made in 1882 to the Society of Biology (No. 3).

In this communication, it concerns a person who, without hysteria and without hypnotism, presented remarkable symptoms of <term>contracture</term> <note>A state of prolonged muscular contraction or rigidity that cannot be voluntarily relaxed.</note> by pressure on the muscle masses—a contracture disappearing by light stimulation such as a puff of air or a sudden noise. Furthermore, by giving the hand a slight oscillatory movement for half a minute, this movement could no longer be stopped by the subject’s will; it continued indefinitely.

The first is the **lethargic state**. It is obtained either by fixing the gaze on an object or by lightly compressing the eyeballs through lowered eyelids. Lethargy obtained in this way is characterized essentially by the appearance of a deep sleep, muscle relaxation, often complete <term>anesthesia</term> <note>The total loss of physical sensation or the ability to feel pain.</note>, and the abolition of intellectual life; suggestions are impossible during this stage. ### ON THE THREE HYPNOTIC PHASES

...contracts; pressure on the <term>ulnar nerve</term> <note>The nerve running near the ulna bone in the forearm</note> causes <term>ulnar clawing</term> <note>original: "griffe cubitale"; a physical contraction where the fingers curl into a claw-like shape</note>, while pressure on the facial nerve causes the distortion of facial features on the corresponding side.

The second state is the **cataleptic state**. To transition the subject from the first state to the second, it is sufficient to lift the eyelids. If only one eye is opened, only the corresponding side of the body enters <term>catalepsy</term>, while the other side remains in <term>lethargy</term>. The cataleptic patient maintains every posture or attitude given to them; <term>neuro-muscular hyperexcitability</term> <note>The physical tendency for muscles to contract upon being touched</note> has disappeared.

In this phase, it is possible to produce **suggestions** through the "muscular sense"; for example, if the subject's hands are brought together as if to blow a kiss, their expression becomes smiling; if the hands are joined as if in prayer, the expression becomes serious and the subject drops to their knees. One can return the subject from the cataleptic state to the lethargic state by closing their eyelids. Finally, this state can occur directly without being preceded by the lethargic phase, triggered by the nervous shock produced by a very bright light or a sudden, violent noise.

The third state is the **somnambulic state**. It can be induced initially by fixing the gaze or through various other practices. One transforms lethargy or catalepsy into somnambulism by applying light or repeated rubbing to the <term>vertex</term> <note>The very top of the head</note> of the subjects. This state is characterized by a typical <term>anesthesia</term> <note>Loss of physical sensation or pain</note> that is more or less pronounced, by <term>sensory hyperacuity</term> <note>Highly sharpened senses</note>, and above all by the fact that the subject is essentially primed for all manner of suggestions.

<term>Neuro-muscular hyperexcitability</term> does not exist in this state. Permanent contractions cannot be triggered through the mechanical stimulation of muscles or nerves; however, through light touches or a gentle breath directed at the skin, one can produce a special **contracture** "different from that which occurs in the lethargic state, in that it is not resolved by the stimulation of opposing muscles, and different from cataleptic immobility, in that it offers resistance when one attempts to change the posture." (<term>Binet</term> and <term>Féré</term>.) <note>Alfred Binet and Charles Féré were colleagues of Jean-Martin Charcot and famous for their early studies in psychology and hypnosis.</note>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Salpêtrière school's rigid classification of hypnotic states. # THE THREE PHASES DO NOT EXIST

One can transform <term>somnambulism</term> <note>A deep state of hypnosis characterized by responsiveness and potential memory loss upon waking</note> in the reverse direction into <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of muscular rigidity where limbs stay in whatever position they are placed</note> by opening the subject's eyes, or into <term>lethargy</term> <note>A state of deep relaxation and apparent unconsciousness</note> by closing and lightly pressing on the eyeballs. These three phases were said to constitute what has been called <term>grand hypnotism</term> <note>original: "grand hypnotisme"; the term used by Jean-Martin Charcot to describe the full range of hypnotic symptoms he believed were specific to hysterical patients</note>, or the **great hypnotic neurosis**.

Observers from Nancy <note>The "Nancy School" was a group of physicians, led by Hippolyte Bernheim, who argued that hypnosis was a normal psychological phenomenon based on "suggestion," rather than a physical disease</note> have been criticized for jumping straight into the psychological realm instead of first studying the somatic or physical characteristics of hypnotized subjects. It is claimed that we have confused and mixed all these various states without distinguishing between them; indeed, we have not stated whether our subjects were in lethargy, catalepsy, or somnambulism.

I reply: If we did not take the three phases of <term>hysterical hypnotism</term> as the starting point for our research, as described by <term>Charcot</term> <note>Jean-Martin Charcot (1825–1893), the influential French neurologist who viewed hypnosis as a manifestation of hysteria</note>, it is because we have been unable to confirm their existence through our own observations. Here is what we constantly observe in Nancy: When a subject—whether hysterical or not—is hypnotized by any method (fixing on a bright object, the operator’s fingers or eyes, passes <note>Slow, sweeping hand movements made by a hypnotist over the subject's body</note>, <term>vocal suggestion</term>, or closing the eyelids), there comes a moment when the eyes remain closed, often—though not always—rolled up under the upper eyelids; sometimes the eyelids are agitated by <term>fibrillary movements</term> <note>small, involuntary twitching of muscle fibers</note>, but this is not constant. We then observe neither <term>neuro-muscular hyperexcitability</term> <note>The physical tendency for muscles to contract instantly upon being touched, which Charcot claimed was a physical proof of hypnosis</note> nor an exaggeration of tendon reflexes. Is this lethargy? 

In this state, as in all hypnotic states—and I insist on this fact—the hypnotized person hears the operator; their attention and ear are fixed upon him. Often, they answer questions; they almost always answer if one insists and tells them they can speak. Even while remaining immobile, insensitive, their face as inert as a mask and apparently detached from the outside world, they hear everything—whether they retain the memory of it later upon waking, or have lost it. The proof is that, without touching them or blowing on their eyes, the simple words: "Wake up," pronounced once or several times before them, awakens them.

<summary>The author rejects Charcot's theory of three distinct physical phases of hypnosis, arguing that the "Nancy School" finds no evidence for these somatic states. Instead, they observe that hypnotized subjects remain mentally connected to the operator and respond to suggestion regardless of their physical appearance.</summary>

# THE THREE PHASES DO NOT EXIST

The subject in this state is capable of manifesting the phenomena of <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of muscular rigidity where limbs remain in whatever position they are placed</note> or <term>somnambulism</term> <note>A deep hypnotic state where the subject is highly responsive to commands</note> without the need for any specific manipulation, provided they have reached a sufficient level of hypnotization.

To place a limb in catalepsy, it is not necessary to open the subject's eyes or expose them to a bright light or a loud noise—methods used at the <term>Salpêtrière</term> <note>The Paris hospital where Jean-Martin Charcot conducted his famous research, claiming hypnosis was a physical condition triggered by external stimuli</note>. It is enough to lift the limb and leave it in the air for a moment, affirming if necessary that the limb can no longer be lowered; it then remains in a state of **suggestive catalepsy**. The hypnotized person, whose will or power of resistance is weakened, passively maintains the posture that has been imparted to them.

To demonstrate the characteristics of somnambulism in subjects capable of manifesting them, it is not necessary to rub the <term>vertex</term> <note>The crown or top of the head; Charcot believed rubbing this spot would move a patient from one hypnotic phase to another</note>, as is done at the Salpêtrière; it is enough to speak to the subject, and they, being suggestible, carry out the action or experience the suggested phenomenon. Touching the skin or blowing air upon it does not cause <term>contracture</term> <note>A state of sustained, involuntary muscle contraction</note> of the underlying muscles in our subjects when suggestion is not involved.

We have not observed that the act of opening or closing the eyes, or rubbing the vertex, modified the phenomena in any way, nor that these actions triggered them in subjects who were not already capable of manifesting them through suggestion alone.

We have only observed varying degrees of <term>suggestibility</term> <note>The core concept of the Nancy School: the idea that hypnosis is purely a psychological response to the words or actions of the hypnotist</note> in hypnotized individuals. Some experience only the closing of the eyes, with or without numbness; others also experience a relaxation of the limbs with inertia or an inability to perform spontaneous movements; others maintain the postures given to them (suggestive catalepsy). Finally, suggestive contracture, automatic obedience, <term>anesthesia</term> <note>A loss of physical sensation or pain produced by suggestion</note>, and induced <term>hallucinations</term> mark the progressive development of this suggestibility. Approximately one subject out of every six or seven of those being hypnotized reaches the highest degree, to the som- <note>The text cuts off here, likely intending to say "somnambulism"</note>

<summary>The author argues that hypnotic phenomena like catalepsy and somnambulism are produced by psychological suggestion rather than physical triggers, contradicting the methods and theories of the Salpêtrière school. He posits that these states are simply different degrees of suggestibility rather than distinct physical phases.</summary>

# SUGGESTIVE HYPNOTIC NEUROSIS

...nambulism with amnesia upon waking; and, when it is not achieved immediately through the sole act of hypnotization, none of the maneuvers we have tried were able to develop it; only continued suggestion could produce it. The degree of hypnotic **suggestibility** <note>The tendency to accept and act on the suggestions of others</note> has always seemed to us to depend on the individual's temperament and the psychic influence exerted, and not at all on the manipulation performed.

This is what I have constantly observed in several hundred people whom I have subjected to hypnotization; all my colleagues in <term>Nancy</term> <note>The "Nancy School" of hypnosis, which argued that suggestion—not physical triggers—was the key to all hypnotic phenomena</note>, and <term>Mr. Liébeault</term> <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), a country doctor whose work with the poor inspired the Nancy School's theories</note>, who has put over 6,000 people to sleep over the last twenty-five years, have never observed anything else.

Never, in any of my subjects, have I been able to produce the three phases of the <term>Salpêtrière</term> <note>The Paris hospital where Jean-Martin Charcot conducted his famous research, claiming hypnosis was a physical condition with universal stages</note>, and it is not for lack of trying; I should add that in Paris itself, I saw hypnotized subjects in three hospitals; they all behaved like our subjects, and the hospital doctors who were treating them absolutely confirmed what we saw.

Only once did I see a subject who perfectly exhibited the three periods: lethargic, cataleptic, and somnambulic. She was a young girl who had spent three years at the Salpêtrière, and the impression I was left with—why not say it?—is that, being subjected to a special training through these manipulations, and imitating through unconscious suggestion the phenomena she saw occurring in other somnambulists of the same school, trained by imitation to perform reflex phenomena in a certain typical order, she was no longer a natural hypnotic subject; she was indeed a case of *suggestive hypnotic neurosis*.

If I am wrong, if these phenomena occur naturally and outside of any suggestion, it must be recognized that this "great hypnotism" is a rare state; <term>Binet and Féré</term> <note>Alfred Binet and Charles Féré, prominent researchers at the Salpêtrière who published influential works supporting Charcot's pathological view of hypnosis</note> state that in ten years, only a dozen such cases have passed through the Salpêtrière. Should these cases, as opposed to the thousands of cases in which these phenomena are absent, serve as the basis for the theoretical conception of hypnosis?

<summary>The author argues that the "three phases" of hypnosis observed at the Salpêtrière are not natural phenomena but are instead "trained" into patients through unconscious suggestion and imitation. He contrasts the rare cases in Paris with the thousands of successful hypnotizations in Nancy that depend entirely on suggestibility.</summary>

# ON TRANSFER EXPERIMENTS

It will be a curious thing in the history of hypnotism to see so many distinguished minds led astray by an initial erroneous conception, led into a series of singular errors that no longer allow them to recognize the truth. These are regrettable errors, for they hinder progress by obscuring a question so simple in itself and where everything is explained, once one knows that **suggestion** is the key to all hypnotic phenomena!

Nothing is more curious to read from this point of view than the numerous experiments on <term>transfer</term> <note>The supposed movement of a symptom, like paralysis or a sensation, from one side of the body to the other</note> by <term>Messrs. Binet and Féré</term> <note>Alfred Binet (1857–1911), later famous for the IQ test, and Charles Féré (1852–1907), both students of Charcot who initially supported his physical theories of hypnosis</note>. It is known that these authors conclude from their experiments that the application of a **magnet** to a hypnotized subject can transfer to the side of the body where it is applied—for example, to the upper left limb—phenomena such as anesthesia, contracture, or paralysis, which were previously provoked on the other side—for example, in the upper right limb. The magnet would likewise transfer sensory anesthesias and hallucinations of smell, hearing, sight, taste, and touch. This transfer supposedly takes place without the intervention of suggestion, by a simple physical phenomenon, in which the subject’s brain, considered as a psychic organ, would play no role.

The authors believe they have eliminated suggestion because they conducted these experiments in the states known as **lethargy** or **catalepsy**.

> "These states," they say, "are, in <term>great hypnotism</term> <note>Le grand hypnotisme: Charcot's term for a supposedly genuine, pathological form of hypnosis he believed was distinct from simple suggestion</note>, unconscious states where the condition of the senses and intelligence makes the subject completely foreign to what is happening around him. However, experience shows that the magnet transfers a large number of phenomena under these conditions."

First error, which has been the source of all the experimental illusions of these authors.

At every level of hypnotization, I repeat, the subject remains conscious, and we have observed thousands of cases in **Nancy**.

If among the only twelve subjects upon whom, in the span of ten years, the phenomena of what is...

...calling it *great hypnotism*, to distinguish it from what is called the *little hypnotism of Nancy* <note>The "Nancy School," led by Hippolyte Bernheim, argued that hypnosis was a psychological phenomenon based on suggestion, whereas the Salpêtrière school in Paris, led by Charcot, believed it was a physical, pathological state with distinct stages.</note>; if in these subjects, one observed an apparent unconsciousness during the so-called *lethargic* state, I am convinced that it was only an appearance. The subject, unconsciously raised in this suggestion, could not react in that state because they believed they could not react; because the idea had been introduced into their brain that, as long as the necessary manipulation had not been performed on them, they could not emerge from that state, nor could they accept any suggestion. Nothing is easier than to artificially create an analogous state in any <term>somnambulist</term> <note>In the 19th century, this referred to a person in a deep state of hypnosis who could perform complex actions while seemingly asleep.</note>.

That being established, I tried to reproduce the experiments of <term>Messrs. Féré and Binet</term> <note>Alfred Binet and Charles Féré, who claimed that magnets could physically "transfer" symptoms from one side of the body to the other without the patient's conscious knowledge.</note>; I tried a very great number of times on a very great number of subjects, in the presence of several of my colleagues, among whom were <term>Messrs. Beaunis and Charpentier</term> <note>Henri Beaunis (1830–1921), a psychologist, and Augustin Charpentier (1852–1916), a physician, both associated with the University of Nancy.</note>, and we never succeeded when suggestion was not at play.

Here, for example, is an experiment I conducted with Mr. Beaunis: We put to sleep a nurse from the ward, who was susceptible to entering <term>somnambulism</term> and who had never participated, either as a witness or an actress, in the type of experimentation I wanted to perform on her. I placed her left upper limb in <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state where the limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed.</note>, horizontally, the thumb and index finger extended, the other fingers flexed; the right arm remained in a state of relaxation.

I applied a **magnet** against it, which I left for eight minutes; no phenomenon occurred.

Then, addressing Mr. Beaunis, I said: "Now I am going to perform an experiment; I am going to apply the magnet (on the correct side) against the right hand, and after one minute, you will see this hand rise with the arm, taking exactly the same position as the upper left limb, while the latter will relax and fall."

I replaced the magnet exactly as I had the first time, and after one minute, the (*suggested*) *transfer* was realized with perfect precision; the face of the hypnotized woman remained impassive; it was an inert mask.

->## ON TRANSFER BY SUGGESTION<-

If I then, without saying anything further, place the magnet back against the left hand after one minute, the transfer occurs in the opposite direction, and so on.

In the same person, I induce a <term>torticollis</term> <note>A stiff neck where the head is tilted to one side; the author is inducing this through hypnotic suggestion.</note> through a contraction of the muscles on one side of the neck; I bring the magnet near the opposite side without saying a word; after one minute, the head turns toward the magnet, and an inverse stiff neck occurs; the transfer is complete.

It had been enough for me to state the phenomenon of transfer just once to Monsieur Beaunis <note>Henri Beaunis (1830–1921), a professor of physiology and a key figure in the Nancy School of hypnosis alongside the author.</note> in front of the subject—who was seemingly inactive—for it to occur thereafter every time and for all physical positions; for the idea of the phenomenon had entered the brain of the subject, who was intelligent and attentive despite their apparent inactivity.

I then say: "I am going to turn the magnet in a different direction and the transfer will occur from the hand to the leg."

After one minute, indeed, the arm falls and the leg rises. I place the magnet against the leg without saying anything, and the transfer occurs again from the leg to the arm.

If, without saying anything to the subject, I replace the magnet with a knife, a pencil, a bottle, a piece of paper, or with nothing at all, the same phenomenon occurs.

The following day, I repeated these experiments on another <term>somnambulist</term> <note>In 19th-century psychology, this referred to a person in a deep hypnotic state who could follow complex instructions while appearing to be in a trance.</note> who had been present during the previous day’s session. Without saying anything to them, and without saying anything in front of those present, the experiments succeeded perfectly; the idea of transfer had been suggested to their brain by the events they had witnessed.

Furthermore, after I had repeated this transfer several times from one arm to the other and then ceased applying the magnet altogether, the transfer continued to happen spontaneously two more times (*consecutive oscillations*)—certainly due to the person’s idea that the experiment was continuing. I should add, moreover, that I had previously tried several times to obtain a transfer in this person without any result, as long as the idea of the phenomenon had not yet entered their brain.

It is worth adding that many <term>somnambulists</term> <note>In this era, the term referred to people in a deep state of hypnotic trance who could still function and speak.</note> possess a very high level of perceptual acuity; the slightest hint guides them. Knowing that they are expected to carry out the <term>hypnotist's</term> <note>original: "hypnotiseur"</note> thoughts, they strive to guess them. If "transfer" experiments have been repeated several times on the same subject, they easily guess that they must transfer such and such a phenomenon; and, without anything being said in their presence, they can grasp from the expectant attitude of the operator, or from any other clue, whether the <term>transfer</term> <note>The supposed movement of a symptom or sensation from one side of the body to the other, often using a magnet.</note> is meant to take place.

If I dwell a little on these facts, and if I emphasize my critical observations, it is because they strike at the very foundation of the doctrine of hypnotic phenomena.

Furthermore, I wish to relate here several experiments that I conducted with my colleague Charpentier <note>Augustin Charpentier (1852–1916), a French physician and physicist known for his work on vision and the "size-weight" illusion.</note> regarding the hallucinatory image; nothing demonstrates better than these experiments how easily <term>suggestion</term> <note>The process by which a subject accepts an idea or sensation presented by the hypnotist as reality.</note> occurs and how deceptive observation can be.

One can suggest to many somnambulists during their sleep that they will see a certain thing upon waking, and the hallucination can be realized with such clarity that the subject confuses it with reality. Now, Messrs. Féré, Binet, and Parinaud <note>Charles Féré and Alfred Binet were leading researchers at the Salpêtrière hospital; Henri Parinaud was a famous ophthalmologist. Another example: if, through suggestion, one colors pieces of cardboard green and red, and if one overlaps these two tints using one of the known methods, the subject sees the resulting grey tint, which is produced by the mixture of these two complementary colors.

Are these results accurate? Does the suggested image truly behave, as has been claimed, just as a real, objective image would—passing through the <term>peripheral visual apparatus</term>, the **retina**, and the **optic nerve** until it reaches the sensory center of the **cerebral cortex**? Or rather...

# REAL IMAGE AND SUGGESTED IMAGE

Is it merely a subjective image, triggered directly like a memory in the <term>sensory center</term> <note>The part of the brain perceived at the time to be responsible for processing physical sensations.</note>, and evoked by the subject's imagination?

To solve this question, we conducted several experiments; we shall relate them in the order in which they were performed.

We chose as subjects women of average intelligence, who were not <term>hysterical</term> <note>In the 19th century, "hysteria" was a common but vague medical diagnosis for various emotional and physical symptoms, often incorrectly linked specifically to women.</note> and possessed balanced judgment. They were suggestible at every level—that is to say, they were susceptible, during their sleep, to <term>anesthesia</term>, <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of muscular rigidity where a person’s limbs remain in whatever position they are placed.</note>, sensory illusions, and both hypnotic and <term>post-hypnotic hallucinations</term>. All of them could be rendered completely <term>analgesic</term> <note>Insensitive to pain.</note> during their sleep; tickling the inside of their nostrils did not make them flinch; there could be no question of <term>simulation</term> <note>The act of faking a trance or symptoms.</note>. Furthermore—and we insist on this fundamental precaution—we conducted all our experiments *without saying a single word, even in a low voice*, that could provide a clue to the sleeping subjects; for, as is easily demonstrated, at every level of <term>hypnotization</term>, they can hear and often record everything with a <term>perception</term> that is sometimes remarkably fine.

This being established, here are the facts:

1. L. C..., aged seventeen and in good health, is easily hypnotized by the simple closing of her eyelids and the command to sleep. We prepared a white cardboard disk and suggested to her that, upon waking, she would see the left half of this disk as red and the right half as green. Once awake, she clearly saw the two colors. We then placed this cardboard on a <term>rotating disk</term> <note>original: "disque rotatif"; a device used to spin color wheels to study how the eye perceives blended colors.</note> and gave it a rapid spinning motion. It is well known that when two real colors reach the <term>retina</term> almost simultaneously in this way, they are perceived as a single color which, through the <term>mixing of colors</term> (specifically red and green), would appear as yellow. However, when we asked L. C... what color she saw, she indicated white.

2. After having put her back to sleep, we suggested to her that she would see another disk, half yellow and half blue. Upon her waking, we presented her with the same disk, which was entirely white: she saw the two suggested colors...

# ACTION OF THE PRISM ON SUGGESTED IMAGES

...certain subjects recognize the doubling of the image by psychically deducing it from the doubling of real objects that pass through the field of the prism.

Let us continue the account of our experiments.

Depending on whether one turns the cylinder containing the prism in one direction or another, the two doubled real objects are seen side by side on the same horizontal line or, conversely, one above the other on the same vertical line. We mark with <term>reference points</term> <note>Fixed markers used by the experimenters to track the physical orientation of the prism.</note> the position of the cylinder corresponding to the horizontal or vertical juxtaposition of the two images.

This established, we place any object in front of the subject at a certain distance—for example, a flask—which we have them look at through the prism; they see it as double. We ask them to turn the cylinder so that the two flasks are side by side, then so that they are superimposed: their indications align with the reference points; they now understand the handling of the prism and are well aware of what they see.

Then we put them to sleep, and during their sleep, we remove the flask, suggesting to them that upon waking, they will still see it in the same place. Once awake, they do indeed see the <term>fictional flask</term> <note>A hallucinatory object created through hypnotic suggestion.</note>; through the prism, they see it as double. We tell them to turn the prism so as to juxtapose them horizontally, then vertically: their indications are then purely imaginary and no longer correspond to the reference points.

Each time that, without their knowledge, we replace the fictional flask with a real flask, the subject—who still believes they are seeing the same flask—gives exact indications consistent with the reference points; each time reality is replaced by the suggested image, these indications become imaginary once more.

However, it happens that some subjects eventually, after a certain amount of experimentation, provide accurate information which they deduce from the doubling—

We took two cylinders of similar appearance: one containing a <term>birefringent prism</term> <note>original: "prisme bi-réfringent" — a type of prism that splits a single ray of light into two, creating a double image.</note>, the other a simple piece of glass. Four other somnambulists gave imaginary indications. The first, submitted to the same test at another time of day, no longer saw anything consistent with the laws of optics.

Another somnambulist was subjected to the same experiment; we were able to convince ourselves that every time they aimed the prism directly at the balloon, they gave false indications; these only became accurate when they found a chimney, a roof, or any object that could serve as a reference point.

Such are the facts, to which we could add others; we have verified them at length. They have not left the slightest doubt in our minds; they impose upon us this conviction—which is, moreover, easy to anticipate—that the suggested image is a fictional image, and that it does not correspond to any physical representation in space. A prism can only double real light rays placed in front of it that pass through it; it cannot double an image seen behind it within the cerebral sensory center. The hallucinatory image may be, for the subject, as clear, as brilliant, and as vivid as reality itself. But, being born entirely within the subject's imagination, the subject sees it as they conceive it, as they interpret it, and as their conscious or unconscious memory causes it to be reborn in the <term>sensorium</term> <note>original: "sensorium" — historically, the part of the brain or mind that receives and interprets sensory stimuli.</note>. It is a psychic, cerebral image and not a physical one; it does not pass through the peripheral visual system, has no objective reality, and does not obey the laws of optics, but only the whims of the imagination.

# CHAPTER VII

**Historical overview.** — Mesmer and mesmerism. — His condem<gloss>n</gloss>ation by the learned bodies <note>Refers to the 1784 Royal Commissions in France, which investigated Franz Mesmer’s claims of "animal magnetism" and concluded there was no scientific evidence for a magnetic fluid.</note>. — Husson’s report <note>A later 1831 report by the Royal Academy of Medicine, led by Pierre Husson, which was more sympathetic to the reality of magnetic phenomena.</note>. — Abb<gloss>é</gloss> Faria and sleep by suggestion. — The doctrine of Alexandr<gloss>e</gloss> Bertrand. — Experiments and fluidic doctrine of General Noizet<gloss>.</gloss> — Second period: Braid and braidism <note>James Braid (1795–1860) was a Scottish surgeon who moved the field away from "animal magnetism" toward a physiological understanding, coining the term "hypnotism."</note>. — Analysis of the doctrine. — Grimes and electro-biology in America and England. — Experiments and doctrine of Durand de Gros. — On the <term>moral medicine</term> <note>original: "médecine morale" — an early term for psychotherapy or psychiatric treatment focused on the mind's influence over the body.</note> of Doctor Charpignon; I have presented the phenomena exactly as I have observed them, just as all those who wish to repeat these experiments will be able to observe them as well; I have said only what I have seen, confirmed, verified, and had verified by others many times. Nothing of what I have seen—I hasten to add—seems to me contrary to the physiological and psychological concepts that science has established to this day. Of the "marvelous," such as lucidity <note>original: "lucidité" — the supposed clairvoyant ability to see without eyes or perceive hidden things.</note>, the prediction of the future, internal vision, vision at a distance or through opaque bodies, the transposition of the senses <note>The belief that a subject could "see" with their fingers or "hear" with their stomach while under hypnosis.</note>, or the instinct for remedies <note>The claim that a hypnotized person could instinctively diagnose illnesses and name their own cures.</note>—is it necessary to say that I have seen none of it?

->MESMER<-

The history of <term>magnetism</term> <note>Specifically "animal magnetism," the theory that a physical force or fluid could be transmitted between living beings.</note> appears as one of the greatest wanderings of the human spirit. Men of science rejected what seemed to be the negation of reason; classical science pushed away what did not belong to its domain. Shameless charlatanism, completing the discredit, alone continued to exploit public gullibility.

Not everything was worthless, however, in the wild and boastful conceptions of <term>mesmerism</term>; a few serious people persisted in seeing a grain of truth in the midst of errors, discerning the wheat from the chaff. Today, <term>magnetism</term> is dead, like alchemy; but <term>hypnotic suggestion</term> was born from <term>magnetism</term>, just as chemistry was born from alchemy.

I will not revisit the history of Mesmer and <term>mesmerism</term>. It has been written by Figuier <note>Louis Figuier (1819–1894), a prolific French writer who popularized science.</note>, by Bersot <note>Ernest Bersot (1816–1880), a philosopher and member of the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences.</note>; it is traced by a master’s hand by Dechambre in the *Encyclopedic Dictionary of Medical Sciences* <note>Amédée Dechambre (1812–1886), a physician and renowned medical editor.</note>. Who does not know Mesmer’s <term>tubs</term> <note>original: "baquets" — large wooden vats filled with water, glass, and iron filings, used by Mesmer to "concentrate" the magnetic fluid.</note>, the patients in silence forming several rows around these tubs, the "animal current" of the magnetizer meeting that of the vat and causing, after a variable amount of time, various nervous disturbances, hysteric-like, or analogous to those of <term>somnambulism</term> <note>At this time, "somnambulism" referred to a state of magnetic trance or "sleep-walking" induced by the practitioner.</note>, truly scenes of convulsions? And the doctrine of a universally diffused <term>magnetic fluid</term>, capable of receiving, propagating, and communicating all the impressions of movement by which a mutual influence is exercised between the celestial bodies, the earth, and living bodies! The learned bodies, the Academy of Sciences and the Royal Society of Medicine, condemned the new doctrines after examination.

> "From the point of view of the curative effect," said the latter, "animal magnetism is nothing but the art of throwing sensitive people into convulsions; from the point of view of the curative effect, magnetism is useless or dangerous."

Despite the discredit that Mesmer’s self-interested charlatanism threw upon his practices, <term>magnetism</term> retained followers; moreover, it did not take long to be transformed by his students. The most famous of all, the Marquis de

# THE QUESTION BEFORE THE ACADEMIES

Puységur <note>Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur (1751–1825), a disciple of Mesmer who discovered "artificial somnambulism."</note> magnetized by movements performed by hand, by touch, by glass rods, and by the influence of a magnetized tree; through these varied maneuvers, he produced in reality the state known as <term>somnambulism</term> <note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, this referred to a magnetic trance or "lucid sleep" rather than simple sleepwalking.</note>, the true knowledge of which seems to be linked to his name. The action of the will upon the vital principle—the focus of electricity, which is to say, of movement—that was for him the essence of <term>animal magnetism</term>.

Numerous magnetic societies were founded little by little in the principal cities of France; that of Strasbourg, the **Society of Harmony**, composed of more than one hundred and fifty members, published the results of its work for several years.

The upheavals of the revolutionary period and the wars of the Empire drew minds toward other ideas; however, innumerable books and memoirs for and against magnetism continued to stir public opinion.

With peace and order restored, the question took on new momentum. Public courses were established; the official world and learned societies became less hostile. In 1820, experiments were conducted by Dupotet <note>Jean-Denis, Baron du Potet (1796–1881), a highly influential French magnetizer.</note> at the **Hôtel-Dieu**, then at the **Salpêtrière** <note>Two of Paris's most famous hospitals.</note>. In 1825, Dr. Foissac sent a note to the two Academies of Sciences and Medicine, calling on them to make a ruling. The latter, at his request, resumed the examination of <term>animal magnetism</term>. At the end of six years, the report, entrusted to Husson <note>Adolphe-Nicolas Husson (1772–1833), the physician who led the 1826-1831 commission into magnetism.</note>, was read to the Academy on June 21 and 28, 1831.

> "The favorable conclusions of this report give," says Dechambre, "a general idea of magnetism as it had been shaped, toward 1831, by the action of time and the numerous trials through which it had passed."

Today, as the question appears to be emerging from the theoretical and charlatan-like clouds that long obscured it, it is interesting to reread the conclusions of this remarkable report, which contains and soundly assesses most of the facts as we have described them.

<header>HUSSON’S REPORT</header>

## Here are some of the conclusions:

The contact of thumbs and hands, frictions, or certain gestures made at a short distance from the body and called <term>passes</term> <note>Specific rhythmic hand movements intended to direct "magnetic fluid" through the patient's body.</note>, are the means employed to establish <term>rapport</term> <note>From the French word for "connection"—the specific psychological and physical link between the magnetizer and the subject.</note>, or, in other words, to transmit the action of the magnetizer to the magnetized subject.

The time necessary to transmit and induce the magnetic effect has lasted from half an hour down to a single minute.

Once a person has been put into a magnetic sleep, it is not always necessary to resort to physical contact and passes to magnetize them again. The gaze of the magnetizer, or their willpower alone, has the same influence over the subject.

There usually occur more or less remarkable changes in the perceptions and faculties of individuals who fall into **somnambulism** <note>In this context, it refers to a deep magnetic trance or "lucid sleep," rather than simple sleepwalking.</note> through the effect of magnetism.

a). Some, amidst the noise of confused conversations, hear only the voice of their magnetizer; many respond precisely to questions addressed to them by the magnetizer or by people with whom they have been placed in <term>rapport</term>; others hold conversations with everyone around them; however, it is rare that they hear what is happening around them. Most of the time, they are completely oblivious to sudden external noises made near their ears, such as the clanging of copper vessels struck close by, the falling of a piece of furniture, etc.

b). The eyes are closed; the eyelids yield with difficulty to efforts made by hand to open them; this operation, which is not without pain, reveals the eyeball convulsed toward the top and sometimes toward the bottom of the socket.

c). Sometimes, the sense of smell is as if annihilated. One can have them breathe <term>muriatic acid</term> <note>An older name for hydrochloric acid; its vapors are extremely pungent and irritating.</note> or ammonia without them being inconvenienced, or even suspecting it. The opposite occurs in certain cases, where they remain sensitive to odors.

d). Most of the somnambulists we observed were completely insensible. We were able to tickle their feet, nostrils, and the corners of their eyes with a feather, or pinch their skin so hard as to cause <term>ecchymosis</term> <note>A medical term for bruising or discoloration of the skin caused by bleeding underneath.</note>, without them showing any sign of feeling it.

...pricking them under the fingernail with pins pushed unexpectedly to a considerable depth, without them noticing it. Finally, one woman was seen who was insensible to one of the most painful surgical operations, and neither her face, nor her pulse, nor her respiration showed the slightest emotion.

We did not see anyone magnetized for the first time fall into somnambulism. Sometimes it was only at the eighth or tenth session that the **somnambulism** <note>A state of "lucid sleep" or deep trance induced by magnetic passes.</note> manifested.

Upon waking, they claim to have totally forgotten all the circumstances of the state of somnambulism and never remember it. In this regard, we can have no guarantee other than their statements.

To accurately establish the relationship between magnetism and **therapeutics** <term>therapeutics</term> <note>The branch of medicine concerned with the treatment of disease and the healing process.</note>, it would have been necessary to observe its effects on a large number of individuals, etc. Since this did not occur, the commission had to limit itself to reporting what it had seen in too small a number of cases to dare pronounce any definitive judgment.

Some of the magnetized patients felt no benefit. Others experienced more or less marked relief, namely: one, the suspension of habitual pain; another, the return of strength; a third, a delay of several months in the appearance of epileptic seizures; and a fourth, the complete cure of a severe and long-standing paralysis.

Considered as an agent of physiological phenomena, or as a therapeutic means, magnetism should find its place within the framework of medical knowledge, and consequently, physicians alone should practice and supervise its use, as is the practice in Northern countries <note>Likely referring to Prussia, Denmark, or Sweden, where animal magnetism was more widely accepted by official medical faculties at the time.</note>.

The Academy did not dare to print Husson's report; it left him with the responsibility for his opinions. Though the reporter's honesty defied all suspicion, a certain reputation for credulity remained attached to his person.

A few years later, in 1837, a magnetizer named Berna performed experiments before a new commission appointed by the Academy concerning the **transposition of sight** <note>The alleged ability of a person in a magnetic trance to "see" with parts of the body other than the eyes, such as the stomach or fingertips.</note>; they convinced no one. Dubois gave a negative report. Another of its members, Burdin the Elder, offered a prize of 3,000 francs to

And starting from October 1, 1840 <note>The OCR reads 1810, but historically this refers to the end of the Burdin Prize in 1840, following Husson's 1831 report.</note>, the date the competition closed, the Academy decided that it would no longer respond to communications concerning animal magnetism. This time again, the truth contained in Husson's report was drowned in the chimerical absurdity of the marvelous.

We now arrive at the second period of the history of **animal magnetism** <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>Also known as Mesmerism; the theory that an invisible natural force (a "fluid") possessed by all living things could be manipulated to heal or induce trance.</note>. The doctrine of the magnetic fluid, considered either as a universal fluid or as an emanation from the human organism—animal heat or electricity—had not been able to withstand scientific observation. The influence of the imagination on the production of these phenomena had struck all the commissioners of the learned societies. Deslon himself, the first student of Mesmer, had written in 1780: "If Mr. Mesmer had no other secret than that of making the imagination act effectively for health, would he not still have a very wonderful one? For if the medicine of the imagination were the best, why should we not practice the medicine of the imagination?"

Around 1815, an Indo-Portuguese priest <note>José Custódio de Faria (1756–1819), a pioneer in the study of hypnosis who moved away from the idea of "magnetic fluids."</note> coming from the Indies, who became famous under the name of Abbé Faria, professed in speeches of a bizarre form, marked by mystical ideas, that the cause of somnambulism resides in the subject and not in the magnetizer, against whose will the sleep can occur. Every day he gathered about sixty people at his home; he attempted his experiments on eight or ten of them and among this number, one, two, sometimes more, fell into somnambulism ¹.

# ABBÉ FARIA #

The person to be magnetized being seated in an armchair, he would invite them to close their eyes and collect their thoughts. Then, suddenly, in a strong and imperative voice, he would say: "Sleep," repeating this order if necessary three or four times. The subject, after a slight tremor, would sometimes fall into the state that Faria referred to as *lucid sleep* <term>lucid sleep</term> <note>original: *sommeil lucide*; a trance state where Faria believed the subject gained heightened clarity or "lucidity."</note>.

The doctrine of suggestion was thus created, at least as the mechanism for inducing sleep, if not yet as the full interpretation for the so-called "lucid" phenomena manifested during this sleep.

In 1819, a former student of the *Polytechnic School* <term>École polytechnique</term> <note>France's most prestigious engineering school, known for its rigorous scientific curriculum.</note> and a Doctor of Medicine, Alexandre Bertrand, announced a public course on animal magnetism. At that time, he attributed all the observed effects to the properties of a magnetic fluid; he was a mesmerist.

At the same time, an officer who became General <note>The text likely refers to General Noizet, who was influential in this era of magnetic study.</note>

<margin>they performed sleight-of-hand tricks, and they regarded as accomplices all the people on whom the experiments were successful. If it happened that, in a group of several people, one of them experienced some effects, fell asleep, and became a somnambulist, this result at first astonished those who could not doubt its reality; but later, the impression became less strong, and the power of the word *charlatan* was so great that soon everything that had been seen was forgotten. Even the person who had experienced these effects would delude themselves like the others, ending up believing that nothing extraordinary had happened within them. The shame of having something in common with a man called a *charlatan* <note>In the 19th century, being labeled a "charlatan" could destroy a person's social and professional standing entirely.</note> often led to the truth being denied, and people dared to claim that they had made a game of deceiving the assembly and the performer himself. What I state here should not surprise anyone who knows the weaknesses of the human heart, and I have been all the more struck by it because I have had the opportunity to verify it myself.</margin>

> "Finally, one day it happened that an actor actually played the role of somnambulism and deceived Abbé Faria. From that moment on, the cry of charlatanism grew even louder, as if it were the mark of a charlatan to expose himself to such mistakes and let himself be caught by a stranger. People stopped following his experiments, and it became a matter of ridicule to believe in them. I believe in them, however, and I shall never blush to proclaim the truth. I do not declare myself the champion of Abbé Faria, whom I barely knew; I do not know what his morality might have been, but I am certain that he produced the effects I have reported."

<page-num>120</page-num>

-> # BERTRAND AND GENERAL NOIZET # <-

Noizet, a disciple of Abbé Faria <note>Abbé Faria (1756–1819) was a pioneer of the scientific study of hypnotism who argued that "magnetic" effects came from the subject's mind, not a physical fluid.</note>, deeply struck by the facts he had witnessed, did not accept the existence of a fluid. He recognized no power other than that of the imagination—the conviction of the person experiencing the effects.

He formed a connection with Bertrand, whom he eventually converted to his ideas.

> "Perhaps too much," adds General Noizet, "in the sense that he even rejects the little I had retained of his system."

Bertrand's definitive ideas were presented in his *Treatise on Somnambulism and the Different Modifications it Presents* <note>original title: *Traité du somnambulisme et des différentes modifications qu'il présente*</note>, written in 1823. He argued that the cause of these phenomena was due to a particular form of nervous exaltation, which the author designated as **ecstasy**. According to him, it was this state that produced the "possessed" women of Loudun <note>The Loudun possessions of 1634 involved a group of nuns who experienced mass hysteria, which Bertrand interpreted as a psychological rather than a demonic phenomenon.</note>, those magnetized at Mesmer's tub <term>tub</term> <note>original: *baquet*; a large wooden vat filled with water and iron filings that Franz Mesmer used to concentrate what he believed was "animal magnetism."</note>, and somnambulists. This nervous state is characterized by insensibility, moral inertia, forgetfulness upon waking, an instinct for remedies, the communication of thoughts, sight without the use of eyes, and an exaltation of the imagination.

A singular thing! While General Noizet was winning Bertrand over to his initial concepts, Noizet himself—dominated by his spiritualist ideas and seeking to reconcile the two diverging opinions (fluidist and anti-fluidist)—soon fell back into the fluidist doctrine. It is through the hypothesis of a **vital fluid** that the author explains the interesting phenomena he relates in a memoir sent in 1820 to the Royal Academy of Berlin (*Memoir on Somnambulism and Animal Magnetism*. Paris, 1854).

While the doctrine of suggestion had its precursors, it was not definitively established and demonstrated until 1841 by James Braid of Manchester¹. It is to him that we owe the discovery of **hypnotism**, and the terms *braidism* and *braidic suggestion* have remained in scientific vocabulary.

<page-num>121</page-num>

<header>JAMES BRAID</header>

...to establish the new doctrine that has arisen in opposition to Mesmerism <note>Mesmerism was the theory of "animal magnetism" proposed by Franz Mesmer, which suggested an invisible fluid connected all living things.</note>.

Braid has proven that no magnetic fluid exists, nor any mysterious force emanating from the hypnotist; the hypnotic state and the phenomena it involves have a purely subjective source within the nervous system of the subject themselves. The fixation on a bright object, coupled with the fatigue of the muscles that lift the upper eyelid <term>levator palpebrae superioris</term> and the concentration of attention on a single idea, induces sleep. Subjects can plunge themselves into this state without any external influence through their own mental tension. In this state, their imagination becomes so vivid that any idea developed spontaneously, or suggested by a person to whom they give particular attention and trust, takes on the full force of current reality. The more frequently these phenomena are induced, the easier and more convenient it becomes to induce them; such is the law of association and habit. The will of the hypnotist, if not expressed through speech or gestures understood by the subject, does not trigger any phenomenon. The physical posture given to the hypnotized person—the state in which one places the muscles of the limbs or the face—can give rise to the feelings, passions, and acts corresponding to these anatomical positions, just as the suggestion of certain feelings or passions creates the correlated physical attitude or mimetic expression.

This part of Braid’s work remains unassailable: observation confirms it in every respect. But is the same true of those phreno-hypnotic <note>Phreno-hypnotism was a practice combining hypnosis with phrenology, the now-discredited "science" that claimed personality traits were located in specific areas of the brain that could be felt as bumps on the skull.</note> experiments, where he claims that by manipulating the neck and face, he can excite certain bodily and mental manifestations depending on the parts touched? Does he thus stimulate, via the sensory nerves of the head, localized organs of the brain corresponding to various passions—benevolence, imitation, theft, etc.?

I believe, along with Brown-Séquard <note>Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (1817–1894) was a famous Mauritian-born physiologist and neurologist known for his work on the spinal cord and "rejuvenation" experiments.</note>, "that Braid did not protect himself from causes arising from suggestions..."
