...when he believed he found proofs of the truth of phrenological doctrines <note>Phrenology was the 19th-century theory that the shape of the skull indicated a person's mental faculties and character traits.</note> among his hypnotized subjects. For those who know that a single word pronounced at a sufficient distance from a hypnotized subject can suggest an entire series of ideas, or develop the most varied feelings or actions, it is easy to understand how Braid committed the errors I am pointing out $^1$."

It seems to me, moreover, that Braid, at the end of his life, conceived a doubt regarding his earlier experiments relating to phreno-hypnotism <note>Braid's earlier attempt to combine phrenology with hypnotism, believing that touching specific parts of the head could trigger specific emotions.</note>. In his last memoir addressed to the Academy of Sciences in 1860, on the occasion of the experiments of Azam and Broca <note>Étienne Eugène Azam and Paul Broca were prominent French physicians whose reports on surgical anesthesia via hypnotism sparked a major revival of Braid's theories in France.</note>—a remarkable memoir that summarizes his work—he passes over his phreno-hypnotic research in silence; he limits himself to saying that his experiments on emotional phenomena triggered by contact with the scalp led him to conclude that the results obtained neither proved nor invalidated phrenological organology <term>organology</term> <note>The phrenological study of specific areas of the brain supposedly governing different mental faculties.</note>: he explains his error regarding a correlation he had supposed to exist between the frontal tissue and memory by the fact that touching the forehead of a hypnotized subject triggers a more effective suggestion by dissipating distraction and daydreams, allowing them to focus their attention more closely on the question and respond correctly.

Braid’s experiments did not cause a great stir in England; in France, they were barely known.

It was in America that the doctrine of magnetism would reappear under a new name. This doctrine, designated by Grimes under the name of *electro-biology* <note>A 19th-century term for a form of hypnotism where suggestions were made while the subject was supposedly in an "electrical" state of the nervous system.</note>, was spread in the United States by a multitude of professors, most of whom—says Dr. Phillips, from whom I borrow these details on electro-biology—were unfortunately not up to the level of a scientific mission. <header>DOCTRINE OF DURAND DE GROS</header>

obscure to move the medical public; then, in 1860, his *Theoretical and Practical Course on Braidism or Nervous Hypnotism* appeared, in which the author's thought and method emerge with great clarity.

Braid had established that the fixity of attention and the concentration of thought obtained by the fixation of the gaze are the determining causes of the hypnotic state; but he did not seek to delve into the physiological or psychological mechanism of the phenomenon. Durand de Gros <note>Joseph-Pierre Durand de Gros (1826–1900), a French physiologist and psychologist who wrote under the pseudonym Dr. Philips.</note> tries to go further and explain the link that exists between this concentration of thought—the first starting point of the Braidic modification—and the appearance of insensibility, of <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A physical state where a person's limbs remain in whatever position they are placed, often associated with trances.</note>, of ecstasy, in a word, of this profound and general revolution of the economy <note>In 19th-century medicine, "economy" refers to the organized system or "machinery" of the living body.</note> which is its point of arrival.

Here is the author's theory, as set forth by him: A general and sufficiently intense activity of thought is necessary for the regular distribution of nerve force in the nerves of sensitivity. If this activity ceases, their innervation is suppressed, and they lose their ability to conduct external impressions toward the brain. We know, in fact, that idiots <note>A historical medical term used in the 19th century to describe individuals with significant intellectual disabilities, whom the author claims had reduced physical sensitivity.</note> are more or less anesthetic, etc. On the other hand, sensation is the necessary stimulant of mental activity.

From this it follows that, to determine insensibility, it is enough to suspend the exercise of thought, and to suspend this, it is necessary to isolate the senses from the external agents that affect them. One cannot suspend thought, but one can reduce it to a minimum by subjecting it to the exclusive stimulation of a simple, homogeneous, and continuous sensation. One thus reduces its sphere of action to a single point. The cerebral cell continues to secrete nerve force; thought no longer consumes more than a small part of this force; this force accumulates in the brain where a "nervous congestion" will take place. This is the first part of the Braidic operation which produces what the author calls the *hypotaxic state* <term>hypotaxic state</term> <note>A term coined by Durand de Gros to describe a preliminary stage of hypnosis where the nervous system is highly concentrated and primed for suggestion.</note>. This state once produced, whether by a door still left ajar in the sensorium <note>The parts of the brain that receive and interpret sensory stimuli.</note>, by way of sight, of hearing, of the mus-

...cular, an impression slips through to the brain, and the point upon which this excitation acts will immediately emerge from its torpor to become the seat of an activity that the tension of <term>nerve force</term> <note>A 19th-century medical concept suggesting the nervous system is powered by a specific energy or "fluid."</note> will increase with all its weight. It is then that the general cessation of <term>innervation</term> <note>The distribution or supply of nervous energy to a body part.</note> will suddenly be succeeded by an excessive local innervation which, for example, will instantly substitute <term>hyperesthesia</term> <note>An extreme, often painful, sensitivity to touch or other stimuli.</note> for insensitivity, and <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of muscular rigidity where limbs remain in whatever position they are placed.</note>, tetanus, etc., for the relaxation of the muscular system.

The available nerve force can be summoned to this or that functional point of the center of innervation by directing toward this point an impression that awakens its own specific activity. For this purpose, a mental impression is employed—that is to say, a suggested idea. This is the second stage of the Braidic operation <note>Referring to "Braidism," the early term for hypnotism named after James Braid.</note> that Durand de Gros calls *ideoplasty* <note>The process by which a suggested idea is transformed into a physical effect.</note>. The idea becomes the determining cause of the functional modifications to be provoked: mental excitation reproduces the sensations previously provoked by organic excitations; these sensations, regenerated by an idea, are called memorative.

The experiments of Doctor Philips (Durand de Gros) did not succeed in lifting the discredit into which magnetism had fallen with the medical public; Braidism remained forgotten. One must, however, cite D<gloss>r</gloss> Charpignon of Orléans, who, starting in 1841, had busied himself greatly with magnetism and "moral medicine" <note>An early term for psychological therapy or treatment involving the patient's mind and willpower.</note> in the treatment of nervous diseases. His memoir, titled: *On the Role of Moral Medicine in the Treatment of Nervous Diseases* (1862) <note>original: "De la Part de la Médecine morale dans le traitement des maladies nerveuses"</note>, was honorably mentioned by the Academy of Medicine; the phenomena of hypnotic suggestion and suggestion in the waking state that are set forth there thus obtained, for the first time, the official sanction of this learned body; this was, in reality, a reversal of the summary decision of October 1, 1840 <note>The date the French Academy of Medicine had previously decided to stop researching animal magnetism.</note>. This memoir was published in 1864 under the title: *Studies on Animic and Vitalist Medicine* <note>original: "Etudes sur la médecine animique et vitaliste"; "Animic" refers to the soul, and "Vitalist" refers to the belief in a non-physical life force.</note>.

One must also mention Victor Meunier, who, as early as 1852, in the journal *The Press* <note>original: "la Presse"</note>, had the scientific courage to popularize experiments that official science condemned at the time.

In 1859, Braidism <note>The early term for hypnotism, named after the Scottish surgeon James Braid, who sought to move the practice away from "mystical" animal magnetism toward a physiological explanation.</note> truly made its entrance into France; a communication from Professor Azam, of Bordeaux, to the Society of Surgery, published in the *Archives of Medicine* <note>original: "Archives de médecine"</note> (1860), gave it a great, though fleeting, resonance. Having learned of the phenomena provoked by the English doctor through one of his colleagues who had read the article *Sleep* <note>original: "Sommeil"</note> by Carpenter in *Todd’s Cyclopaedia* <note>referring to the "Cyclopaedia of Anatomy and Physiology" edited by Robert Bentley Todd.</note>, he successfully repeated these experiments on several healthy people.

Demarquay and Giraud-Teulon (*Research on Hypnotism or Nervous Sleep* <note>original: "Recherches sur l’hypnotisme ou sommeil nerveux"</note>, Paris, 1860), and Gigot-Suard (*The Mysteries of Animal Magnetism and Magic Unveiled, or the Truth Demonstrated by Hypnotism* <note>original: "Les Mystères du magnétisme animal et de la magie dévoilés ou la Vérité démontrée par l’hypnotisme"</note>, Paris, 1860), published interesting observations. Surgeons primarily sought in hypnotism a means of <term>anesthesia</term> <note>The practice of inducing a loss of sensation or consciousness to prevent pain during surgery.</note> suitable for replacing chloroform <note>A chemical anesthetic that was effective but often dangerous or even fatal in the 19th century.</note>; a satisfactory observation (concerning the incision of an anal abscess by Broca <note>Paul Broca, the famous French physician best known for his research on the brain's speech center.</note> and Follin) was presented, in 1859, to the Academy of Sciences. A few days later, Dr. Guérineau, of Poitiers, announced to the Academy of Medicine that he had amputated a thigh during hypnotic anesthesia (*Hospital Gazette* <note>original: "Gaz. des hôpitaux"</note>, 1859).

The application of hypnotism to surgical anesthesia was, moreover, not a new thing. # APPLICATION TO SURGICAL ANESTHESIA

...by Dr. Loysel, of Cherbourg; in 1845, the amputation of two thighs by Drs. Fanton and Toswel, of London; in 1845, the amputation of an arm by Dr. Joly, in London; in 1847, the removal of a jaw tumor by Dr. Ribaud and Kiaro, a dentist in Poitiers.

Despite these successful attempts, surgeons soon observed that hypnotism only rarely succeeds as an anesthetic; absolute insensibility <term>insensibility: the total loss of physical feeling or pain, necessary for surgery before the invention of modern chemical anesthetics</term> is the exception among hypnotizable subjects, and hypnotization itself most often fails in people who are distressed by the anticipation of an operation. Braidism, appearing to lack practical interest, fell back into oblivion.

If Lasègue had pursued his research further, he might have definitively revived Braidism. In a memoir titled *On Partial and Temporary Catalepsies* <note>original: "Des Catalepsies partielles et passagères"</note> (*General Archives of Medicine* <note>original: "Arch. génér. de médecine"</note>, 1865), he notes that the simple closing of the eyes in certain hysterical patients—and even in some men not suffering from hysteria—determines varying degrees of sleep, ranging from simple numbness to complete lethargy with anesthesia. These various states are accompanied by a cataleptic rigidity <term>cataleptic rigidity: a physical state where a person's limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed, as if the muscles have turned to wax</term> of the limbs, which ceases abruptly as soon as the awakened patient regains their sense of sight.

But Lasègue went no further; he did not think to identify these phenomena with those of hypnotic sleep, as Braid had described it.

In 1866, Dr. Liébeault, who had been studying the question for many years, published a book titled *On Sleep and Analogous States Considered Especially from the Point of View of the Action of the Mind on the Body* <note>original: "Du Sommeil et des états analogues considérés surtout au point de vue de l'action du moral sur le physique"</note>; it is the most important work published on Braidism. A proponent of the doctrine of suggestion <note>The idea that the hypnotist's words or influence can trigger physical or mental changes in the patient.</note>—which he pushed further than Braid and applied successfully to therapeutics—and an enemy of the supernatural and mysticism, the author seeks to interpret the observed phenomena through psycho-physiological perspectives.

His doctrine is similar to that of Durand de Gros: the concentration of thought on a single idea—that of sleeping—facilitated by fixing one's gaze, leads to

# DOCTRINE OF LIÉBEAULT

the immobilization of the body, the deadening of the senses, their isolation from the outer world, and finally the cessation of thought and the unchanging nature of states of consciousness. Suggestive catalepsy <term>suggestive catalepsy: a state where a patient's limbs remain in any position the hypnotist places them, driven here by the "suggestion" or command of the doctor</term> is the consequence of this cessation of thought: the hypnotized person remains, with a fixed idea, in rapport <term>rapport: a specialized psychological connection where the subject remains sensitive only to the hypnotist while ignoring other people or distractions</term> with the person who put them to sleep, whom they hear and from whom they receive impressions. Incapable by themselves of passing from one idea to another, their mind sticks to the idea that is finally suggested to them; and from the moment it is, for example, that of having the arms extended, they keep them extended.

Ordinary sleep does not differ fundamentally from hypnotic sleep: both are due to the immobilization of attention and nervous force <note>19th-century scientists believed "nervous force" was a physical energy or fluid that moved through the body to power thought and movement</note> on the idea of sleeping. The individual who wants to sleep isolates their senses, withdraws into themselves, and remains immobile; the nervous influx, concentrating so to speak on one point of the brain—on a single idea—abandons the sensory, motor, and sensitive nerves.

But the ordinary sleeper, once their state of consciousness is immobilized, is no longer in rapport with anyone but *themselves*; the impressions brought to the brain by the nerves of sensitivity or the nerves of organic life can awaken various sensations or memorial images which constitute dreams. These dreams are spontaneous, that is to say, suggested by the self.

The hypnotized sleeper falls asleep with the idea immobilized *in rapport with the one who put them to sleep*; hence the possibility for this foreign will to suggest dreams, ideas, and acts to them.

Forgetfulness upon waking after deep hypnotism <note>This refers to "post-hypnotic amnesia," where a subject cannot remember what happened during the trance</note> comes from the fact that all the nervous force accumulated in the brain during sleep is diffused again throughout the organism upon waking; as this force decreases in the brain, it is then impossible—with a lesser quantity of it—for the subject who has returned to themselves to grasp again in their memory what they were conscious of before.

In ordinary sleep, or in light hypnotism, the nervous force accumulated toward the seat of the idea...

<summary>Dr. Liébeault explains that hypnotic sleep and ordinary sleep are physiologically similar, differing only in "rapport"—the mental connection between the subject and the hypnotist that allows for external suggestion.</summary>

# THE HYPNOTIC STATE IN ANIMALS

fixed point is less intense; the other parts of the nervous system are not as inactive; dreams are brought about by peripheral impressions <note>Sensory inputs from the limbs or skin, like a touch or a sound, rather than internal thoughts</note>. Furthermore, waking is not sudden, but progressive; the nervous force accumulated in the brain gradually decreases, and when the movement of thought begins to establish itself, it recovers memories of at least the end of the sleep.

The work of the physician of Nancy <note>Referring to Dr. Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), the founder of the Nancy School of hypnotism</note> went unnoticed: hypnotism remained a mere scientific curiosity. People were satisfied with knowing that the fixation of a bright object produces sleep with anesthesia <note>A loss of physical sensation or pain</note> in certain subjects, and in some, <term>catalepsy</term> <note>catalepsy: a condition where a person’s limbs remain in whatever position they are placed, as if the muscles have become wax-like</note>, and researchers did not push their investigations any further.

In Germany, Czermak¹ published his observations on the hypnotic state obtained in animals in 1873. As early as 1646, Athanasius Kircher had shown that a hen, placed with its legs tied before a line drawn on the ground, remains motionless after a certain amount of time; it retains this attitude even when the binding is removed and it is stimulated. Czermak obtained the same phenomenon without the binding and without drawing a line on the ground; it is enough to hold the animal motionless for some time, with the neck and head gently extended over the abdomen. Other animals—birds, salamanders, crayfish, pigeons, rabbits, sparrows—were hypnotized, some <term>cataleptized</term>, by the simple fixation of an object, such as a finger or a match, placed before their eyes.

Preyer² considered this state to be caused by fear and called it <term>cataplexy</term> <note>cataplexy: here used to describe a "tonic immobility" or playing dead, a state of paralysis triggered by extreme shock or fright</note>. The tightening of newts when they are seized, the effects of lightning, the shock experienced by patients during surgery, paralysis due to fright, and the stupor of animals wounded by a firearm, were all seen as phenomena analogous to those produced by the hypnotization of animals; they were said to be due to the excitation of the moderating apparatuses—

### EXPERIMENTS OF CHARLES RICHET

In horses, similar hypnotic states have been observed. A Hungarian, Constantin Balassa¹, had pointed out, in 1828, a method for shoeing horses without force:

> "By staring at it squarely, the horse is led to back up, to lift its head, to stiffen the cervical column <note>The vertebrae of the neck</note>, and one can so overawe some of them to such an extent that they do not move, even if a gunshot is fired in the vicinity. Gentle friction with the hand, in a cross pattern on the forehead and eyes, would also be a precious auxiliary means to calm and drowse the gentlest horse, as well as the most violent."

In 1839, Dr. Wilson, in England, produced this state which he called *trance* on the animals at the London Zoological Garden; finally, more recently, in 1881, Beard, in Boston, compared these so-called trance or "trancoidal" phenomena in animals to human hypnotism and showed that they can be obtained by various methods: fear (a fixed posture imposed on animals that makes them unable to resist, lying them on their backs, or binding them), magnetic passes <note>Hand movements made by a practitioner near the subject's body, once thought to transmit a 'magnetic' fluid</note>, staring into their eyes, bright light (as seen in fishing with torches or insects attracted to a flame), or music. All of these are methods that disturb the psychic balance by concentrating cerebral activity toward a single idea².

In 1875, Charles Richet³ resumed experiments on humans and once again studied induced somnambulism <note>A state of deep trance or "sleepwalking" brought on by hypnosis</note>; he showed that through so-called magnetic passes, through the fixation of a shiny object, and other procedures...

### EXPERIMENTS OF CHARCOT

Although difficult to achieve the first time, it almost always occurs if one has the patience to conduct several sessions; according to Richet, this magnetic neuropathy would, moreover, offer few therapeutic applications.

This author had the merit of recalling the medical world's attention to hypnotic phenomena; he is one of those who best studied and highlighted the psychological phenomena of somnambulism.

In 1878, Charcot¹ studied induced somnambulism in hysterical patients. These memorable research studies are well known: the production of <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A trance-like state where the person remains in a fixed position with rigid muscles</note> accompanied by anesthesia through the fixation of a bright light, and, in this state, the phenomena of suggestion—that is to say, the physical posture imposed on the limbs being reflected by the expression of the face (a smile, or a look of prayer). He also noted the sudden disappearance of light replacing the catalepsy with a sleep characterized by muscle relaxation or <term>lethargy</term> <note>In this clinical context, a deep state of unconsciousness where the muscles are completely limp</note>, the muscular hyperexcitability manifesting in this state (the contraction of a muscle by light stimulation of it or its nerve)—and finally, the friction of the vertex <note>The top of the head</note> transforming this lethargic state into somnambulism, with the possibility of walking, responding, etc.

Bourneville and Regnard retraced and illustrated these experiments in the *Iconography of the Salpêtrière* <note>A famous collection of photographs and descriptions documenting patients and clinical states at the hospital</note>. Charcot and his students did not formulate any theory for the interpretation of these phenomena. We also know of the interesting experiments communicated by Dumontpallier to the Society of Biology.

### GERMAN THEORIES

[...ly] to his experiments, he found four or five susceptible to being put into <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of physical rigidity where a person's limbs remain in whatever position they are placed</note> and receiving all sorts of suggestions. These experiments were repeated by professors in university towns: in Chemnitz by Weinhold, Ruhlmann, and Opitz; in Breslau by Heidenhain, Grützner, Berger, and others¹.

Various theories arose: some were purely physiological, such as that of Rumpf², who assumed reflex changes in the cerebral circulation giving rise to phenomena of cerebral <term>hyperemia</term> <note>An excess of blood flow to the brain</note> or <term>anemia</term> <note>A decrease in blood flow to the brain</note>. Others were purely chemical, such as that of Preyer³, who believed that the concentration of thought causes an exaggerated activity of brain cells. This activity would result in easily oxidizable products, such as <term>lactates</term> <note>Compounds like lactic acid produced during metabolic activity</note>, which numb the brain by withdrawing oxygen from its various regions. However, the speed with which one enters hypnosis and the instantaneous nature of the awakening do not align well with these chemical theories.

Finally, other doctrines are psycho-physiological. Schneider, in Leipzig, sought to interpret these phenomena through the exclusive and abnormal concentration of consciousness on a single idea. According to him, intellectual excitement, the exaggerated sharpness of the senses, and the vividness of the imagination are due to the fact that all psychic activity, instead of being spread over a wide area, is concentrated on a small number of points⁴. This theoretical view had already been put forward in France, as we have previously seen,

### THE DOCTRINE OF PROSPER DESPINE
8
<meta>catchword: SUGGESTION.</meta>

...by Durand de Gros and Liébeault. Berger, from Breslau, also believes that the concentration of the entire thinking being on a single idea gives rise to an inertia of the will that constitutes the core of the hypnotic state; **cataleptiform** <term>cataleptiform</term> <note>Resembling catalepsy, a condition where the body remains in a fixed, rigid posture</note> rigidity would be a concurrent phenomenon caused by the fact that psychological excitement spreads to the **excito-motor centers** <note>The parts of the brain that trigger muscle movement</note> of the brain.

Heidenhain, of Breslau, putting forward a similar view, suggests that the weak and continuous stimulation of the sensory nerves—whether acoustic or optical—leads to a suspension of activity in the cells of the **cerebral cortex** <note>The outer layer of the brain associated with higher-level thought and consciousness</note>. To this is added an excitement of the motor reflex centers lying beneath the cortex, either because the cortex is paralyzed and its ability to moderate reflexes is missing, or because, due to this same paralysis, any sensory stimulation transmitted to the brain spreads within a more limited nervous area and therefore acts more effectively on that excito-motor domain.

Mr. Espinas, a professor at the Faculty of Arts in Bordeaux, developed similar psychological views. Studying sleep specifically in **hysterics** <note>In the 19th century, "hysteria" was a common medical diagnosis for a wide range of psychological and physical symptoms, often attributed to nervous system instability</note>, he suggests that these subjects possess a state of unstable equilibrium in the nervous system and a subsequent prompt exhaustion of the higher centers under the influence of prolonged or depressing sensations¹.

# RECENT STUDIES

...without any "self," without personality. Psychological faculties can, in certain pathological brain states, manifest in the absence of the self, the mind, or consciousness, and produce acts similar to those normally manifested by the initiative of the self. This is automatic cerebral activity; that which, on the contrary, manifests the "self" is conscious cerebral activity. In the normal state, these two activities are intimately linked to each other; they form but one and always manifest together; in certain pathological nervous states, they can separate and act in isolation.

Somnambulism <note>In this 19th-century context, "somnambulism" refers both to sleepwalking and the deep hypnotic trance state</note> is characterized, physiologically, by the exercise of the brain's automatic activity alone during the paralysis of its conscious activity. The somnambulist's ignorance of everything they did during somnambulism does not, therefore, come from forgetting, but from the non-participation of the "self" in their actions. We shall see in the following chapter if this opinion is well-founded.

Admitting the (hypothetical!) doctrine of Luys <note>Jules Bernard Luys (1828–1897), a French neurologist who sought to map specific mental functions to layers of the brain</note> that the different layers of the cortical gray matter have different functions—that the most superficial governs the **sensorium** <term>sensorium</term> <note>The sensory apparatus of the body as a whole, through which an individual perceives the environment</note>, the middle layer the intellectual faculties, and the deepest the transmission of the will for action—the author believes it necessary to deduce that active somnambulism would be physiologically determined by the nervous paralysis of the most superficial layer of the gray matter of the **convolutions** <note>The folds or ridges on the surface of the brain, also known as gyri</note>, with the persistence of activity in the middle and deep layers; but if the middle layer is also paralyzed, one has inactive somnambulism, which manifests no psychological faculty.

In a study by D<gloss>octor</gloss> Ladame, of Geneva, published in 1881 titled: *Hypnotic Neurosis, or Magnetism Unveiled* <note>Original title: "La Névrose hypnotique ou le Magnétisme dévoilé"</note>, one finds a very well-executed, clear, and complete account of the question as it presented itself at that time. Let us also note a publication by Mr. Emile Yung, of Geneva, appearing in 1883, titled:

# ON AUTOMATISM

...sees only what he sees, does only what he wants, and obeys only his own spontaneous and personal suggestions! That is the first impression. And yet, if one reflects a little, one soon becomes convinced that the contradiction is not absolute; nature does not deviate from its laws; those that govern the normal organism also govern the organism modified experimentally and pathologically.

Many acts are performed automatically, without our will or without our consciousness, in our habitual life. The specific functions of the spinal cord are carried out without our knowledge; the complex phenomena of vegetative life <note>The basic biological functions that sustain life without conscious effort</note>—circulation, respiration, nutrition, secretion, excretions, the movements of the digestive tract, the living chemistry of the organism—operate silently through a mechanism of which we are not conscious. It is known that the impression transmitted by a sensory nerve can be reflected through the gray horns <note>Referring to the "cornes grises," the interior sections of the spinal cord that process signals</note> of the spinal cord, without passing through the brain; movement follows the unperceived impression, or the sensation, without being willed: this is the <term>spinal reflex act</term>; it is spinal automatism that commands this movement. Tickling the sole of the foot determines reflex movements, even when a damaged spinal cord no longer allows the transmission of stimuli to the brain; a decapitated frog continues to execute adapted, appropriate, defensive movements with its four limbs and its trunk; one places a drop of acetic acid <note>A common chemical used in 19th-century physiology experiments to test nerve reactions</note> on the upper thigh, and the hind limb flexes so that the foot comes to rub the irritated spot; one presses the region of the flanks between the jaws of a pair of forceps, the frog brings the tip of its corresponding hind limb in front of the forceps, presses the toes of that limb, and seeks—sometimes repeatedly—to push it away with force (Vulpian) <note>Alfred Vulpian (1826–1887) was a prominent French physician and physiologist known for his work on the nervous system</note>. Here, the brain does not intervene; the animal machinery, unconscious of itself, is sufficient to carry out the complex acts intended to protect the organism against attacks from the outside. ## REFLEX ACTIONS

...a person when, deeply absorbed in profound meditation—"functionally decapitated," as Mathias Duval says—swats away a fly that lands on his hand or moves an annoying object without being conscious of it and without retaining any memory of it, through the action of simple, perfectly coordinated <term>medullary reflexes</term> <note>Reflexes controlled by the spinal cord or the medulla, rather than the conscious brain</note>.

The brain may provide the initial impulse; the act then continues while the thoughts and the will are occupied elsewhere, driven solely by <term>spinal automatism</term> <note>The body's ability to perform complex physical movements automatically without conscious direction from the brain</note>. When we walk and various ideas distract our minds, we forget that we are walking, yet the journey continues by simple reflex; the contact of the sole of the foot with the ground is enough to trigger, through a centrifugal path in the spinal cord, the phenomena of <term>muscular coordination</term> that carry out this act. Relieved by this subordinate automatic mechanism of the duty to constantly monitor the execution of this complex function, our brain works with complete freedom on other concepts; mechanically, we keep walking, so much so that we may overshoot the goal assigned by the will that commanded the first step, if the latter—taking a break from our distractions—does not intervene to stop the impulse. It is the same with swimming, fencing, horse-riding, and music. An artist performing a long piece of music often allows themselves to be absorbed by outside ideas; their thought is no longer on the music; their fingers still wander over the keyboard and mechanically continue—under the influence of spinal stimuli linking together spontaneously—what the distracted brain no longer directs.

Furthermore, what the psychic organ <note>Referring here to the brain as the seat of conscious thought</note> has forgotten, spinal automatism can rediscover. An artist may no longer recall all the phrases of a musical composition; gaps exist in his mind; he would be unable to complete the piece using the hazy memories of his brain; yet, <term>spinal memory</term> <note>A historical term for what we now commonly call "muscle memory"</note> compensates, if I may say so, for <term>cerebral memory</term>; often the fingers rediscover on the keyboard the difficult arrangement of...

# AUTOMATISM IN THE NEWBORN

> ...mobile, the limbs and the torso sway in a thousand ways. This tendency, which invites mockery, is observed especially in women. <note>This reflects 19th-century medical biases that often associated "automatic" or "hysterical" physical behaviors more strongly with women.</note>

To these instinctive acts, let us add certain movements that may follow impressions received and perceived by the <term>sensorium</term> <note>The parts of the brain that receive and interpret sensory stimuli</note> and which are nonetheless due to automatic brain action. An unpleasant odor that makes us contract our nostrils, a sudden noise that makes us turn our head, a weapon pointed at us that makes us extend our hand to push it away—these are examples of defensive movements, adapted to the goal of repelling a danger or a hostile impression. The impression was perceived by the olfactory, auditory, or visual center; but it was perceived in its "raw" state, so to speak. It did not have the time to be processed or interpreted by the psychic centers of the cerebral hemispheres; the defensive movement was unconscious, non-deliberate, and involuntary. We were not free to *not* do it. From the sensory <term>medulla</term> <note>The author uses *noyau bulbaire* (bulbar nucleus), referring to the medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem responsible for automatic functions</note> where the impression was received, or from the sensory cortical center where it was perceived, the reflex reaction occurred instantaneously, before the will came into play, toward the motor centers corresponding to the complex movement to be carried out in the instinctive interest—that is to say, the unreflective interest—of self-preservation.

In the animal throughout its entire existence, as our distinguished friend Mr. Netter has well demonstrated in an excellent book¹, and in the newborn child, <term>cerebro-spinal activity</term> <note>The combined functioning of the brain and the spinal cord</note> is almost entirely automatic. The life of the nervous system is, in a sense, exclusively concentrated in the medulla, the spinal cord, and its intra-cerebral extensions. Voluntary determinations do not exist, and yet complicated acts, such as sucking, are accomplished by the sole reflex mechanism of the cerebro-spinal centers. # AUTOMATISM IN THE CHILD

...shown that the brain of the newborn, of gelatinous consistency and uniform gray coloration, contains barely a few sketched nerve tubes; the excitable parts of the brain, the so-called <term>psychomotor zone</term> <note>The area of the cerebral cortex involved in the planning, control, and execution of voluntary movements</note>, do not yet exist in humans and animals deprived of voluntary movements (Soltmann) <note>Otto Soltmann (1844–1912), a German pediatrician known for his research on the physiology of the central nervous system in infants</note>; the white coloration corresponding to the completed structure of the nerve tubes (the axon <note>Original: *cylindre-axe*</note> covered by its myelin sheath) will only appear later; anatomically and physiologically, the brain is embryonic. Then consciousness, the will, and the psychic faculties of the brain <note>Original: *encéphale*</note> come into play, developing gradually through the progress of age and education; the automatic cerebrospinal activity, which alone dominated the organism during the first months, and which predominates throughout existence in animals, becomes associated with conscious and reflective activity. Automatic phenomena always persist and are found in all acts of life, sometimes isolated, often dominated and modified by the state of consciousness. The child is impulsive <note>Original: *primesautier*, meaning acting on the first impulse without reflection</note>; he acts by instinct, which is to say he is entirely abandoned to his automatism; he leaps, laughs, cries, grimaces, and weeps at the whim of the impressions he receives; he sings when a familiar tune awakens in him the idea of singing. # AUTOMATISM IN THE ADULT

When the driving chords <note>Original: *cords*, likely an OCR error for *accords* (chords)</note> of a waltz vibrate in certain ears, does not the idea of dancing suggested to the brain tend to involuntarily produce the corresponding swaying of the body and limbs? One feels swept away, and for the slightest reason, one would let oneself go, if the state of consciousness developed by education, if the habit of a certain reserve imposed by social customs, if the attention concentrated on ourselves did not intervene as a moderator, as a regulator, to impose a brake on the **cerebral automatism** <term>cerebral automatism</term> <note>The 19th-century theory that the brain can execute complex movements or behaviors without the intervention of the conscious will</note> awakened by a **sensory suggestion**. Are not all the acts of our life, all our actions in the world, regulated by education and social conventions, the result of the mastery that our consciousness, directed by practice, has managed to take over the long term over our unthinking instincts, over our "beast" <note>Original: *notre bête*. This refers to the animalistic or primitive nature believed to reside within the human psyche</note>? In even the most enlightened man, the one most accustomed to self-mastery, it often happens that a perceived impression is so intense that it transforms into an automatic act before the moderating influence of consciousness has had time to prevent it. A soldier, violently shaken by a superior, loses control and strikes him; this physical assault <note>Original: *voie de fait*. A legal term for a physical act of aggression or violence</note> instantly follows the perceived impression: it is a **reflex act**. The soldier regrets it, for he exposes himself to a terrible punishment. But reason comes too late; anger is blind and does not reason.

The brain, as a **psychic organ** <note>In this period, the brain was often referred to as the physical organ through which the "psyche" or soul manifested its functions</note>, does not intervene only to moderate reflex action; it also intervenes to correct, to interpret, to rectify our impressions, whether they be impressions imperfectly transmitted by our sensory organs, or memory-based impressions <note>Original: *impressions mémoratives*</note> reviving directly as if in the...

-># HYPNAGOGIC HALLUCINATIONS<-

...the shock of reminiscence <note>The sudden, involuntary return of a memory or past impression</note>, or perhaps the impressions suggested by an external influence. The wind whistling through a crack provides the acoustic image of a groan; the psychic organ <note>A 19th-century term for the mental faculties or the parts of the brain responsible for processing thoughts and sensations</note> interprets it and restores it to its true cause; an imaginary vision surprises us during our daydreams; consciousness regains possession of itself and restores reality. Are we not all, through the imperfection of our conscious being and our sensory impressions, exposed to illusions, to varying suggestions? What happens in a dream—where our numbed senses no longer correct the incoherent ideas that arise, where the most fantastic things seem like realities, where we believe everything because judgment, being absent, no longer controls anything—this also happens to some during the period of psychic concentration that serves as a prelude to sleep. > “My hallucinations,” he says, “are more numerous and above all more vivid when I have—which is frequent for me—a tendency toward **cerebral congestion** <term>cerebral congestion</term> <note>A 19th-century medical diagnosis involving an excess of blood flow to the brain, believed to cause irritability or sensory disturbances</note>. The appearance of these hallucinations then brought me back to myself, and I resumed the course of my thoughts, only to fall back soon after into new visions, and this several times in succession until I was completely asleep. One day, I was able to observe these singular shifts. I was reading aloud a travelogue about southern Russia. I had barely finished a paragraph when I instinctively closed my eyes. In one of these short moments of sleepiness, I saw **hypnagogically** <term>hypnagogically</term> <note>occurring in the transitional state between wakefulness and sleep</note>, but with the speed of lightning, the image of a man dressed in a brown robe and wearing a hood like a monk from the paintings of Zurbaran <note>Francisco de Zurbarán (1598–1664) was a Spanish painter famous for his stark, realistic depictions of monks and religious figures</note>. This image immediately reminded me that I had closed my eyes and stopped reading; I suddenly reopened my eyelids, and I resumed my reading. The interruption was of such short duration that the person to whom I was reading did not notice it, etc. ¹. »

Who has not had these hallucinations, more or less clearly defined, when the attention withdraws from the objects on which it was fixed; when the mind, losing clear consciousness of the **self**, becomes the plaything of images evoked by the imagination? A stranger to the reality of things, it is entirely surrendered to the artificial concepts that obsess it, until consciousness, regaining possession of itself, dissipates these daydreams, erases the **chimeras** <note>In this context, "chimeras" refers to groundless illusions or fantastic fabrications of the mind</note> and re-establishes reality.

Our errors, our illusions, our hallucinations are not all spontaneous, born within ourselves, based on memory, or following a defective sensory impression; they can be suggested to us by other people; our brain, sometimes, accepts them without scrutiny.

Undoubtedly, when an order is formulated for us by someone who has no authority over us, the impression produced is too weak for our brain to carry it out automatically without evaluating its appropriateness; our judgment debates it, our reason fights the instinct of passive obedience. > "One evening," relates Maury <note>Alfred Maury (1817–1892) was a French physician and scholar whose self-observation of his own dreams was foundational to the study of the unconscious.</note>, "I had dozed off in my armchair; my ear still vaguely perceived sounds. I heard these words, it seems, but without realizing it was my brother who had said them; and in the dream I was having at the time, I imagined myself going to fetch a match. Waking up a few seconds later, I was told what my brother had said. I had already forgotten hearing it, even though I had responded to it at the moment; my response had been entirely mechanical. Yet, in the dream, I believed I was going to get a match of my own accord; I did not suspect I was carrying out an order."

## INCREASED IDEO-MOTOR EXCITABILITY

and the will are weakened: the more intense the sleep, the less spontaneity the sleepers have, and the more they are docile to suggestions; but this deep sleep, this weakening of the will and consciousness, are not necessary for the manifestation of suggestive phenomena. This important fact emerges, without question, from the preceding study.

The only certain thing is that there exists in hypnotized subjects, or those impressionable to suggestion, a particular aptitude for transforming a received idea into an act. In the normal state, every formulated idea is discussed by the brain, which only accepts it with the benefit of inventory <note>original: "sous bénéfice d'inventaire." A legal metaphor meaning the brain evaluates information before fully accepting it, much like an heir checks an estate's debts before accepting an inheritance.</note>; perceived by the cortical centers, the impression spreads, so to speak, to the cells of the neighboring convolutions <term>convolutions: the folds or ridges on the surface of the brain’s cerebral cortex</term>; their own activity is set in motion; the various faculties assigned to the gray matter of the brain intervene; the impression is processed, controlled, and analyzed by a complex cerebral labor that leads to its acceptance or its neutralization; the psychic organ opposes its veto to the injunction if necessary. In the hypnotized person, on the contrary, the transformation of the idea into an act, sensation, movement, or image occurs so quickly, so actively, that intellectual control does not have time to occur; when the psychic organ intervenes, it records an accomplished fact <note>original: "fait accompli"</note> often with surprise, which it confirms by the very fact of observing its reality, and its intervention can no longer prevent it. If I say to the hypnotized person: "Your hand remains closed," the brain realizes the idea as soon as it is formulated. From the cortical center where this idea—introduced via the auditory nerve—is perceived, a reflex occurs immediately toward the motor center corresponding to the central origins of the flexor nerves of the hand; the flexion into a contracture <note>A state of prolonged muscular contraction.</note> is achieved. There is therefore *an exaltation of the ideo-motor reflex excitability which carries out the unconscious transformation, unbeknownst to the will, of the idea into movement.*

## IDEO-SENSORY AND SENSORY EXCITABILITY

[...received] through hearing is reflected upon the center of olfactory <note>relating to the sense of smell</note> sensitivity, where it reawakens the sensory memory-image of a nasal tingling, just as previous impressions created it and left it as a latent imprint; this memory-sensation, thus revived, can be intense enough to trigger the reflex act of sneezing. There is, therefore, also an intensification of the *ideo-sensitive or ideo-sensory reflex excitability, which brings about the unconscious transformation of the idea into a sensation or sensory image*.

The visual, acoustic, and gustatory <note>relating to the sense of taste</note> images likewise follow the suggested idea.

The negative suggestions <note>A "negative suggestion" is a command given to a subject to *not* perceive something that is actually present, such as telling them they cannot see a specific person in the room or feel a specific pain.</note> are more difficult to conceive. If I say to the hypnotized subject: "Your body is insensitive, your eye is blind," the impression propagated by the auditory nerve to the center of tactile or visual sensitivity creates the image of tactile or visual anesthesia <term>anesthesia: a temporary loss of sensation or awareness</term>; the skin nerves receive the stimulation; the retina receives the image; retinal vision exists, and the light makes the pupil contract; but the cerebral perception of the tactile impression or the retinal image no longer exists. It appears that this is a *reflex paralysis of a cortical center produced by the suggested idea in this case*. Such nervous "stopping" actions are, moreover, well known—if not well explained—in physiology and pathology: stimulation of the pneumogastric nerve <term>pneumogastric nerve: now more commonly called the Vagus nerve, it carries signals between the brain and the heart, lungs, and digestive tract</term> stops the heartbeat; a violent emotion paralyzes; a profound trauma produces bodily insensibility (surgical stupor); speech fails under the effect of a vivid impression; and sudden functional blindness manifests in cases of hysteria.

The organism possesses dynamic mechanisms by which a property or activity can be suddenly suspended; this is what Brown-Séquard <note>Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (1817–1894) was a pioneering physiologist and neurologist who identified the "inhibition" of nervous functions.</note> calls *inhibition*; conversely, these properties or activities can be reinforced, which Brown-Séquard calls *dynamogeny* <term>dynamogeny: the production or increase of nervous energy or functional activity in an organ</term>. "This inhibitory or dynamogenic faculty belongs to many parts of the nervous system, and it can be put into play either in a direct manner or through reflex action." As examples of inhibitions,

# THE IDEA BECOMES ACTION

Brown-Séquard <note>Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (1817–1894) was a pioneering physiologist known for his work on the spinal cord and neurology.</note> cites the stopping of the heart under the influence of the excitation of the abdominal sympathetic ganglia, the stopping of respiration by irritation of the laryngeal nerves, and the inhibition of mental activity or loss of consciousness by a simple puncture of the medulla <note>original: "bulbe"; the medulla oblongata is the part of the brainstem that controls automatic functions like breathing</note>, even while the heart continues to beat. He also notes reflex amaurosis <note>a type of vision loss or blindness</note> following a lesion of the trigeminal nerve <note>the nerve responsible for sensation in the face</note> and other nerves, or from the partial sectioning of the restiform bodies <note>structures in the medulla that connect to the cerebellum</note> in rabbits$^1$. The negative suggestions we mentioned previously belong to this same order of facts.

The mechanism of suggestion, in general, can therefore be summarized in the following formula: *an increase in ideo-motor, ideo-sensitive, and ideo-sensory reflex excitability*. Just as through certain influences—strychnine <note>In the 19th century, researchers used small doses of strychnine to study how it drastically increased the sensitivity of spinal reflexes.</note>, for example—sensory-motor excitability is increased in the spinal cord so that the slightest impression at the periphery of a nerve is immediately transformed into a contraction, without the moderating brain being able to prevent or hinder this transformation; so too, in hypnotism, "ideo-reflex" excitability is increased in the brain. In this state, any received idea is immediately transformed into an act, without the "psychic organ of refinement"—the higher level of the brain—being able to prevent this transformation.

This is merely a formula, I am aware; I do not claim to put forth a complete theory. In the psychological domain, the cause and the essence of phenomena escape us. Such as it is, this formula, if I do not...

$^1$ "The initial act itself," says Brown-Séquard, "by which an individual is thrown into hypnotism, is nothing but a peripheral irritation (of one of the senses or the skin) or a central one (by the influence of an idea or an emotion) which produces a decrease or an increase of power in certain points of the brain, the spinal cord, or other parts; and braidism <note>An early term for hypnotism, named after James Braid (1795–1860), who first coined the term "hypnosis."</note> or hypnotism is nothing other than the very complex state of loss or increase of energy into which the nervous system and other organs are thrown under the influence of the primary peripheral or central irritation. -># ON SLEEP INDUCED BY SUGGESTION<-

...deceives, it serves at least to help us conceive of a mechanism that the mind cannot otherwise rigorously interpret. A bit of light arises, it seems to me, from this theoretical conception, however imperfect it may be: we understand that these curious phenomena can exist normally, in the waking state <note>original: "état de veille"; the state of being fully awake and conscious</note>, in certain subjects who, by a particular disposition of their nervous centers, have more open, more easily "cleared" pathways for intracerebral reflectivity <note>the brain's ability to automatically reflect an idea into a physical sensation or movement</note>. These individuals also experience a weakening of the conscious state that normally moderates reflex automatism. It is also understandable that those who have been frequently hypnotized may have acquired through habit—that is, through the frequent repetition of these induced phenomena—an increase in this ideo-reflex <term>ideo-reflex: the process where an idea automatically triggers a physical reflex without conscious will</term> excitability. The pathways, being more frequently cleared, offer the nervous influx an easier and faster release; the impression follows this path by preference, even in the waking state. This is why subjects trained and educated by prior hypnotizations can, without being hypnotized anew, manifest the same phenomena and perform the same acts under the influence of suggestion, which becomes all-powerful over them.

Sleep itself is born from a conscious or unconscious suggestion. The person who affirms to themselves that they are going to sleep, or to whom it is affirmed by word or gesture, immobilizes their thought on the idea of sleep. They gradually feel all the symptoms: heaviness of the eyelids, visual clouding <note>original: "obnubilation visuelle"; a darkening or blurring of sight often preceding a loss of consciousness</note>, and numbness of the limbs. They isolate their senses, withdraw from all external impressions, their eyes close—sleep is there.

The various methods of hypnotization act partly through suggestion; the fixation on a shiny object or the convergent squinting of the eyes develops a fatigue and numbness of the eyelids, which instills the idea of sleep; the closing of the eyelids is itself an invitation to sleep. It is said that Breton <note>referring to people from Brittany, a cultural region in northwest France</note> women put their infants to sleep by hanging a small, shiny glass ball from the canopy of the cradle where it sparkles before their eyes. <header>SPONTANEOUS AND INDUCED SLEEP</header>

...certain practices for determining religious ecstasy make use of this suggestion through visual fatigue; such as the contemplation of an imaginary point in space, or the tip of their nose by the <term>yogis: practitioners of meditation and asceticism in India</term> or devotees of India, and the contemplation of their navel by the monks of Mount Athos, also known as <term>omphalopsychics: from the Greek for 'navel' and 'soul,' referring to those who practice navel-gazing as a meditative aid</term>. Let us add that monotonous, weak, and continuous impressions on any one of the senses produce a certain intellectual torpor in most people, which is the prelude to sleep. The brain, entirely absorbed by a gentle, uniform, and incessant perception, becomes a stranger to every other impression; being too weakly stimulated, it allows itself to grow numb. "If the mind," says Cullen <note>William Cullen (1710–1790), a Scottish physician known for his influential work on the nervous system</note>, "attaches itself to a single sensation, it soon reaches an almost total absence of impressions, or, in other words, the state closest to sleep."

The prolonged and monotonous sound of tambourines struck with the same cadence in the darkness of night produces ecstatic hypnotism among the Arabs of the Aïssaoua <note>A Sufi order in North Africa known for ritual practices involving music and trances</note> sect. The impression made on the hearing by the continuous murmur of waves, or by a slow and monotonous delivery, leads to drowsiness. "The child is hypnotized aurally by the monotonous songs of its nurse; the regular oscillations of its cradle, by communicating a long series of slight shocks, all similar to one another and separated by equal intervals, hypnotize it through the muscular sense. Incantation with its charms <note>original: "carmina"; Latin for songs, chants, or ritual verses</note>, whose simple and invariable rhythm murmurs to the ear and captivates it without speaking to the intelligence, must be considered a particular form of <term>Braidism: an early term for hypnotism named after James Braid, who focused on the physical causes of trance like eye strain</term> acting on the sense of hearing instead of addressing the sense of sight" (Dr. Philips <note>The pseudonym of Jean-Philippe Durand de Gros, a French polymath and pioneer in psychology</note>).

### SUGGESTION WITHOUT SLEEP

...incoherent impressions that constitute dreams. Have those who deny the psychic phenomena of hypnotism, or who only admit their existence in "sickly nervous temperaments," ever reflected on what happens in normal sleep? In that state, even the most balanced brain goes adrift, faculties dissociate, and the most bizarre ideas and fantastic concepts impose themselves. Poor human reason has taken flight; the proudest spirit allows itself to be hallucinated and becomes, during this sleep—that is, during a third of its existence—the plaything of dreams evoked by the imagination.

In induced sleep <note>Often referred to as "somnambulisme provoqué" in 19th-century French medical literature</note>, the idea of the person who induced the sleep remains present in the mind of the hypnotized subject. This allows the "hypnotizer" to put that imagination into play, to suggest dreams themselves, and to direct actions that are no longer controlled by a weak or absent will.

By virtue of this <term>paresis: a state of diminished or weakened mental control or muscle power</term> of voluntary psychic activity—which normally regulates our <term>cerebro-spinal automatism: the body's capacity to perform complex actions without conscious thought</term>—the latter becomes exaggerated and takes the lead. Thus, sleep favors the production of suggestive phenomena by suppressing or weakening the moderating influence of the will. However, sleep is not indispensable to their production; sleep itself is already, I repeat, a phenomenon of suggestion. Certain subjects are resistant to the idea of sleep, yet they still reach a <term>cataleptiform: referring to catalepsy, a state of rigid posture and unresponsive senses</term> closing of the eyelids. In the case of one female patient in my service, I provoke neither sleep nor the closing of the eyelids, but rather the closing of her hand in a state of muscle contraction by simple affirmation. Hypnotism is therefore not the *obliged* prelude to suggestion; it facilitates it when it can be induced, but other suggestions can sometimes succeed even when the suggestion of sleep remains ineffective.

We established at the beginning of this study that the hypnotic state involves various degrees. In a memoir full of interest that reveals an ingenious mind, M. Chambard <note>Ernest Chambard (1848–1906), a French physician who specialized in the study of dreams and somnambulism</note> has classified the different periods of hypnotic sleep in a different manner. This division is based on...

# ON THE PERIODS OF HYPNOTIC SLEEP

This section concerns the concepts of Alfred Maury <note>Alfred Maury (1817–1892) was a French polymath and pioneer in the study of dreams; he is best known for identifying "hypnagogic hallucinations"—the visions we see just before falling asleep.</note> regarding the succession of phenomena that result in physiological sleep.

Sight disappears first; the other senses, initially heightened, then cease to function, with touch being the last to go.

The intellectual functions, having become momentarily more active because they are no longer distracted by sensory impressions, then dissociate; the first to disappear are the coordinating faculties that decide and direct: the will, attention, judgment, and finally memory. The imaginative faculties that suggest and carry one along, being the only ones persisting for a time, leave the brain accessible to dreams, hallucinations, and bizarre concepts.

They extinguish in their turn. For an instant, the *ego* <note>original: *moi*</note> keeps watch alone above the intellectual faculties and the drowsy senses, then, suddenly, it vanishes. Sleep is complete.

Equipped with these data, Mr. Chambard <note>Ernest Chambard (1848–1901) was a French physician who collaborated with Charcot to define the "three stages" of hypnotism.</note> establishes the intermediate degrees from the most complete sleep to waking in the following order.

The deepest degree is *lethargy*; it first takes hold of the hypnotized subject, who then, waking in a more or less complete fashion, stops at one of the intermediate degrees.

1° In lethargy, the subject is inert, without consciousness, and without relation to the outside world: only <term>vegetative life: the basic biological functions necessary for survival, such as breathing and circulation, that occur without conscious effort</term> persists.

The <term>relational functions: the mental and physical processes that allow an individual to interact with their environment</term> are then reborn: first, those that establish an unconscious link between the organism and outside impressions; this is *automatism*: every sensory or sensitive excitation provokes simple or complex movements, the same as it would determine in the waking state, if the coordinating faculties did not intervene to prevent or moderate them.

2° This is first motor *automatism* giving rise to the phenomena described by Charcot under the name of *neuro-muscular hyperexcitability* <note>A state where muscles contract or react intensely to even slight physical stimulation, often associated with the "lethargic" stage of hypnosis in Charcot’s school.</note>. The brain being still func-

3rd. As these unconscious—or at least minimally conscious—relational functions become more active, and the senses of touch, hearing, and muscle awareness gradually awaken, we reach **passive somnambulic automatism**: the subject continues movements they are placed into (**motor inertia**), performs acts related to sensory impressions (**motor suggestion**), reproduces spoken sounds or movements they see or hear (**automatic imitation**), and carries out orders (**automatic obedience**).

4th. As memory and the imaginative faculties awaken in their turn, we reach **active somnambulic automatism**: the brain, lacking spontaneity, is open to dreams. These differ from ordinary dreams due to the unconscious nature of the psycho-motor and psycho-sensory phenomena. These include ambulatory <note>walking while dreaming</note> dreams, professional dreams <note>dreams where the person acts out their daily job</note>, instinctive and passionate dreams, **anamnestic** <term>anamnestic: related to the recall of past memories or history</term> dreams, intelligent dreams (during which the subject performs complex acts, writes, plays music, etc.), and suggested dreams.

5th. The coordinating faculties return incompletely; since the imaginative and instinctive faculties continue to dominate the scene and prevail over the former "reasoning" faculties, this is **somnambulic life**; the subject appears awake and performs all the actions of daily existence; however, their weakened will and heightened imagination leave them vulnerable to suggestions and obedient to commanded acts.

6th. Finally, the coordinating faculties are fully restored; balance is regained; the awakening is complete.

This ingenious concept does not seem to me to conform to the facts.

From all observations, as has been seen in the description of these phenomena, it appears that active somnambulism (which Chambard calls active somnambulic automatism and somnambulic life) implies the most profound influence, the most advanced degree of hypnotism,

# ->LONG-TERM SUGGESTION<- #

The division of the hypnotic state into degrees, as I have established according to Mr. Liébault <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébault (1823–1904) was a French physician who founded the "Nancy School" of hypnosis, which emphasized the role of suggestion over physical causes.</note>, seems to me more consistent with the data of observation.

The weakest influence manifests as a simple torpor, with the closing of the eyelids.

If the *suggestibility* <note>The degree to which a person is inclined to accept and act upon the ideas or instructions of another.</note> is greater, it is the motor function that first feels the effects; this is suggestive contracture <note>A state where muscles are triggered to remain in a fixed, rigid position through suggestion.</note>, followed by suggestive automatic movements appearing on the scene. Automatic obedience, anesthesia, sensory illusions, and finally provoked hallucinations mark the progressive stages of the development of this suggestibility, the pinnacle of which is constituted by active somnambulism and by somnambulistic life.

I will not attempt to interpret the mechanism of all hypnotic phenomena more deeply.

Among them, however, there is one that is particularly interesting and has called in vain upon all the insights of psychology for some attempt at *interpretation*; I refer to the problem of *long-term suggestions* <note>original: "suggestions à longue échéance"; these are suggestions given during hypnosis to be carried out at a specific time in the future, often days or even months later.</note>.

Let us try, in our turn, to shed a little light on this obscure question.

Before approaching it, it seems necessary to me to develop some considerations regarding *latent memories*.

The study of hypnotic phenomena highlights *latent memories*; I do not say unconscious memories. Impressions are deposited in the brain during hypnotic sleep. At the moment the subject receives them, they are aware of them. Upon waking, this awareness has disappeared. The memory is momentarily latent, like many memories—like all the memories that, since we have been living and thinking, sleep in our brain. But these latent memories of the hypnotic state can be awakened or awaken spontaneously through certain influences. Let us cite a few examples.

# ->LATENT MEMORIES<- #

1° One day, a photograph is taken of one of my <term>somnambulists</term> <note>In the context of 19th-century hypnosis, a "somnambulist" refers to a person who enters a deep hypnotic state where they can act and speak but will have no memory of it upon waking.</note> in her waking state; then she is hypnotized, and her photograph is taken again in various attitudes suggested during this state: anger, fear (due to the imaginary sight of a snake), joy (tipsiness), disdain (the sight of mocking students), and ecstasy. Upon waking, she remembers nothing. A few days later, having hypnotized her again, I say to her: "When you wake up, you will open the book at your bedside and you will find your photograph." I say only this to her. Upon waking, she takes the book, opens it, and finds her photograph there (a hallucinated one! there was none), asking if she may keep it and send it to her son. "Do you find it a good likeness?" I ask her. — "Very much so; I look a little sad." — "Well," I say, "turn the page." She turns and recognizes her photograph (imaginary!) in the attitude of anger. — "Turn again." — And, continuing to turn the pages one by one, she recognizes her various photographs with as much clarity as if they truly existed, in her various attitudes of fear, joy, disdain, and ecstasy; she describes each of these poses to me with perfect precision, exactly as she sees them—which is exactly how she had posed during her hypnotic sleep—without having any recollection of having struck those poses, nor of the suggestion corresponding to each one. She appears greatly astonished when I tell her that these attitudes had been communicated to her during her sleep. Thus, the latent memory of facts performed during somnambulism was awakened by a sort of association of "memory-ideas."

2° In a sleeping somnambulist, I produce suggestive phenomena of transfer; for example, I place his left arm in <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state where a person's limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed, as if the person were a wax statue.</note> in a horizontal position; and bringing a <term>stethoscope</term> <note>While usually a tool for listening to the heart, early hypnotists often used medical instruments as "props" to focus a patient's attention or to symbolize the "transfer" of symptoms from one side of the body to the other.</note> near the other arm, I say that the catalepsy is going to transfer to that side; after a minute, this arm moves into a horizontal position, while the left arm falls limp. If I bring the stethoscope back to the left arm, that one resumes the horizontal position, the other falls, and so on. I can...

# THE AWAKENING OF HYPNOTIC MEMORIES #

...even produce a <term>torticollis</term> <note>A stiff neck or "wry neck" where the head is tilted to one side.</note>, a paralysis, or a <term>suggestive contracture</term> <note>A state of prolonged muscle contraction or stiffness caused by mental suggestion rather than physical injury.</note> and transfer them from one side to the other, solely by the idea suggested to the subject that the stethoscope produces this phenomenon. # THE CAUSE OF AMNESIA UPON WAKING #

...will never remember anything spontaneously. Now, nothing is easier than to evoke in all <term>somnambulists</term> <note>In this historical context, "somnambulist" refers to a person in a deep state of hypnosis, not just a sleepwalker.</note> the memory of all the impressions experienced during their sleep, and this experiment succeeds with all somnambulists. It is enough for me to say to them: "You are going to remember everything that happened, everything you did during your sleep." I place my hand on their forehead if necessary to concentrate their attention; they reflect for a moment on themselves without falling asleep, and all the **latent memories** are reborn with great precision: they repeat my words, their own, relate their actions and gestures one after another, and their hallucinations; nothing is forgotten. I have awakened the latent memories by a simple affirmation.

These facts being well established, before going further, let us seek to interpret, if possible, the mechanism of <term>amnesia</term> <note>The loss of memory; here specifically referring to the "post-hypnotic amnesia" where a subject forgets what happened while they were entranced.</note> or the absence of memory upon waking from deep sleep.

# THE SKEPTICS AND THE PARTISANS OF THE DEVIL

...executes the act or experiences the commanded hallucination, without knowing its origin.

To my knowledge, no explanation has been attempted for this singular phenomenon, which is of an undeniable reality. Some, unable to explain it, have denied it, stubbornly refusing to bow before the evidence of the facts; others—such as that <term>Abbé</term><note>A title for a priest in France. During this period, the Catholic Church was often in conflict with new psychological and medical discoveries.</note> who wrote in *L’Univers* regarding hypnotic phenomena—finding no plausible explanation, have considered it supernatural. They suggest a <term>cunning spirit</term><note>original: "esprit malin"; a common euphemism for a demon or the Devil.</note> would emerge from hell to come to the aid of the operator. In this instance, the former lack a scientific spirit; the latter err through a lack of modesty and humility. To deny what one cannot understand, or to invoke God or the Devil to explain what the poor human brain cannot conceive, demonstrates a certain intellectual arrogance that does not belong to a truly <term>enlightened mind</term><note>original: "esprit fort"; historically referring to a freethinker or someone who relies on reason rather than religious dogma.</note>. The transmission of the human voice, articulated with its tone and inflections through a wire and a vibrating plate, is a marvelous phenomenon that we witness even better than we can explain. The problems of the infinite, of the eternal without beginning, and of space without limits, appear to our human understanding as riddles for which it can conceive no solution—and yet, that solution exists. All phenomena of a <term>psychic nature</term><note>original: "l'ordre psychique"; here referring to the study of the mind and spirit, which was then a burgeoning field between philosophy and modern psychology.</note> are mysteries whose mechanisms escape us, but which occur nonetheless. Let us remain humble with the sense of our own insufficiency, and modestly resign ourselves to not overstepping the boundaries of our intelligence.

If I dare to formulate here an attempt at interpretation, or at least a few ideas that might serve the conception of the phenomenon I am pointing out, it is not because I claim to solve the question: my conception is perhaps not the truth. At the very least, I will have shown that a certain conception of the phenomenon is possible, and thus stripped the question of that mysterious and supernatural appearance which is so repugnant to any scientific mind.

# ON WAKING AT A FIXED HOUR

->SUGGESTION. 10<-

Can we explain suggestions with a long delay by an organic change imprinted on the nerve substance, which serves as the <term>substratum</term><note>The underlying layer or foundation; here, the physical brain matter that supports mental activity.</note> for psychic phenomena? Could it be said that, in the hypnotic state, the brain has the property of receiving the imprint of the suggested idea and undergoing a change similar to a spring-loaded mechanism, wound or tightened to release at a given moment—like an alarm clock set to ring at a specific hour? This is a concept that does not, it seems to me, rely on any known anatomical or physiological data.

As an argument for this comparison of the psychic apparatus governing memory with an alarm clock, one might point to the fact that many people have the power to wake up at the time they designated for themselves before falling asleep. The brain would thus have the property of regulating its sleep in advance for a variable number of hours determined by itself.

The explanation seems different to me. The person who falls asleep with the idea of waking at a fixed time continues to have this idea during sleep; for natural sleep, no more than induced sleep, does not result in the abolition of thought or consciousness. We are conscious of ourselves during sleep: we think, we dream, we work. Many subjects speak while sleeping; they answer questions put to them. It has often happened to me, finding a patient sleeping naturally in my clinical ward, to say to him: “Do not wake up, continue to sleep.” Then I raise his arms in the air; they remain there passively in <term>suggestive catalepsy</term><note>A state in which a person's limbs remain in whatever position they are placed, as if the muscles are temporarily frozen.</note>. I give him a suggestion for when he wakes. He carries it out without remembering anything, without knowing that I spoke to him. General Noizet and Mr. Liébeault <note>General Noizet and Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault were pioneers of the "Nancy School" of hypnotism, which emphasized that hypnosis was a normal psychological phenomenon based on suggestion rather than a product of magnetism or disease.</note> have reported the same fact. Natural sleep is transformed into hypnotic sleep; or to put it better, I have put the subject <term>in rapport</term><note>original: "en rapport"; a technical term in early psychology referring to a state of intense focus and communication between the subject and the practitioner.</note> with me; for, in my opinion, nothing—absolutely nothing—differentiates natural sleep from induced sleep; one can exploit natural sleep just as one exploits hypnotic sleep. If they do not have a sense of time, what happens? Preoccupied with the idea of not missing the hour, they wake up several times during the night, lighting a candle each time...

Our ideas are conscious while we sleep; they have become latent when we are awake; we do not remember that we thought all night about not missing the hour, and we believe that the waking was spontaneous or unconscious.

It is through this order of ideas that I seek to account for the mechanism of **long-term suggestions**. The <term>somnambulist</term><note>In 19th-century psychological texts, this term refers not just to sleepwalkers, but to subjects in a deep state of hypnosis who remain active and responsive.</note> who must, at the end of three months for example, perform an act suggested during sleep, manifests no idea of the order received during those three months; and when they have accomplished it, they believe and affirm they had no idea related to that act during those three months.
