One must have seen these singular psychic phenomena to grasp their full significance. And one cannot help but think then that a similar phenomenon occurs spontaneously in <term>somnambulists</term><note>In 19th-century psychology, "somnambulist" referred specifically to a person in a deep hypnotic trance, not just a sleepwalker.</note> and without their knowledge; somnambulists pass easily from one state of consciousness to the other, the memories of the second being erased in the first. Deposit an idea in their brain during the state called somnambulism—an idea that must manifest on a fixed day. During the so-called **waking state**, the idea seems extinguished; but it does not remain latent until the day it is due. It is reborn and becomes conscious again every time the same nervous concentration, every time the same psychic state is reproduced. It is enough for their attention to fold back upon itself, for the brain to become absorbed in an idea or an image, for a sort of *passive somnambulism* to occur within them—passive only because it is not forced out of its passiveness. And this is so true that many somnambulists are suggestible in the waking state; every formulated idea, every evoked image is realized by them in the waking state; they are subject to hallucinations by mere speech; they are somnambulists normally and without any artifice of preparation, so to speak.

The operator can do nothing other than exploit this state of special psychic receptivity.

There is therefore reason to believe that the somnambulist often spontaneously enters the state of somnambulistic consciousness, in which impressions deposited in the same prior state can be reawakened. He then remembers the order received, the commanded suggestion; he knows that such a phenomenon must take place on such a day; he "sets his stages," if I may put it that way; he confirms himself in his idea

-># THE AWAKENING OF HYPNOTIC IMPRESSIONS<-

...not to forget it and to carry it out at the appointed time, just as a normal sleeper might hold the intention not to miss the hour they must wake up. At that moment, the idea is perfectly conscious within the <term>somnambulist</term><note>In 19th-century medicine, this referred to a person in a deep hypnotic trance.</note>. However, when they cease to concentrate—when we speak to them, when we call their nervous activity back to the outside world—we return them to full possession of themselves. We restore their normal state of consciousness, just as we might tell a child to open their eyes and look at the world with their brain. The concentration vanishes; the memory is once again extinguished or latent. And, at the moment the somnambulist carries out the suggested act, they believe in perfectly good faith that the idea has freshly hatched—spontaneously hatched—within their brain; *they no longer remember that they had remembered it.*

I was able to verify this directly with two somnambulists. To one, I said during her sleep: “Next Thursday (in five days), you will take the glass that is on the nightstand and you will put it in the suitcase at the foot of your bed.” Three days later, having put her to sleep again, I asked her: “Do you remember what I ordered you to do?” She replied: “Yes, I must put the glass in my suitcase Thursday morning, at eight o'clock.” — “Have you thought about it since I told you?” — “No.” — “Think back carefully.” — “I thought of it the following morning at eleven o'clock.” — “Were you awake or asleep?” — “I was <term>drowsy</term><note>The original French "assoupie" suggests a state of light sleep or a semi-conscious "nodding off," indicating she briefly re-entered a state similar to the trance where the memory lived.</note>.”

To another, I said one morning, having put him to sleep: “Tomorrow morning, during the <term>rounds</term><note>The "visite" refers to the daily rounds made by the head physician to check on hospital patients.</note>, you will ask me if you should continue taking <term>potassium bromide</term><note>A common 19th-century sedative and anti-seizure medication.</note>; you will ask me this as a request for information, without knowing that it was I who told you to ask me.”

The following morning, in the presence of D<gloss>octor</gloss> Voisin, who did me the honor of attending my clinic, I had forgotten my own suggestion. I was leaving the man's bed when he called me back and asked if he should continue taking the bromide. “Why are you asking me that?” I said to him. — “Because I believe I will soon be leaving the hospital and I would like to know if the bromide is useful to me.” —

-># CONSCIOUSNESS OF LATENT MEMORIES<-

“Why do you ask me that now?” — “I don’t know. It’s just an idea that came to me.” Then, I put him back to sleep and ask him: “Why did you ask me if you should continue the <term>bromide</term><note>Potassium bromide was a common 19th-century sedative used to treat "nervous" disorders and epilepsy.</note>?” — “To know if it was useful to me!” — “But why this question this morning?” — “Because you told me yesterday to ask you.” — “Have you thought, since yesterday morning when I put you to sleep, that you had to ask me this question?” — “I thought of it last night during my sleep. I dreamed that my legs hurt and that I should ask you if I should continue the bromide.” I wake him up and he no longer remembers anything. The idea of asking me this question had come to him, he believed, spontaneously.

Therefore, the <term>suggestion</term><note>An instruction given to a subject under hypnosis to be carried out later.</note> deposited in the brain during sleep, remaining as a <term>latent memory</term><note>A memory that is present but not currently active or conscious.</note> upon waking, is capable of becoming conscious again spontaneously; if the suggestion is not to be carried out for several weeks, the idea does not remain latent and unconscious until the day it is due.

I summarize my findings in the following conclusions:

1° Impressions produced by <term>artificial sleep</term><note>A common 19th-century term for hypnosis.</note> or induced sleep are always conscious at the moment they are produced;

2° The consciousness of these impressions, extinguished upon awakening from the induced sleep, can always be evoked by simple affirmation;

3° Latent memories of the hypnotic state can awaken spontaneously in certain states of <term>psychic concentration</term><note>A focused mental state where the "barrier" between the conscious and subconscious mind becomes thin.</note>;

4° The idea of suggestions to be carried out at a later date does not remain unconscious until that day; the consciousness of the idea deposited in the brain during the hypnotic state can awaken at times, like other latent memories, in these same states of psychic concentration.

# CHAPTER IX

->General applications of the doctrine of suggestion. — Moral and psychological perspective. — On education. — Legal perspective. — Criminal suggestions. — Observation. — Retroactive hallucinations. — The Tisza-Eslar affair. — Instinctive imbecility. — Response to Mr. Paul Janet.<-

From every perspective, the doctrine of <term>suggestion</term><note>The process by which an idea is introduced into the brain and accepted as a reality or an impulse to act.</note>, as we have established it through observed facts, raises the most thrilling questions. In psychology, it is a revolution! How many problems is this study, still in its infancy, destined to solve? To what extent does suggestion take hold on the most diverse brains, chosen from the intelligent classes refined by education as well as from the modest classes offering less cerebral resistance? To what extent can passions, instincts, tastes, and psychic faculties be modified by a prolonged and skillfully conducted suggestion, whether in the waking state or the <term>hypnotic state</term><note>A state of altered consciousness, often called "artificial sleep" in the 19th century, where a subject is highly responsive to the influence of the hypnotist.</note>? 

Is not the education of a child—the notions and principles instilled into their brain by word and example, the philosophical and religious doctrines in which they are cradled from their earliest age—already a true suggestion in the <term>waking state</term><note>Suggestion given to a person who is fully awake and alert, rather than in a trance.</note>? If this is practiced methodically, directed in a uniform way, and not countered by contradictory ideas or examples, does it not often impose itself with irresistible force? Mature men, whose personal experience has later liberated their brains, often retain—despite all their independence of spirit and free reason—an old foundation of ideas they can no longer discard, because these ideas have become incarnated in their

### SUGGESTION THROUGH EDUCATION

...brain by means of a long-standing prior suggestion, even though these ideas seem to clash with the new trends of their psychic state.

> “Without realizing it,” says Mr. Liébeault, “we acquire moral and political notions, family or racial prejudices, etc.; we are permeated by the ideas that form the atmosphere around us. There are social and religious principles that ought not to withstand common sense, let alone reason, yet which we believe in good faith and defend as our own property. These principles were those of our ancestors; they are even national; they have been embodied from fathers to sons; destroying them through reasoning is impossible and, by force, it is dangerous; no matter how much one demonstrates their falsehood, there are thoughts in men born of imitation which, as absurd as they may be, are one with themselves, and end up being transmitted from generation to generation, in the manner of instincts.”

What a suggestion in the waking state can achieve on certain young and virgin brains, hypnotic suggestion—which suppresses control—carries out by force, so to speak, and as if by breaking and entering while the masters of the house are away, with a much more powerful effectiveness. Is it true to say, with Durand <note>Joseph-Pierre Durand de Gros (1826–1900), a French physiologist who wrote under the pseudonym Dr. Philips and was a proponent of Braidism.</note>, that <term>braidism</term><note>A 19th-century term for hypnotism, named after the Scottish surgeon James Braid, who focused on the physiological process of "nervous sleep" induced by staring at a fixed object.</note> provides us with the basis for an intellectual and moral orthopedics <note>Here used metaphorically to mean the "straightening" or correction of the mind and character, much like orthopedics straightens the limbs.</note> that will certainly one day be inaugurated in educational houses and penitentiary establishments?

From a legal and medico-legal point of view, how many applications there are! When one sees a subject who has fallen spontaneously or been artificially placed into a <term>somnambulistic</term><note>A deep state of hypnosis where the subject can act and speak as if awake but remains under the influence of the hypnotist and usually has no memory of the events afterward.</note> life—a docile instrument without will in the hands of another—undergoing all influences and performing all acts, one cannot help but feel a deep emotion! # LEGAL APPLICATIONS

Spinoza’s <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher who argued that human beings believe they are free only because they are conscious of their actions but ignorant of the causes that determine them.</note> famous phrase: “Our illusion of free will is only the ignorance of the motives that make us act.”

It is the duty of moralists, psychologists, and forensic doctors to courageously examine the great questions of this nature that weigh upon the human conscience.

I wish only to show, by means of an example, how much the phenomena of psychic suggestion—as experimentation has achieved them with our subjects—can be exploited for nefarious purposes. The following observation, which I report according to Professor Despine <note>Prosper Despine (1812–1892), a French physician and pioneer in forensic psychiatry who studied the relationship between "nervous states" and criminal behavior.</note>, is extracted from the trial records of July 29 and 30, 1865, at the Assize Court of Draguignan:

> “On March 31, 1865, a beggar arrived at the hamlet of Guiols (Var). He was approximately twenty-five years old; he was crippled in both legs. He asked for hospitality from a man named H..., who lived in this hamlet with his daughter. She was twenty-six years old, and her moral character was beyond reproach. The beggar, named Castellan, faking <term>deaf-mutism</term><note>The historical term for being unable to hear or speak; in this context, the beggar feigned the condition to appear more mysterious or pitiable.</note>, made it understood through signs that he was hungry; he was invited to supper. During the meal, he engaged in strange acts that caught the attention of his hosts: he made a show of only having his glass filled after tracing the sign of the cross over the object and over his own face. During the evening gathering, he signaled that he could write. He then traced the following sentences: ‘I am the son of God, I am from heaven and my name is: Our Lord! For you see my little miracles, and later you will see greater ones. Fear nothing from me, I am sent by God.’ He claimed to know the future and announced that civil war would break out in six months. These absurd acts impressed those present, and Joséphine H... was deeply moved by them: she went to bed fully dressed, out of fear of the beggar. The latter spent the night in the hayloft, and the following day, after having breakfasted, he left the hamlet. He soon returned, after ensuring that Joséphine would remain alone for the entire day. He found her busy with household chores and spoke with her for some time...”

Having said this, I change the course of her ideas, I induce more cheerful suggestions; upon her waking, I no longer speak to her of this event. 

Three days later, I ask my friend, Mr. Grillon, a distinguished lawyer, to interrogate this woman as if he were an <term>examining magistrate</term><note>French: *juge d'instruction*. In the French legal system, this is a judge who performs the initial investigation into serious crimes.</note>. In my absence, she tells him the facts in all their details, giving the names of the victim and the criminal, and the exact hour of the crime; she maintains her statements energetically; she knows the gravity of her testimony; if she is called to appear before the <term>assizes</term><note>The criminal court that handles the most serious offenses.</note>, despite the emotion she feels, she will tell the truth, since it is necessary; she is ready to swear before God and men! 

Having approached her bed after the deposition, the lawyer, acting in his capacity as a magistrate, had her repeat it before me. I asked her if it was indeed the truth, if she had not dreamed it, or if it was not a vision like those I was accustomed to giving her during her sleep; I urged her to be wary of herself. She maintained her testimony with unshakeable conviction.

This done, I put her to sleep to uproot this suggestion. "Everything you said to the examining magistrate," I told her, "is not true: you saw nothing on August 3rd; you no longer know anything at all; you will not even remember that you spoke to the examining magistrate; he asked you nothing and you told him nothing." 

Upon her waking, I said to her: "What did you say to this gentleman just now?" 

— "I said nothing." 

— "What? You said nothing," said the magistrate, "you spoke to me of a crime that took place in your house on August 3rd; you saw the man named X..., etc."

There is even more. # FALSE TESTIMONY OF A HALLUCINATING CHILD

Moritz—this was the child's name—had heard a cry, gone outside, pressed his eye to the temple's lock, and seen Esther lying on the ground; three men were holding her; the butcher was bleeding her from the throat and collecting her blood in two plates! <note>This description matches the "blood libel," a centuries-old false accusation that Jews murdered Christian children to use their blood in religious rituals.</note> Held in isolation for three months, entrusted to a guard who never leaves his side, the child, upon reaching the hearing, persists in his confessions: the sight of his wretched father and of his twelve co-religionists threatened by the gallows, the most ardent pleas to urge him to tell the truth, the tears and the curses—nothing moves him; he tirelessly repeats the same things in the same terms: he has seen it. How can we explain the child's confessions? Two hypotheses are possible. Terror, violence, and threats could have extracted a false deposition; and we know how, in children and even in adults, stubbornness in a lie becomes obstinate, simply because one has lived for weeks with the habit of that lie; add flattery following violence, the promise of a life strewn with roses to reward perseverance in the imposed lie. This is possible! And yet, I do not readily conceive of a moral perversion so monstrous, so rapidly developed in a child who, until then, had shown no bad instincts.

That terror might wrest a false testimony from a weak-willed soul is in the nature of things! But placed in the presence of a father who suffers and implores, that the child, deaf to all pleas, should consciously maintain his deposition, knowing that it will lead to the death penalty <term>capital punishment</term>, that he continues notwithstanding...

Here is the other hypothesis: The child is brought before the examining magistrate <term>juge d'instruction: a judicial officer who conducts the initial investigation into a crime</term>: humble, depressed by the poor environment in which he was raised, he trembles before the figure representing Power and Justice. In colorful language, full of assurance, he tells him detailed and realistic accounts of similar scenes. The imagination of the poor nervous child, fascinated by terror, is vividly struck: he is all eyes, all ears; his faculties of reason are paralyzed by emotion. The official's words make an impression on his weak mind; and little by little, the deep and persistent impression becomes an image; under the influence of this vigorous suggestion, the hypnotized brain constructs from scratch the scene that the commissioner evokes: everything is there: the child sees the victim lying down, held by three people, the sacrificer plunging his knife into the throat, the blood flowing: the child has "seen" it. The retroactive hallucination <term>hallucination rétroactive: a false memory suggested by an external influence that the subject eventually accepts as a real event they witnessed</term> is created, just as one is created experimentally in deep sleep, and the memory of the fictional vision is so vivid that the child cannot escape it. Just as a dramatic scene vigorously sketched by a novelist imposes itself on the imagination with as much clarity as reality itself.

I do not know if this hypothesis is the true one: the very fact of the child's rapid conversion, due to the skillful maneuvers of his instructors, seems to denote a brain accessible to suggestions. A psychic study of this witness by a commission of doctors well-versed in these facts would undoubtedly have allowed for the measurement of the suggestibility...

# ->INSTINCTIVE IMBECILITY<-

...of this brain, to determine if he was hypnotizable, and perhaps to bring the truth to light.

I have sought to establish that hypnotism does not actually create a new state: nothing happens during induced sleep that cannot also occur at a rudimentary level in many people—and to an almost equal degree in a few—while in a waking state. Certain people are naturally suggestible; from a psychological point of view, they exist normally in that state we have called <term>hypotaxy</term> <note>A state of heightened suggestibility or "light hypnosis" where the subject remains conscious but is highly responsive to the influence of others.</note> or <term>fascination</term> <note>original: "charme"</note>, which renders them incapable of conducting their own lives and which weakens or suppresses all moral resistance within them. Men who are distinguished in many respects, gifted with brilliant artistic or intuitive qualities, are often "big children," as if their entire intellectual power were concentrated into one or two imaginative faculties. Everyone has known those child prodigies—those mental calculators, for example, such as Mondeux or Inaudi <note>Henri Mondeux (1826–1861) and Jacques Inaudi (1867–1950) were famous "calculating prodigies" who could perform complex arithmetic in their heads but often lacked general education or other cognitive skills.</note>—who, through a prodigious native power of abstraction, solved the most complicated problems in their heads, yet were incapable of intellectual effort in any other regard. Here, at least, an immense talent that borders on genius compensates for the disharmony of cerebral functions. Others have no such compensation.

Who has not seen these "disinherited" beings? They are not devoid of intelligence; they are capable of absorbing common ideas, and can even shine in a social gathering and create an illusion of their own worth. When they are well-directed, they fulfill their social duties well, but in reality, they are devoid of initiative and will. Lacking moral resistance, they move as the wind blows—that is to say, as suggestion pushes them. I would go so far as to say they are afflicted with *instinctive imbecility*.

Under the names <term>instinctive insanity</term>, <term>insanity of action</term>, <term>moral insanity</term>, <term>lucid insanity</term>, or <term>reasoning mania</term>, <term>alienists</term> <note>A 19th-century term for psychiatrists or doctors who studied mental "alienation."</note> describe "a morbid state that manifests less through intellectual delirium than through disorder in the...

## ->LUCID IMBECILES<-

...ideas and words as by the extravagance of feelings and actions which appear to be the result of an instinctive, automatic, thoughtless impulse, without reflection or reasoning intervening to direct them, as occurs in a person of sound mind." > "These patients are mad," says Trélat, <note>Ulysse Trélat (1795–1879) was a French physician who wrote extensively on "lucid madness" (*la folie lucide*), describing people who seem sane in speech but are erratic or dangerous in their behavior.</note> "but do not appear mad, because they express themselves with lucidity. Their lack of reason is known only in their private lives and does not manifest outwardly. It is among them that we find a fairly large number of beings sometimes considered insane, sometimes criminal, and who have alternately resided in asylums or in prisons."

Among them, one sees individuals with a rare strength in discussion, who have the gift of the retort and constantly seek the opportunity to let their wit shine.

All her answers were put through the crucible of analysis, and this with a depth of vision that astonished everyone."

# INSTINCTIVE WEAKNESS

but the instinctive, affective, and sentimental part of the <term>moral being</term> <note>In 19th-century psychology, the "moral being" referred to the part of the human personality responsible for ethics, willpower, and social behavior, as opposed to the "intellectual being" responsible for logic.</note>, which governs the acts of life, is as if atrophied. They lack **moral spontaneity**; they do not know how to conduct themselves; like sleepwalkers from a psychic point of view, they obey every suggestion and easily succumb to all external impulses. This psychic state, moreover, involves varying degrees: from simple <term>instinctive weakness</term> to absolute **instinctive idiocy** <note>At the time this was written, "idiocy" was a technical medical classification for various levels of cognitive or moral impairment, rather than a simple insult.</note>. Under good direction, these beings who have been disinherited of their moral sense can achieve a happy and beneficial career, made fruitful by honest inspirations. Others fail sadly in the mire or before the courts.

Consider a young girl raised with good principles whom everyone agreed was gentle and honest. She marries, and the first years are happy; she appears to be a devoted wife and a good mother. A young man captures her imagination; her husband, struggling with the difficulties of existence, neglects her; she gives herself to this young man. Later, the husband broods over ideas of vengeance against this young man who, after seducing his wife, founded a rival business that prospers, while his own founders. To satisfy his vengeance, he recaptures his wife’s mind, persuades her that his rival is the cause of their misfortune, and insinuates to her that he must be killed—that her moral rehabilitation comes at the price of this murder. She gives in to this suggestion; docile, yielding to threats, she sets a rendezvous with her former lover and, under the pretext of renewing their interrupted relationship, coldly, without emotion, she leads him to her husband, who murders him; no remorse, no regret disturbs her conscience; she does not seem to suspect the enormity of her crime.

Nothing in her past allowed one to foresee this monstrous perversion of the moral sense. Before the jury, her boarding school headmistress affirmed that she was the most docile, the best-disciplined student. A witness, whom the audience laughed at because they did not understand him, said of her:

->### NATIVE ABSENCE OF THE MORAL SENSE<-

"...than to virtue." <note>This phrase completes the sentence from the previous page: "She was as prone to vice as to virtue."</note> Translated into psychological language: she possessed a suggestible brain; she was docile to every suggestion, and I would add that her <term>moral sense</term> <note>In this context, the "moral sense" is the internal faculty that allows an individual to distinguish right from wrong and resist harmful impulses.</note> provided no counterweight to her excessive suggestibility. It was perhaps less a perversion than a **native absence of the moral sense**; it was an **instinctive imbecility**.

I do not claim that my interpretation is the only truth; it is enough for my thesis that it is plausible. It is far from my thought, moreover, that all criminals are insane or unconscious; every act must be studied within its circumstances, its causes, its antecedents, and the moral state of the person who perpetrated it. For who would dare to claim that the degree of <term>culpability</term> <note>Legal and moral guilt.</note> is measured solely by the gravity of the act committed?

I shall stop here! I only intended to touch upon a question that concerns the gravest interests of justice and society, leaving it to those more competent than myself to scrutinize further and deduce conclusions. It seemed to me that the experimental study of **hypnotic phenomena** could shed some light on this still-obscure field of <term>moral responsibility</term>. It is with prudence and reserve that one must venture onto this dangerous ground; I have set forth my doubts and my scruples, though I dare not call them my convictions.

# RESPONSE TO MR. PAUL JANET

...only with a certain reserve what emanates from elsewhere. For you, everything there is demonstrated; there, thanks to a truly scientific method, nothing is contestable:
> “we start from the simplest and most elementary facts to rise to the more complex and delicate facts, from the physical and apparent facts to the more internal psychological facts that are more difficult to interpret.”

In Nancy, on the contrary, you seem to say that by neglecting the more elementary and coarse physical phenomena, we seek above all to highlight the most extraordinary facts—those most striking to the imagination. We perhaps push suggestion too far; and perhaps, too, the doctor’s own imagination plays a part in the therapeutic results or psychological phenomena we claim to obtain.

I am responding to this fundamental objection, for it is the guiding idea of your study.

No one does more justice than I to the works coming out of the <term>Salpêtrière School</term> <note>The medical school centered at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, led by Jean-Martin Charcot, which viewed hypnosis as a physical symptom of hysteria.</note>. I am too much a student of Mr. <term>Charcot</term> <note>Jean-Martin Charcot (1825–1893), the "Napoleon of the Neuroses," a pioneering French neurologist.</note>, and I owe him too great a share of my medical education not to pay the tribute due to this eminent master, whose name will always honor French medicine.

But I do not blindly accept—does the master himself accept them?—all the scientific assertions emanating from all the students who have succeeded one another in this fertile field of observation. Science progresses slowly, through a thousand difficulties; new facts come to contradict or modify every day the acquisitions believed to be certain the day before: the true truth is long in emerging from the <term>gangue</term> <note>A geological term used metaphorically here to mean the worthless rock surrounding a gemstone; the "clutter" or "waste" obscuring the truth.</note> that obscures it.

If I have not accepted as the starting point of my studies the three phases of <term>hysterical hypnotism</term> <note>Charcot’s theory that hypnosis followed three rigid physiological stages: lethargy, catalepsy, and somnambulism.</note>, as Charcot describes them—<term>lethargy</term>, <term>catalepsy</term>, and <term>somnambulism</term>—it is because I have been unable to confirm through my own observations the existence of these various states as distinct phases.

# OUR METHOD OF OBSERVATION

As I told the <term>Society of Biology</term> <note>The Société de biologie, a prestigious French learned society founded in 1848.</note>, suggestion—that is, the penetration of the idea of a phenomenon into the subject's brain through speech, gesture, sight, or imitation—has appeared to me to be the key to all the hypnotic phenomena I have observed. The alleged physiological or physical phenomena appeared to me to be, for the most part if not entirely, **psychic phenomena**. I do not claim to explain through suggestion the facts observed by other researchers; I only wish to say that I could not produce them without suggestion. Therefore, was I required to take as the starting point for my research the elementary, physical, and apparent facts—as you call them—that I myself could not observe? Have I departed from the truly scientific method because I only reasoned based on what I saw?

And besides, I admit that these facts of a purely physical or physiological order may be accurate and constant! Is it true to say that they are simpler and more elementary, easier to interpret, than the psychological facts we have observed? Is it true that one can rise from the simpler ones to the more complex and delicate ones? I answer: *Not at all*, because these facts are of an absolutely different order.

The suggestive phenomena have their analogues in normal and pathological life; nature produces them spontaneously. Paralysis, <term>contractures</term> <note>Prolonged, involuntary muscle contractions.</note>, anesthesia, sensory illusions, and hallucinations occur in natural sleepwalking, in hysteria, in <term>mental alienation</term> <note>A historical term for mental illness or insanity.</note>, in alcoholism, and in other intoxications; they occur in all of us during normal sleep. When naturally asleep, we are all suggestible and prone to hallucinations through our own impressions or through impressions coming from others. Mr. <term>Alfred Maury</term> <note>Louis Ferdinand Alfred Maury (1817–1892), a French physician and scholar famous for his work on dreams.</note> has well studied the so-called <term>hypnagogic</term> <note>The state of consciousness leading into sleep.</note> hallucinations, those that occur in the period preceding sleep; some people continue to be obsessed by them in the period immediately following waking.

<summary>Bernheim argues that "suggestion" is the fundamental mechanism of hypnosis, refuting the idea that physical symptoms are more "scientific" or "elementary" than psychological ones. He highlights that hypnotic-like states (hallucinations and paralysis) occur naturally in sleep and various medical conditions.</summary>

# NATURAL SLEEP TRANSFORMED INTO SOMNAMBULISM

...tention, those who are absorbed by emotion, those whose brains are preoccupied by diverse ideas, offer a conscious or unconscious moral resistance to suggestion. The will or the idea of sleeping must be present! Common people, former soldiers, artisans, and subjects accustomed to passive obedience—docile minds—have seemed to me more apt to receive suggestion. Intelligent, well-balanced men of <term>lymphatico-sanguine</term> <note>original: "lymphatico-sanguins"; a 19th-century medical classification of temperament, combining calm, steady traits (lymphatic) with active, energetic ones (sanguine).</note> temperament, who know how to apply their attention without preoccupation or hidden motives, sleep better when they wish to than certain <term>neurotics</term> <note>original: "névropathes"; a historical term for patients with functional nervous disorders, often considered "agitated" or "unstable" by doctors of the era.</note> whose agitated brains cannot focus on any one point.

Recently, in my hospital ward, I found a poor <term>consumptive</term> <note>original: "phtisique"; a person suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis, a common and often fatal wasting disease at the time.</note> woman who was sleeping; I had never hypnotized her. Thus, we have a case of natural sleep during which I was able to establish a connection with the sleeping subject; and that alone constituted hypnotic sleep! How could the connection have been established? I suppose there was a beginning of awakening, but my injunction to continue sleeping prevented the awakening from being completed; the person fell back into so-called hypnotic sleep—that is, in <term>rapport</term> <note>A technical term in hypnosis describing a state where the subject is selectively attentive only to the hypnotist.</note> with me. A mother finds her child asleep; she speaks to him, the child answers; she gives him a drink, the child drinks, then falls back into his inertia, and upon waking, has forgotten everything: the child has, in reality, been hypnotized—that is, in rapport with his mother. # SUGGESTIBILITY IN PARIS AS WELL AS IN NANCY

...we do not know the processes capable of hypnotizing everyone. The day we discover a sure and constant <term>soporific</term> <note>original: "agent soporifique"; a substance or method that induces sleep.</note> agent that provokes sleep rapidly without modifying the psychic disposition—so that the subject can sleep while their thoughts remain fixed on the person present—then perhaps no one will escape the suggestive influence of others, just as no one escapes the hallucinatory suggestions provoked by one’s own impressions in normal sleep.

# COMPLIANCE OR SIMULATION

...and had realized everything; but as he had promised himself to obey without resistance, he had obeyed. “Could you have resisted?” I asked him. “When I placed your arm in the air, could you have lowered it, despite my assertion to the contrary?” — “I believe so,” he said, “without being certain. For a moment I began to lower my arm (which had indeed been visible). Along the way, a sense of remorse seized me. I raised it again, saying to myself: No, I must not lower it.”
Was this a matter of <term>compliance</term>? <note>original: "complaisance"; in this context, it refers to a subject "going along" with the doctor's suggestions out of politeness or a desire to be a "good" patient, rather than being truly under hypnotic influence.</note>

This young man did not know what to think of it himself. Curious and absolutely desiring to be enlightened, he begged me half an hour later to hypnotize him again. In less than a minute, he was under. I placed his legs and his arms in the air: they stayed there. Then I said to him: “Now, perform the experiment; try to lower your arm and your legs, if you can; if you have any willpower, apply it. But I warn you that you will not be able to.” He tried in vain and did not succeed, despite all his visible efforts, in modifying the suggested posture. I made his two arms rotate one around the other: “Try to stop,” I said, “you will not be able to.” Indeed, he could not stop this <term>rotatory automatism</term>. <note>A phenomenon where the subject's limbs continue a repetitive motion (like circling hands) involuntarily until told to stop.</note> When he was awakened, he was convinced that it was not merely compliance, but that there was a physical impossibility of resisting the suggested act.

This experiment, I have repeated with a great number of subjects. <term>Charles Richet</term> <note>A French physiologist (and later Nobel Prize winner) who, like Bernheim, studied the psychological aspects of hypnosis and helped move it away from the realm of occultism.</note>, recounting similar examples, has well described this singular psychic state. Many imagine they have not been influenced because they heard everything; they believe in good faith that they have <term>simulated</term> <note>Feigned or faked the hypnotic state.</note>; it is sometimes difficult to demonstrate to them that they were not free *not* to simulate.

This digression supports my conclusion: that hypnosis is not a variant of <term>hysteria</term>; it is not a diseased state grafted onto a <term>neuropathy</term>. <note>Bernheim is arguing against the famous neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot, who believed hypnosis was only possible in "hysterical" (mentally ill) patients. Bernheim insists it is a normal brain function.</note> It is a physiological state, in the same category as natural sleep, from which it can derive; it can be produced to a certain degree in the majority of subjects.

# MORAL RESPONSIBILITY

the most intense degree, deep somnambulism, is neither rare nor difficult to encounter.

Must we conclude that these revelations should throw the masses into terror, that the population is doomed to universal hallucination, or that a mere glance at a passerby is enough to hypnotize them? This is an exaggeration against which you, as a moralist and philosopher, have wisely warned the public.

There is no such thing as a "magnetizer"; there is no "magnetic fluid." <note>Bernheim is arguing against the older theory of "animal magnetism," which suggested that a physical fluid or energy passed from the doctor to the patient. He believes the power lies entirely in the patient's mind.</note> Neither <term>Donato</term> <note>Alfred d'Hont (1845–1900), a famous Belgian stage hypnotist who performed under this name.</note> nor <term>Hansen</term> <note>Carl Hansen (1833–1897), a Danish hypnotist whose public demonstrations influenced many scientists of the era.</note> possess special hypnotic virtues. Induced sleep does not depend on the hypnotist, but on the subject: it is their own faith that puts them to sleep; no one can be hypnotized against their will if they resist the command. I am happy to join you in reassuring the public against any chimerical fear that a false interpretation of the facts might cause.

Does this mean, therefore, that justice and human morality should not be moved by these revelations? That everything has been said, everything foreseen, and that everything is for the best in the best of judicial organizations? To say so would perhaps be to willfully close one’s eyes to a fruitful truth. You did not fear to say that legal experts and philosophers have much to gain from these studies, and we should be grateful to <term>Mr. Liégeois</term> <note>Jules Liégeois (1833–1908), a law professor who worked with Bernheim to study how hypnosis might be used to commit or be a victim of a crime.</note> for having brought the question frankly to the academic forum.

Induced somnambulism shows extreme cases, those where the suggested act imposes itself with an irresistible command. But nothing happens in deep sleep that does not have its analogue—its diminutive form, if I may say so—in the waking state. Sleep exaggerates <term>physiological automatism</term> <note>Involuntary actions or behaviors performed without conscious intention.</note>; it does not create it. Between a fatal suggestion and an absolutely voluntary determination, every degree can exist. And who could analyze all the suggestive elements that intervene without our knowledge in the acts we believe to have come from our own initiative! Will, free will, moral responsibility: grave and thrilling questions! A painful philosophical doubt that grips the human conscience!

<summary>Bernheim reassures the public that hypnosis requires the subject's cooperation rather than "magical" powers, while simultaneously warning that the study of suggestion challenges our traditional understanding of free will and legal responsibility.</summary>

# THE DANGERS OF IGNORANCE

Truth is never dangerous! Only ignorance is defenseless! You speak of universal hallucination! It existed in the past, when we did not know, when we did not even suspect the singular ease with which artificial hallucination can be produced! It existed when a naive faith in witchcraft—as if implanted in the human brain by centuries of suggestion—blinded the finest minds; when the Sabbath <note>original: "sabbat"; referring to the "Witches' Sabbath," a folkloric gathering of those practicing witchcraft.</note>, sorcerers, succubi, incubi <note>In medieval folklore, these were demons believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping humans.</note>, gnomes, evil spirits, and all those phantoms conjured by the imagination were considered realities; when trembling science did not dare, in the face of the burning stake, to challenge all-powerful religious superstition! How many crimes, how many catastrophes, how many judicial errors would have been spared poor humanity, if scientific truth had been able to come to light! The history of the devil, of witchcraft, of possessions, the history of demonic epidemics—these suggested collective hallucinations—weigh like a frightful nightmare upon the centuries that preceded our own! And even in our day, how many superstitions suggested by the blindness of a crude law will disappear like shadows under the torch of scientific truth!

To conclude this all-too-long response, allow me to add, most honored master, that I have deeply meditated upon these words of <term>Bacon</term> <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), the English philosopher who pioneered the scientific method. This is a translation of his famous aphorism from "Novum Organum."</note>:

> "The human mind does not receive the light of things with sincerity, but rather mixes it with its own will and passions; thus it creates a science to its own liking; for the truth that man receives most willingly is the one he desires."

*hallucination, witchcraft, sabbath, succubi, incubi, gnomes, superstition, scientific truth, Bacon*

> “Paracelsus,” this author further adds, “that great partisan of occultism, had recognized the cause of the effects of amulets and similar things, for he wrote these judicious words: ‘Whether the object of your faith be real or false, you will nonetheless obtain the same effects; thus, if I believe in a statue of Saint Peter as I would have believed in Saint Peter himself, I will obtain the same effects that I would have obtained from Saint Peter himself; but that is a superstition. It is faith, however, which produces these miracles, and whether it be true or false, it will always produce the same wonders.’” <note>original: "Que l'objet de votre foi soit réel ou faux, vous n'en obtiendrez pas moins les mêmes effets..." Let us compare these words to those spoken by a sixteenth-century author, Pietro Pomponazzi of Milan, which are reported by Hack Tuke¹:

> “One can easily conceive of the marvelous effects that confidence and imagination can produce, especially when they are reciprocal between the sick and the one who acts upon them. The healings attributed to certain relics are the effect of this imagination and confidence. Skeptics and philosophers know that if, in place of the bones of a saint, one put those of any other skeleton, the sick would be no less restored to health, if they believed they were approaching true relics.”

The loadstone <note>Natural magnetic ore, also known as magnetite.</note> which served the Egyptians in the preparation of their prophylactic amulets has at all times cured gouty pains, headaches, toothaches, and hysteria. In the last century, artificial magnets manufactured by Father Hell, a famous astronomer from Vienna, and employed in the form of magnetic armatures, cured spasms, convulsions, and paralysis. Applied by Abbé Lenoble as constant and habitual armatures, they were no less effective in serious nervous affections.

->ABBÉ LENOBLE'S MAGNETS<-

Let us dwell a little on magnet therapy <note>original: "magnétothérapie"</note>, for it was—along with Burcq's metal therapy <note>Victor Burcq (1822–1889) was a physician who claimed that placing different metals on the skin could cure various nervous disorders.</note>—a true precursor to hypnotic therapy; Father Hell's medicinal magnetism preceded Mesmer’s animal magnetism; modern magnet therapy preceded therapeutic suggestion.

Abbé Lenoble, who had achieved more perfect methods of creating artificial magnets of a force unknown until then and who had observed their therapeutic applications, established a depot for his magnets in Paris in 1771. He advertised pieces designed to be applied to the wrists, the chest, etc., as well as bracelets and magnetic crosses. In 1777, he entrusted the Royal Society of Medicine with the task of verifying the accuracy of his claims. The Society commissioned Andry and Thouret to repeat his experiments. The remarkable report by these authors, included in the society's memoirs, is marked by a judicious and truly scientific spirit.

Andry and Thouret reported forty-eight observations in which the magnet was tested by them or in their presence; these involved toothaches, nervous pains in the head and lower back, rheumatic pains, facial neuralgia, <term>tic douloureux</term> <note>A chronic pain condition affecting the trigeminal nerve in the face, causing sudden, intense exhaustion or burning pain.</note>, stomach spasms, convulsive hiccups, palpitations, different kinds of tremors, convulsions, <term>hystero-epilepsy</term> <note>A historical diagnosis, popularized by Jean-Martin Charcot, describing patients who exhibited symptoms of both hysteria and epilepsy.</note>, etc.

Among the observed effects, many occurred shortly after the application of the magnet. In several cases, sharp neuralgic pains in the face were calmed each time by contact with the magnet. Spasmodic and convulsive symptoms disappeared rapidly after its application; a nervous cough was calmed instantly and did not return. In one case, convulsive movements of the arm and a <term>contracture</term> <note>A permanent shortening of a muscle or joint, often resulting in deformity or limited movement.</note> that prevented the use of the hand were suspended or significantly diminished during the course of the day. Rheumatic pains were calmed, and those which some patients felt returning by...

In other patients, similar pains, calmed by the action of the magnet, would reappear in different regions of the body; it was sufficient to apply a few magnetic pieces there to dispel them. Finally, against toothaches, the application of magnets was sometimes followed by prompt and noticeable relief. Other variable sensations were noted at each renewal of the fittings: a sensation of heat in the affected parts, vertigo, nausea, palpitations, headaches, itching, tugging, bowel movements, etc. In summary, without exaggerated enthusiasm, and by the irrefutable observation of facts, the commissioners of the Royal Society of Medicine recognize that medicinal magnetism has a real, effective action—not against organic diseases <note>Conditions involving physical damage to organs</note>, but against nervous disorders of various natures that further observation would have to define more precisely.

-># BURCQ’S METALLOTHERAPY<-

I have seen neuralgic pains modified, attacks of nervous dyspnea <note>shortness of breath caused by nervous disorders</note> rapidly stopped, etc. Laennec <note>René Laennec, the French physician who invented the stethoscope</note> praises magnets in the treatment of angina pectoris. The discredit that attached itself to the practices of "animal magnetism"—which, instead of bearing fruit as it could have on the grounds of scientific observation, had collapsed with Mesmer <note>Franz Mesmer, whose theories on "animal magnetism" led to the development of hypnotism but were often dismissed as fraud</note> into a dangerous charlatanism—this discredit appears to have also enveloped the practices of magnetotherapy. The magnet lost its place in the therapeutic arsenal. When, thirty-five years ago, Dr. Burcq spread his doctrine of metallotherapy to the medical public, he found only skeptics. Metallotherapy, and with it magnetotherapy, were resurrected. The magnet, like metals, often restores lost sensitivity.

I myself have begun a series of investigations to determine the value of magnetotherapy in various nervous disorders; these investigations were published in the *Revue médicale de l'Est*, 1881.

### MISCELLANEOUS PRACTICES AND HEALERS

But during the course of these researches, I came to know the <term>suggestive method</term> <note>the practice of influencing a patient's physical or mental state through verbal or mental hints</note> of Mr. Liébeault <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), a French physician and a father of the Nancy School of hypnotism</note>; I observed therapeutic results that were far more consistent and far more rapid. What the magnet produces, simple suggestion always produces, and I wondered if the therapeutic virtue of metals and magnets might not be a purely suggestive virtue. One of my observations, which will be read later, points in this direction. However, I do not wish to claim that this is absolutely the case. It belongs to further observation to provide the answer. What is certain is that suggestion plays a very large role in the dynamic effects obtained. The medicine of magnets and metals is perhaps only a medicine of the imagination. And if Trousseau <note>Armand Trousseau, the influential physician mentioned on the previous page</note> had been able to see what the imagination achieves in <term>hypnotic sleep</term> <note>a state of trance or deep relaxation where the subject is highly responsive to suggestion</note>, he would undoubtedly not have attributed the therapeutic influence of magnets to any other mechanism.

And now, without it being necessary to insist, one will easily understand the possible effectiveness of the various practices that have succeeded one another from antiquity to the present day, applied to the healing of diseases. Let us cite the invocations of the Egyptian priests to obtain from each <term>genius</term> <note>a guardian spirit or minor deity believed to govern specific parts of the body</note> the healing of the limbs subject to its influence; the magic formulas that taught the use of <term>simples</term> <note>medicinal herbs or plants used individually rather than in a mixture</note> against diseases; and the medicine of the descendants of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note> in the <term>Asclepieia</term> <note>healing temples dedicated to Aesculapius</note> or temples of that god. Let us also cite the sympathetic powder of Paracelsus <note>a 16th-century remedy believed to heal a wound by being applied to the weapon that caused it</note>, the metallic tractors of Perkins <note>Elisha Perkins, an American physician who used metal rods to supposedly "draw out" disease</note>, and the pseudo-metallic tractors (made of wood) no less effective, used by Drs. Haygarth and Falconer <note>British doctors who proved Perkins's rods were a placebo by achieving the same results with wooden replicas</note>; and in our own day, homeopathic medicine and the medicine of Mattei <note>Count Cesare Mattei, founder of "electro-homoeopathy," a popular 19th-century alternative treatment</note>. Must we speak of the <term>Royal Touch</term> <note>the tradition of monarchs touching subjects to cure "the King’s Evil," or scrofula</note>, the miraculous healings at the tomb of Deacon Paris <note>François de Pâris, a Jansenist whose grave became a site of religious ecstasy and alleged miracles in the 1730s</note>, and the no less miraculous healings at Knock in Ireland and especially at Lourdes in France? And the numerous healers—some of whom were honest—who believed themselves gifted, like certain magnetizers, with supernatural properties, and who were practicing suggestion without knowing it: the Irishman Greatrakes <note>Valentine Greatrakes, known as "The Stroker" for his healing touch in the 17th century</note>, the German priest Gassner <note>Johann Joseph Gassner, a famous 18th-century exorcist and healer</note>, and the Prince-Abbot of Hohenlohe <note>Prince Alexander of Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst, a 19th-century priest famous for his "miraculous" distant healings</note>.

# THE ROLE OF SUGGESTION IN MEDICATION

Father Mathew <note>Theobald Mathew (1790–1856), an Irish teetotalist reformer who was often credited with miraculous cures</note>, the peasant healer from the surroundings of Saumur, the Zouave Jacob <note>Auguste-Henri Jacob (1828–1913), a famous French healer who claimed to cure through the power of his gaze and presence</note>, and so many others who exist everywhere, whose fame does not extend beyond the region where they exercise their mysterious power!

Does suggestion not claim a share in the effectiveness of certain pharmaceutical, hydrotherapeutic, and electrical treatments? "Dr. John Tanner," says Hack Tuke <note>Daniel Hack Tuke (1827–1895), a prominent British physician and expert on the influence of the mind on the body</note>, "has advocated the treatment of <term>hysterical aphonia</term> <note>the loss of one's voice due to emotional or psychological distress rather than physical injury</note> by the application of electro-magnetism to the tongue alone. He establishes that in more than fifty cases he applied this treatment without success failing him even once. He specifically cites four instances. In the first, the return of the voice was manifested by a great cry; in the second, the voice returned immediately; in the third, the voice was recovered, but lost again within ten minutes; a new application of the treatment brought about a definitive recovery; in the fourth case, there was also an instantaneous return of the voice." Dr. Tanner adds the following considerations: "It is very important, before applying electro-magnetism, to persuade the patient *that he will be cured*; if the efforts of persuasion do not succeed, it is probable that it will be ineffective."

In a witty study dedicated by Dr. Lisle to "imagination medicine" in the *Medical Union* (October 24 and 26, 1861) and entitled: *Orthodox Homeopathy*, this influence of the <term>moral on the physical</term> <note>in 19th-century medicine, "the moral" referred to the psychological or mental state, while "the physical" referred to the body</note> is elegantly presented. Let us also point out to readers who wish to delve deeper into this subject the article *Imagination* by Virey in the *Dictionary of Medical Sciences* in 60 volumes, the works of Padioleau (*Moral Medicine*) and of Charpignon (*Studies on Animic and Vitalist Medicine*), the book by Mr. Liébeault (*On Sleep and Analogous States Considered Especially from the Perspective of the Action of the Mind on the Body*), and especially the recent work by Hack Tuke (*The Body and the Mind: Action of the Psychological and the Imagination on the Physical*).

# HEALING THROUGH IMAGINATION

...readers some observations of healing obtained through the influence of the imagination; these are well-known facts, but it is useful to have them before our eyes, for they show that what we are doing has always been done: <term>suggestive therapy</term> <note>the practice of treating ailments by influencing a patient's expectations or beliefs</note> is not new; what is new is its method of systematic application and its definitive adoption by mainstream medicine.

Sobernheim <note>Joseph Friedrich Sobernheim (1803–1846), a German physician and pharmacologist</note>, cited by Charpignon <note>Jules Charpignon, a 19th-century French physician and author of works on medical psychology</note>, recounts that a doctor was treating a man suffering from a paralysis of the tongue that no treatment had been able to cure. He wished to try an instrument of his own invention from which he expected an excellent result. Before proceeding with the operation, he placed a pocket thermometer in the patient's mouth. The patient imagined that this was the life-saving instrument; after a few minutes, he cried out with joy that he could move his tongue freely.

One will find among my own observations a case of the same kind. A young girl admitted to my clinical service had suffered from complete <term>nervous aphonia</term> <note>the loss of one's voice due to psychological or emotional factors rather than physical injury</note> for nearly four weeks. After formulating this diagnosis, I told the students that nervous aphonia sometimes yields instantly to <term>electrification</term> <note>the medical application of electric current, popular in the 19th century</note>, which can act through its purely suggestive influence. I sent for the induction apparatus. Before using it, I wanted to try simple suggestion through affirmation. I placed my hand on the larynx, applied a few movements to the organ, and said: "Now you can speak aloud." In an instant, I had her say successively: *a*, then *b*, then *Marie*. She continued to speak distinctly; the aphonia had disappeared.

### RELIGIOUS SUGGESTIONS

...this imaginary rhubarb <note>rhubarb root was a common 19th-century laxative</note>, she woke up and had easy evacuations five or six times.

A similar result was reported by Demangeon <note>Jean-Baptiste Demangeon (1764–1844), a French physician interested in the intersection of physiology and the soul</note> (*On the Imagination*, 1879). "A monk was supposed to purge himself the next morning; he dreamed that he had taken the medicine, and as a result, he woke up to yield to natural urges: he had eight abundant <term>bowel movements</term> <note>original: "gardes-robes," an archaic French medical term referring to the contents of a commode or stool</note>."

But among all the psychological causes that, by appealing to the imagination, set in motion the brain's mechanism for possible cures, none is as effective as religious faith. To it are certainly owed many authentically recorded healings.

The Princess of Schwartzenberg <note>likely Princess Pauline von Schwarzenberg, a prominent member of the Austrian nobility</note> had suffered for eight years from <term>paraplegia</term> <note>paralysis of the lower half of the body</note> for which the most famous doctors in Germany and France had been consulted. In 1821, the Prince of Hohenlohe <note>Alexander Leopold Franz Emmerich, Prince of Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst, a priest known for his "miraculous" healings</note>, a priest since 1815, brought to the princess a peasant who had convinced the young priest of the power of prayer in healing the sick. The paralytic woman was freed from the mechanical braces that had been applied to her for several months by Dr. Heime to combat the <term>contracture</term> <note>a condition of shortening and hardening of muscles or tendons, leading to rigid joints</note> of her limbs. The priest invited the paralyzed woman to join her faith with his own and that of the peasant. 

— Do you believe yourself already relieved? 

— Oh! yes, I believe it with a sincere faith. 

— Well then, get up and walk.

At these words, the princess rose, walked around the room several times, and attempted to go up and down the stairs. The next day she went to church, and from that moment on, she retained the use of her limbs (Charpignon <note>Jules Charpignon, a French physician who wrote extensively on medical psychology and animal magnetism</note>).

The reader has understood that this was a case of one of those <term>nervous paralyses</term> <note>today often referred to as functional neurological disorder (FND) or conversion disorder, where physical symptoms arise from psychological stress rather than structural nerve damage</note>, which are so common, often stubborn, and sometimes capable of being cured by a violent emotion.

The same can occur for <term>hysterical contractures</term>. "A vivid psychological emotion," says Charcot <note>Jean-Martin Charcot (1825–1893), the "founder of modern neurology" and teacher of Sigmund Freud</note>, "a set of events that strike the imagination forcefully, or the reappearance of <term>menstruation</term> <note>original: "règles"</note> after a long absence..."

Hypnotism, like natural sleep, exalts the imagination and makes the brain more accessible to suggestion; even the strongest minds cannot escape the hallucinatory suggestions of their dreams. It is a physiological law that sleep puts the brain in such a psychic state that the imagination accepts and recognizes as real the impressions transmitted to it. To induce this special psychic state through hypnotism and to exploit the <term>suggestibility</term> <note>The quality of being inclined to accept and act on the suggestions of others.</note> thus artificially heightened for the purpose of healing or relief—this is the role of hypnotic psycho-therapeutics.

# ->INHIBITION AND DYNAMOGENY<-

depending on the individual, the phenomena commanded; docile in some even in the waking state, it becomes so in almost everyone when a hypnotic state, or one analogous to it, has put to sleep or numbed the faculties of reason, judgment, and control which moderate and restrain <term>cerebral automatism</term> <note>The concept that the brain can execute complex actions or respond to stimuli without the conscious intervention of the will.</note>. Then the brain, more effectively impressed by the formulated order, accepts the idea and transforms it into an act. We have seen hypnotic suggestion produce paralysis, <term>contracture</term> <note>A state of continuous, involuntary muscle contraction that prevents normal movement.</note>, anesthesia, pain, coughing, nausea, etc.; we have seen these dynamic effects of suggestion persist upon waking, or occur only upon waking (post-hypnotic suggestion). The brain refuses to perceive the <term>centripetal</term> <note>Moving toward the center; in biology, this refers to nerve impulses traveling from the limbs or organs toward the brain.</note> impressions of tactile, visceral, or sensory feeling; it refuses to activate the motor cells of the spinal cord that produce movement; from this come motor paralysis, anesthesia, and psychic blindness or deafness—these are *phenomena of inhibition*. Or, on the contrary, it perceives centripetal impressions with greater intensity; it sends a supplement of activity to the motor cells; from this come sensory and sensitive hyperesthesia, more energetic muscular work, or contracture—these are *phenomena of dynamogeny* <note>Derived from the Greek for "power" and "creation"; refers to the generation of increased nervous or muscular energy.</note>. Other psychological processes (<term>moral emotions</term> <note>In 19th-century medical terms, "moral" refers to psychological or emotional states rather than physical ones.</note>) or experimental ones (the experiments of <term>Brown-Séquard</term> <note>Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (1817–1894), a pioneering neurologist and physiologist famous for his studies on the spinal cord and "rejuvenating" effects of organ extracts.</note>) can trigger this cerebral mechanism of inhibition and dynamogeny; such is the paralysis or the impossibility of speaking produced by fright (**"the voice stuck in the throat"** <note>original Latin: *vox faucibus hæsit*, a quote from Virgil's Aeneid describing the physical effect of intense fear</note>), or the ten-fold increase of strength through anger or unusual excitement.

Observation having thus demonstrated what simple hypnotic suggestion can achieve in a state of health, it was natural to apply these findings to the pathological state and to use the nervous activity concentrated by suggestion to neutralize morbid phenomena. ### ->HEALINGS OBTAINED BY THE MAGNETIZER<-

...to suppress the anesthesia, contracture, or paralysis created by disease; to increase weakened muscular strength; and to favorably modify or restore functional dynamism that has been perverted or diminished by a pathological state—provided, of course, that the organic state of the body permits such restoration.

This idea, so simple that it seems it should have been obvious to the first doctors who learned about suggestion, took a long time to come to light.

In the early days of <term>Mesmerism</term> <note>A healing system developed by Franz Mesmer in the 18th century, based on the belief in an invisible "animal magnetism" or fluid that could be manipulated to cure patients.</note>, therapeutic effects were frequently observed. 

> "Some of the magnetized patients," says the report by Husson <note>Henri-Marie Husson (1772–1853) was a French physician who led a famous 1826 investigation into animal magnetism for the Royal Academy of Medicine, which—unlike earlier reports—was somewhat favorable to its existence.</note>, "experienced no benefit. Others felt a more or less marked relief: namely, one experienced the suspension of habitual pains; another, the return of strength; a third, a delay of several months in the appearance of epileptic seizures; and a fourth, the complete cure of a severe and long-standing paralysis."

Mesmer, Puységur, Dupotet, and many other magnetizers obtained cures without knowing exactly what they were doing. Rostan <note>Léon Rostan (1790–1866) was a prominent French physician and member of the Academy of Medicine who argued that magnetic phenomena were real physiological effects rather than just imagination.</note> was able to say, despite the skepticism of the Academy: "They were hardly physicians, and hardly physiologists, those who denied that magnetism caused changes in the organization [of the body] and that it could possess some power in the cure of diseases."

As long as magnetic phenomena were considered the effect of a <term>fluid</term> <note>The "magnetic fluid" was thought by early practitioners to be a physical substance, similar to electricity or heat, that flowed from the healer's body into the patient.</note> acting on the organism, cures were attributed to this fluidic action. Magnetism, through its mysterious influence on the <term>vital principle</term> <note>A historical medical concept that a non-physical force or "spark of life" governs the functions of living organisms.</note>, restored the harmony of bodily functions; it was considered beneficial, much like heat, light, or electricity.

Since the time of Braid <note>James Braid (1795–1860), a Scottish surgeon often called the "Father of Hypnotism," who proved that the effects of magnetism were caused by the subject's own nervous system and "suggestion," not by an invisible fluid.</note>, the idea of a magnetic fluid has retained only a few followers; hypnotic suggestion has replaced magnetism. It is the imagination of the subject alone that is activated and produces all the phenomena.

A strange thing! Braid—who was the first to establish the doctrine of suggestion on unshakeable foundations, a concept briefly glimpsed by Bertrand <note>Alexandre Bertrand (1795–1831) was one of the first theorists to argue that "animal magnetism" was actually a psychological state driven by the patient's own mind.</note>—did not yet think to apply...

### MECHANISM OF HEALING ACCORDING TO BRAID

...to ignore suggestion itself, in its most natural mode, suggestion *by word of mouth* <note>original: "par la parole"</note>, to achieve hypnosis and therapeutic effects. He induces sleep by fixing the eyes on a shiny object; he induces therapeutic effects through *special manipulations*.

These manipulations are based on this fact: that the <term>cataleptiform</term> <note>A state of muscle rigidity similar to catalepsy, often seen in hypnotic trances, where limbs remain fixed in whatever position they are placed.</note> rigidity of a limb produces, according to Braid, an acceleration of the pulse, which becomes small and contracted. This acceleration of the pulse during the effort to keep the limbs extended for five minutes is much greater in a state of hypnotism than during the same effort normally. If one returns the muscles to their <term>flaccid</term> <note>Relaxed or limp; the opposite of rigid or contracted.</note> state while the subject is still in hypnotism, the pulse quickly drops to the level it was before the experiment, and even below it.

With this established, Braid varies the manipulations according to the goal in view.
> "To decrease the force of circulation in a limb and reduce its sensitivity," he says, "one must put the muscles of that limb into activity, leaving the others in flaccidity. — If one wants to increase the force and sensitivity in a limb, it must be kept in flaccidity and the others put into catalepsy. — If one wants to obtain a general depression <note>In this context, "depression" refers to a lowering of physiological activity or sedation, rather than a psychological state.</note>, after holding one or two limbs extended for a short time, they are carefully returned to a normal position and the entire body is left at rest. To obtain a general excitation, all limbs are put into catalepsy, causing difficulty in the free transmission of blood to the limbs, and consequently an increase in cardiac activity, an influx of blood to the brain, and excitation of the nervous centers."

Furthermore, by keeping a particular organ in action while the others remain asleep, there is a considerable increase in its activity through the concentration of nervous energy; by keeping the other organs active and the one that is too active at rest, the activity of the latter is reduced.

->### BRAID’S MANIPULATIONS<-

> “Whether I have been right or wrong,” the author adds, “in my theoretical views, it cannot be doubted that in many cases I have succeeded in the application of hypnotism as a curative agent; and the successful results of the operations were so immediate and so clear that one could not fail to recognize the relationship of cause and effect. However, it seems demonstrated to me that success depends largely on the impression produced by the modification in the circulation.”

Braid reports about sixty instances of healing or improvement obtained by his method. While the facts of these cases remain, his theoretical views are certainly erroneous. I have been unable to confirm the accuracy of his assertions regarding the changes in cardiac activity produced by <term>catalepsy</term> <note>A state of muscular rigidity where the subject maintains a fixed posture.</note>. Even if they were accurate, moreover, these modifications would not be enough to explain healings as rapid as those that were observed.

It is quite singular that after having so well established that the source of all hypnotic phenomena lies in the imagination of the subject—that all these phenomena are purely psychic—Braid did not think to explain the curative effects obtained by this same psychic influence. The pioneer of the doctrine of suggestion, Braid, forgetting his own guiding principle, was still practicing—just like all his predecessors, and as many of his successors still do today—suggestion without knowing it. His patients knew they were being hypnotized for a curative purpose; they held onto this idea during their sleep; they knew the manipulations performed on them were intended to deliver them from their ailments; therapeutic suggestion was taking place within the brain.

Braid does not seem to have had successors in his own country. In France, Dr. Charpignon is one of those who has best studied the influence of faith and suggestion in the hypnotic state. But alongside the moral influence, he still believes in a "magnetic fluidic" <note>An older belief in a physical fluid or "aura" that passed from the healer to the patient to restore health.</note> influence that tends to restore destroyed harmony.

One must, in reality, wait until 1860 to find the doctrine of suggestion entirely freed from...

->## LIÉBEAULT’S VOCAL SUGGESTION<-

...all the elements that still distorted it in the hands of Braid himself, and applied it in the simplest possible way to <term>therapeutics</term> <note>The branch of medicine concerned with the treatment of disease and the action of remedial agents.</note>. Previously, Durand de Gros had, like Abbé Faria, used simple vocal suggestion—the spoken word—to produce the phenomena of hypnosis. Dr. Liébeault had the idea of applying this same vocal suggestion to medical treatment.

The patient is put to sleep through suggestion, which is to say, by causing the idea of sleep to penetrate their brain. They are treated by suggestion, which is to say, by causing the idea of healing to penetrate their brain. Dr. Liébeault’s method consists of affirming out loud, while the subject is asleep, the disappearance of the symptoms they feel. One seeks to establish in them the conviction that these symptoms no longer exist or will disappear; that the pain is dissipating, that sensation is returning to the limbs, that muscle strength is increasing, that the appetite is being restored. One takes advantage of the special psychic receptivity created by hypnotism—of the brain's docility, of the increased suggestibility, and of the heightened <term>ideomotor</term> <note>The process where a thought or mental image triggers an automatic physical movement.</note>, <term>ideosensitive</term> <note>The process where a thought triggers a physical sensation, like warmth or tingling.</note>, and <term>ideosensory</term> <note>The process where a thought triggers a sensory perception, such as a sound or vision.</note> reflexivity—to provoke useful reflexes, and to invite the brain to do what it can to transform the accepted idea into reality.

Such is the method of therapeutic suggestion for which Dr. Liébeault is the pioneer. He was the first to clearly establish that the cures obtained by the old <term>magnetizers</term> <note>Followers of Franz Mesmer who believed they could heal patients using a "universal magnetic fluid."</note> and even by Braid’s hypnotic operations are not the work of a mysterious fluid, nor the work of physiological modifications due to special manipulations, but solely the work of suggestion. The entirety of magnetic medicine is nothing more than "medicine of the imagination"; the imagination is placed by the hypnotic state into such a condition that it cannot escape suggestion.

Dr. Liébeault’s method remained ignored for a long time, even by the doctors of Nancy. In 1884, Charles Richet <note>A Nobel Prize-winning physiologist who investigated both traditional medicine and psychic phenomena.</note> was content to say only that magnetism often has advantages, that it calms nervous agitation, and that it can cure or improve certain types of insomnia.

<summary>This page describes Dr. Liébeault's revolutionary "vocal suggestion" method, which replaced the physical rituals of earlier hypnotists with simple spoken affirmations. He argued that the true power of hypnotic healing came from the patient's own imagination and the brain's ability to turn an idea into a physical reality.</summary>

<keywords>Liébeault, vocal suggestion, Nancy School, therapeutic suggestion, James Braid, imagination, ideomotor, Charles Richet, hypnotism history</keywords>

# OVERVIEW OF <term>SUGGESTIVE THERAPEUTICS</term> <note>A method of medical treatment where the doctor uses the power of suggestion—the spoken word and mental influence—to alleviate physical and psychological symptoms.</note>

Since 1882, I have experimented—at first timidly and without any confidence—with the suggestive method that I had seen employed by Mr. Liébeault. Today, it is in common use at my clinic; I practice it in front of my students. There is perhaps not a day where I do not show them some functional disorder, pain, <term>paresis</term> <note>A condition of muscular weakness caused by nerve damage or partial paralysis.</note>, discomfort, or insomnia, moderated or instantly suppressed by suggestion.

Here, for example, is a child brought to my consultation with rheumatic muscle pain in the arm dating back four or five days; the arm is painful to the touch, and the child cannot lift it to his head. I say to him: “Close your eyes, my child, and sleep.” I hold his eyelids closed and I continue to speak to him. “You are sleeping, and you will continue to sleep until I tell you to wake up. You are sleeping very well, just as in your own bed; you are quite well, at ease; your arms, your legs, everything is asleep and you can no longer move them.” I withdraw my fingers from his eyelids; they remain closed. I put his arms in the air, and they stay there. Then, touching the painful arm, I say: “The pain is disappearing; you have no more pain at all; you can move your arm without any pain; and when you are awake, you will no longer feel the pain; it will not return.” To increase the force of the suggestion by embodying it, so to speak, in a material sensation, I suggest—following the example of Mr. Liébeault—a feeling of heat *in the painful spot* <note>original Latin: "loco dolenti"</note>. The heat replaces the pain. I say to the child: “You feel heat in your arm, the heat is increasing, and you no longer have any pain.”

After a few minutes, I wake the child; he remembers nothing; the sleep was deep. The pain has almost completely disappeared; the child easily lifts his arm to his head. In the following days, I see the father; he is the mailman who brings me my letters. He tells me that the pain has completely disappeared, without returning.

Here now is a tall twenty-six-year-old boy, a worker at the forges. For a year, following an effort made to bend an iron bar, he has felt a sensation...
