### VARIOUS MODES OF SUGGESTION

...in deep sleep. It is in *somnambulism that suggestion acquires its maximum efficacy*, where healings are often instantaneous and appear miraculous. Some subjects resist for many sessions; they only fall into a state of drowsiness; the effect obtained is slight or doubtful. With perseverance, some end up—after a more or less lengthy period of several days or even several weeks of unproductive <term>hypnotizations</term> <note>The process of inducing a hypnotic state.</note>—falling into a deeper sleep; and then the therapeutic action of suggestion can be rapid and lasting.

The mode of suggestion must also be varied and adapted to the specific <term>suggestibility</term> <note>The degree to which an individual is receptive to the ideas or commands of the practitioner.</note> of the subject. The simple word is not always enough to impose an idea. Sometimes, it is necessary to reason, demonstrate, and convince; for some, one must affirm with force; for others, insinuate with gentleness. For in the state of sleep, as in the state of wakefulness, the moral individuality of each subject persists, with their own character, inclinations, and specific impressionability. Hypnotization does not cast all subjects into a uniform mold to turn them purely and simply into <term>automata</term> <note>Beings that act mechanically without conscious will; robots.</note>, moved by the sole will of the <term>magnetizer</term> <note>A historical term for the hypnotist, referring to the older belief in "animal magnetism."</note>; it increases <term>cerebral docility</term> <note>The brain's readiness to accept and act upon external suggestions.</note>; it makes automatic activity prevail over voluntary activity. But the latter persists to a certain extent; the subject thinks, reasons, discusses, and accepts more easily than in the waking state, but does not always accept, especially in the lighter stages of sleep. In these cases, one must know the character of the patient and their particular psychic state in order to *make an impression* on them.

The use of touch, frictions, movements applied to the diseased area, and suggested heat often contribute effectively. I have seen—this is noted in one of our clinical observations—the <term>electrification</term> <note>The application of an electric current for medical purposes.</note> of the painful part, materializing the suggestion through a new sensation, succeed where simple affirmation had been insufficient. ## FAILURES DUE TO THE NATURE OF THE ILLNESS

...forward; he is absolutely unable to walk. Nothing works. This has lasted for weeks. When he tries to walk, these tremors repeat with stubbornness and he is forced to stop and lean on something to keep from falling.

Simple suggestion does not always succeed in stopping these tremors; but if I make him walk, whether in a state of sleep or a state of wakefulness, by energetically affirming that he no longer has tremors—if I make him trot actively, without truce or rest—the tremors disappear and he manages to run for hours on end without feeling any tendency toward the <term>tic</term> <note>A repetitive, involuntary muscle contraction or habit.</note>. *Active suggestive training succeeds where simple passive suggestion has failed.*

Suggestive therapy, fertile in happy results in a very great number of cases, is not infallible. Even when it is handled with intelligence and stubbornness, it can fail; the cause of the failure is inherent *either to the illness or to the subject.*

I am not speaking of incurable diseases, some of whose manifestations can nonetheless be favorably improved by suggestion. Even in minor conditions, appearing simply functional, hypnotic psychotherapy sometimes fails, even though the subject is perfectly suggestible. I remember an Italian mason, who following a <term>contusion</term> <note>A medical term for a bruise or injury caused by a blow that does not break the skin.</note> had violent <term>lumbar pain</term> <note>Pain located in the lower back.</note> for several weeks. Suggestion continued with persistence for a long time achieved no more, even though this man easily fell into a deep sleep and appeared very suggestible.

I tried to hypnotize her again; to escape my persistent efforts <note>original: "obsessions"; in this clinical context, it refers to the doctor's repeated and insistent hypnotic suggestions</note>, she simulated sleep.

However, the persistent contracture led to a shortening of the Achilles tendon and <term>equine clubfoot</term> <note>original: "pied bot équin"; a deformity where the foot is fixed in a downward-pointing position, resembling a horse's hoof.</note>; on several occasions, it was necessary to put her under chloroform to straighten the foot and finally to sever the Achilles tendon. The contracture of the knee eventually subsided spontaneously; that of the leg and foot persists, and a fixed brace constantly keeps her foot flexed.

Against the urinary retention, I tried intimidation, electrical treatment <note>original: "électrisation"</note>, and the most varied methods in vain. Nothing worked. Recently, I have proceeded with a gentler approach; I hypnotized her again; she was cooperative and entered a deep sleep without simulation. She is distressed by her situation; she certainly wishes to be cured; she becomes irritated when accused of being unwilling. In March of this year, after I had hypnotized her several times while trying to instill the idea that she would soon be cured, she seemed to accept this idea; she even fixed, while in her sleep, the precise day when she would urinate spontaneously: in two weeks, on a Wednesday. The prediction was not realized: the urinary retention persisted.

This is certainly a case of contracture and <term>psychic paralysis</term> <note>A loss of motor function caused by psychological or "hysterical" factors rather than organic nerve damage.</note>. The rooted idea, the **unconscious auto-suggestion**, is such that nothing has yet been able to uproot it. At the beginning of the treatment, she seems to have convinced herself that hypnotism would not cure her. Is it this idea, so deeply etched <note>original: "encrée"; likely a play on "ancrée" (anchored) and "encre" (inked), implying a permanent mark on the mind.</note> into her brain, that paralyzes our efforts and her own desire to be cured?

I have made a point of showing failure alongside success,

# 233

<header>->PUBLISHED CASES OF HEALING<-</header>

...the shadow alongside the light. Suggestive therapeutics <note>original: "psycho-thérapeutique suggestive"</note> may fail, just like other treatments; but it often succeeds when other treatments have failed; often, it performs wonders—I do not say miracles.

I will now recount a fairly large number of clinical observations of suggestive therapeutics. These are not selective cases. I could, by publishing only those where the cure was complete and instantaneous, embellish the picture and strike the reader's mind more forcefully; I insist on remaining within the strict truth and presenting an idea as accurate as is currently possible regarding the results provided by therapeutic suggestion. Among our observations, some show rapid and radical cures, others slow and gradual; others show suggestion suppressing only certain symptoms of the condition; still others show it struggling for a long time against stubborn disorders that are improved but return with tenacity; and in this struggle of the mind against the body—persistent and prolonged—it is often one, and at other times the other, that prevails.

Only a few physicians, until today, have followed the <term>Nancy School</term> <note>A group of doctors in Nancy, France, led by Bernheim and Liébeault, who argued that hypnosis was a result of suggestion, a normal psychological process, rather than a symptom of hysteria.</note> in its trials of suggestive therapeutics, according to the method of Mr. Liébeault <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), a country doctor who is considered the father of the Nancy School of suggestive medicine.</note>. Let us cite Mr. Auguste Voisin who, at the congresses of Blois and Grenoble, called attention to its application in the treatment of mental illnesses. A very agitated hysterical woman was calmed by hypnotic suggestion, and affectionate and moral feelings were awakened in her, at least for a certain time. Three new observations recounted in the *General Bulletin of Therapeutics* <note>original: "Bulletin général de thérapeutique"</note> (April 15, 1886), are titled:

1st <term>Hystero-epilepsy</term> <note>A historical diagnosis, largely associated with Jean-Martin Charcot, describing patients who exhibited symptoms of both hysteria and epilepsy, often including dramatic seizures.</note>. Erotic delusion with hallucinations of sight and hearing. Treatment by hypnotic suggestion. Cure.

2nd <term>Melancholic delusion</term> <note>original: "délire mélancolique"; a clinical term used at the time to describe what we might now call severe clinical depression with psychotic features.</note>. Hallucinations of sight and hearing. Refusal of food. Cure by hypnotic suggestion.

<header>->PUBLISHED OBSERVATIONS OF CURES<-</header>

### 3. Hysteria. Hysterical insanity. Hallucinations of sight and hearing. Ideas of suicide. Hemianesthesia and hemidyschromatopsia. Cure by hypnotic suggestion.

<note>Hemianesthesia refers to a loss of sensation on one side of the body. Hemidyschromatopsia is a condition where color vision is impaired in only half of the visual field. Both were common symptoms associated with "hysteria" in 19th-century clinical reports.</note>

Let us also note an interesting observation of suggestive therapy followed by success in a hysterical patient, published by Mr. Séglas (*Archives of Neurology* <note>original: "Archives de Neurologie"</note>, November 1885), and one by Mr. Lombroso (*The Experimentalist* <note>original: "lo Spérimentale"</note>, November 1885).

In Germany, Mr. Berger (*Breslau Journal* <note>original: "Breslauer Zeitschrift"</note> 1880) reports that a hysterical contracture of the fingers was cured during the hypnotic state.

Preyer (*Hypnotism* <note>original: "der Hypnotismus"</note>, Berlin, 1882) says that his assistant, Dr. Creutzfield, used hypnotism to stop neuralgic pains.

Dr. Fischer (*So-called Magnetism or Hypnotism* <note>original: "der sog. Magnetismus oder Hypnotismus"</note>, Mainz, 1883), saw a similar result. Rieger (*Hypnotism* <note>original: "der Hypnotismus"</note>, Jena, 1884), also says he obtained very good effects from it, notably in a young girl in a state of contraction and excitation.

Dr. Wiebe, from whom the preceding citations are borrowed, has four times had recourse to hypnotism as a therapeutic means in the service of Professor Baumler in Freiburg im Breisgau; here are the results he obtained. (*Berlin Clinical Weekly* <note>original: "Berl. Klin. Wochenschr"</note>, 1884, no. 3):

In three of these cases, hypnotism brought about a prompt and lasting cure; in the fourth, the effect was not complete, but nevertheless useful. In the first case, hypnotism cured an anesthesia; in the second, a neuralgia; in the third, clonic convulsions <note>Involuntary, rhythmic muscle contractions and relaxations.</note> were suppressed; finally, in the fourth, convulsions that were also clonic were improved.

I borrow the account of these facts from a review on hypnotism inserted by Professor Lépine in the *Monthly Review* <note>original: "Revue mensuelle"</note> (1884, p. 829).

Despite these isolated facts, suggestive therapy has few adherents. I would be happy if the observations I am about to relate could contribute to popularizing the new method established by Mr. Liébeault.

**CASE STUDY I.** — *Left <term>hemiplegia</term> <note>Paralysis of one side of the body.</note> with <term>sensory-sensorial hemianesthesia</term> <note>Loss of sensation and impairment of the special senses, like sight and hearing, on one side of the body.</note> dating back one year. — Transient right hemiplegia. — Lesions in each hemisphere. — Bilateral post-hemiplegic tremor simulating <term>multiple sclerosis</term> <note>original: "sclérose en plaque"</note>. — Bilateral <term>reflex trepidation</term> <note>A rhythmic shaking or muscle spasm, known today as clonus.</note> and <term>contracture</term> <note>Persistent shortening of muscles or tendons, leading to rigid joints.</note> of the left limbs. — Cure of the hemianesthesia, tremor, and trepidation by a single application of a magnet to the face. — Return of the contracture of the left limbs with flexion of the hand; twenty months later, cure of the contracture by hypnotic suggestion. — Decrease in breathlessness. — Survival for three years. — Autopsy.*

In December of last year, there was a man in my service who, at first glance, appeared to be suffering from multiple sclerosis. A significant tremor shook his limbs as soon as he tried to move them, and it intensified as the intentional movement approached its goal. Upon examining him more closely, it was soon noted that he had left sensory-sensorial hemianesthesia, and we concluded that this was not a case of multiple sclerosis, but rather a bilateral post-hemiplegic tremor. Here is his story:

H..., a <term>marcaire</term> <note>A traditional mountain dairy farmer and cheese maker, particularly in the Vosges region of France.</note>, sixty-four years of age, now worn down by illness, suffering from emphysema and <term>catarrh</term> <note>Inflammation of the mucous membranes, especially in the airways.</note>, enjoyed good health until the night of December 3, 1879. Having gone to bed feeling unwell and wanting to rise at 3 a.m. to milk his cows, he felt a sense of vertigo, believed everything was spinning around him, and fell unconscious. Taken to the hospital at Saint-Nicolas-du-Port, he did not emerge from his coma until four days later. He was suffering from left hemiplegia with facial drooping and difficulty with speech. Around January 15, his left arm became stiff, and a tremor developed there which soon invaded the left leg and has continued to worsen since that day.

On January 18, the patient, staying with a family of workers, was still confined to his room; the hemiplegia had diminished slightly; he could pronounce a few words. That day, wanting to reach his bed, he again experienced a dizzy spell, believed everything was spinning around him, and, fearing he would fall, he

# HEMIPLEGIA AND HEMIANESTHESIA

In the lower limbs, the trembling is less marked; the patient performs all commanded movements well without <term>ataxia</term> <note>A lack of muscle control or coordination of voluntary movements.</note>, and he walks without incoordination or trembling; only a certain stiffness is noted on the left in the movements of the knee. The tendon reflexes are exaggerated; the sudden flexion of the foot triggers a *reflex trepidation <note>A rhythmic, involuntary shaking of the limb (clonus) caused by a sudden stretch of the muscle.</note> which lasts about a minute* and ceases with the sudden extension of the foot; percussion of the <term>patellar tendon</term> <note>The tendon just below the kneecap; the "knee-jerk" reflex.</note> gives rise to the same phenomenon. General sensitivity is abolished on the left, for touch as well as for pain and temperature. On the right, it is present but somewhat dulled. Here are the distances on this side at which two distinct sensations are obtained with the two points of a compass:

Arm, 3.5 cm; forearm, 4. — Hand: palm, 1.5; back, 2.5; fingertips, 1. — Thigh: anterior face, 4.5. — Calf, 8. — Back of the foot, 9.5; sole, 3. — Thorax: anterior face, 5.5. — Abdomen, 3. — Cheek, 2.5. — Forehead, 1.5. Intelligence is clear; no <term>cephalgia</term> <note>Headache.</note>, no vertigo, nor any abnormal sensations in the limbs; articulation of words is normal.

Rather intense oppression. Thorax bulging forward; exaggerated resonance on both sides near the sternum. Rough and dry inspiration, prolonged and <term>sibilant</term> <note>A whistling or wheezing sound.</note> expiration in the front.

*On December 30th*, the sensitivity persists, though dulled, in the lower limb.

### INTERPRETATION OF SYMPTOMS

was it the subject’s expectant attention, turned inward and suggesting to itself the return of sensation, that set the brain's healing mechanism into motion? The question does not yet seem definitively resolved to me.

Be that as it may, how are we to explain the disappearance—whether through a specific action of the magnet or the psychic action of suggestion—of phenomena as persistent as **hemianesthesia** <term>hemianesthesia: a total loss of sensation on one side of the body</term>, tremors, exaggerated **tendon reflexes** <term>tendon reflexes: involuntary muscle contractions in response to a stimulus, such as the common knee-jerk test</term>, and **contracture** <term>contracture: a condition where muscles or tendons become shortened and rigid, often fixing a limb in a distorted position</term>, all of which seem at first glance to be directly commanded by a physical injury to the organ?

Could the centripetal <note>Inward-moving, or traveling from the limbs toward the brain.</note> conductivity of sensory impressions, which was interrupted by the lesion involving the **internal white capsule** <term>internal white capsule: a vital bundle of nerve fibers deep in the brain that acts as a highway for sensory and motor signals</term> in its posterior third, have been re-established through other pathways? Or was it via the *white fibers still intact in this region, on the third section, toward the base of the brain?* Was it thanks to the fibers of the **sensory crossroads** <term>sensory crossroads: a specific region in the brain where various sensory pathways converge</term>, which were still preserved but affected only in their functional operation, that the magnet—whether through suggestive influence or otherwise—was able to restore muscular and tactile sensitivity? This is possible.

Let us also note that the anterior part of the **internal white capsule** was not destroyed, and that the **medullary tract** <term>medullary tract: a bundle of nerve fibers within the spinal cord</term> had not undergone descending degeneration <note>This refers to "Wallerian degeneration," where nerve fibers die off downstream from a brain injury. Moreover, it is well known that secondary contracture is not—as **Charcot** <note>Jean-Martin Charcot (1825–1893), the "father of modern neurology," who was the author’s contemporary and likely supervisor.</note> so aptly puts it—a direct function of the **pyramidal tract** <term>pyramidal tract: the primary pathway for voluntary movement signals from the brain to the limbs</term>; rather, the lesion or irritation of this tract resonates—due to the direct anatomical relationships that seem to exist between them—upon the motor cells of the **anterior horns** <term>anterior horns: the front sections of the spinal cord's gray matter that contain the nerves responsible for muscle movement</term>. From this arises the contracture or the increase in muscle tone; and from this, the exaltation of the **excito-motor** reflex action of the **spinal cord** manifesting as the exaggeration of **tendon reflexes**.

## OBSERVATION

**motor cells** <term>motor cells: nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that transmit signals to the muscles to create movement</term>, instead of remaining localized, may spread to one or several neighboring groups; the result is that intentional movement becomes complicated by more or less disordered involuntary movements. And one will see appear—depending on the more or less intense degree of this over-stimulation of the **spinal cord**, and according to the variable way each individual reacts—either a **hemitremor** <term>hemitremor: a persistent trembling or shaking affecting only one side of the body</term> or **hemichorea** <term>hemichorea: a condition characterized by involuntary, jerky, "dancing" movements on one side of the body</term>. Tremor, **contracture** <term>contracture: a condition where muscles become permanently shortened and rigid, often fixing a limb in a stiff position</term>, and **reflex trepidation** <term>reflex trepidation: a rapid, rhythmic shaking of a limb triggered by a simple reflex stimulus</term> are therefore three phenomena caused by a common pathogenic mechanism: the over-stimulation of the excito-motor ganglionic gray matter associated with the **pyramidal tract** <term>pyramidal tract: the main "highway" of nerve fibers that carries commands for voluntary movement from the brain to the spinal cord</term>.

The magnet—acting in the first instance by suspending these phenomena at the same time as the **anesthesia** <term>anesthesia: in this context, a total loss of sensation (touch, pain, etc.) rather than a drug-induced state</term>—did it act directly on the spinal cord by diminishing its exaggerated excitability? I do not think so. The tremor and the contracture disappeared after the return of sensitivity; and I am inclined to think that the disappearance of these symptoms was linked to the restoration of the tactile and muscular senses. By what mechanism?

Physiologists admit that the brain has a moderating influence on the **reflex excitability** <term>reflex excitability: the speed and intensity with which the spinal cord reacts to a stimulus without waiting for a command from the brain</term> of the spinal cord. Warned by the impressions reaching it regarding what is happening in the muscles and the organs set in motion—the position of the limbs, the degree of muscle contraction, the speed of movements, etc.—the brain can act with full knowledge of the situation, so to speak (though without our conscious realization), through a reflex mechanism and contribute to directing the harmony and regularity of movements. Undoubtedly, in a healthy subject whose spinal cord functions normally, once these complex movements of grasping, walking, etc., repeated every day, have been "assimilated" by the spinal cord, they continue to occur almost exclusively through the **spinal mechanism**, automatically as it were, without the conscious or unconscious intervention of the **brain** <term>original: "encéphale" (the brain as a whole, including the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem)</term> being necessary. But this is no longer the case when the spinal cord functions abnormally, when the abnormal excitability of its ganglionic gray matter—

# DYNAMIC ACTION OF THE MAGNET

...the ganglionic <note>likely referring to the gray matter of the spinal cord</note> dysfunction prevents it from fulfilling its **excito-motor** <term>excito-motor: relating to the nerve functions that stimulate muscles to move</term> functions with regularity and precision. Consequently, movements become disordered; nerve centers unrelated to the intended movement, excited by **irradiation** <note>the spreading of a nerve impulse beyond its usual path to neighboring areas</note>, add unintended muscular movements to the original goal; this is what constitutes trembling; this is **chorea** <term>chorea: a neurological disorder characterized by involuntary, jerky, "dancing" movements</term>.

In these conditions, the intervention of the brain becomes useful: it moderates the excito-motor influence of the **spinal cord**, regulating the movements that the cord—left to its own devices—can no longer direct properly; it corrects, at least to a certain extent, the imperfection of the spinal mechanism. However, it can only correct this if it is able to perceive what is happening during muscular movements. When these sensations are missing, when the **sensorium** <term>sensorium: the sensory apparatus of the brain that receives and interprets stimuli</term> is unaware of the position of the limbs, their contraction or relaxation, their flexion or extension—when the "nerve wires" are broken through which the organs of movement normally report their status and needs at every moment—then the brain becomes powerless to remedy the disorders of **motility** <term>motility: the body's capacity for movement</term>, and the spinal cord rules as master.

If the broken wire is reconnected and the brain is placed back in contact with the skin and muscle surfaces, it will restore order and re-establish, as much as possible, the muscular harmony compromised by the actions of the spinal cord. Now, this appears to us to be the therapeutic influence of the **magnet**. By restoring the tactile sense and the muscular sense, it allows the brain to correct the aberrations of spinal excitability that manifest as trembling, **reflex trepidation** <term>reflex trepidation: a rapid, rhythmic shaking of a limb triggered by a reflex stimulus</term>, and chorea.

It is through a mechanism similar to the one by which it appears to moderate reflex trepidation and **hemichorea** <term>hemichorea: chorea affecting only one side of the body</term> that the magnet was able to simultaneously moderate muscle rigidity. I cannot emphasize this fact enough, as it explains the effectiveness of suggestion in many circumstances. *Functional trouble in diseases of the central nervous system often exceeds the scope of the anatomical lesion; the lesion impacts the functions of neighboring zones through shock or dynamic irritation. And it is against this modified dynamism, which is independent of a direct material alteration, that psychotherapy can be all-powerful.* It remains ineffective, or has only a fleeting and limited effectiveness, when the functional disorder is maintained directly by the lesion. **CASE STUDY II.** — *From September 1, 1882, to February 15, 1884, four major apoplectiform <term>apoplectiform: describing symptoms that resemble a stroke (apoplexy), such as sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis</term> cerebro-spinal attacks, the first with predominant paraplegia <note>paralysis of the lower half of the body</note> on the left side; the others with paralysis of the left lower limb, ulnar neuritis <term>ulnar neuritis: inflammation of the ulnar nerve, which runs near the "funny bone" and controls sensations in the hand and certain finger movements</term>, girdle pains, headache, etc. — Numerous small attacks of isolated left ulnar neuritis. — Effectiveness of suggestion. — Total recovery through a series of suggestions.*

P... (François), fifty-two years old, a worker at the ironworks in Pompey <note>a town in northeastern France famous for its industrial history; its iron was used to build the Eiffel Tower</note>, admitted to the hospital on September 3, 1882.

Well-built, usually in good health, having no history of syphilis or alcoholism, and never having had rheumatism; he says that at the age of eleven, following a fright caused by the sight of a bear, he had epileptiform <term>epileptiform: seizures or attacks that resemble epilepsy but may have psychological or other non-epileptic causes</term> attacks which occurred daily for thirty-six days. Then they stopped, only to return in 1856, at the age of twenty-six. He had them for fourteen years, three or four times a day. Since 1870, he has had no more. # LOCAL LESION AND DYNAMIC RADIATIONS 265

what role functional dynamism plays in cerebro-spinal <term>affections</term> <note>Conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord</note>.

The first attack, leaving in its wake <term>paraplegia</term> <note>Paralysis of the lower half of the body</note> with <term>rachialgia</term> <note>Spinal pain</note>, girdle pains, and shooting pains, seemed to indicate acute <term>meningo-myelitis</term> <note>Inflammation of both the spinal cord and its surrounding membranes</note>. The rapid disappearance of the symptoms through suggestion showed that this was not the case.

The total recovery occurring after each attack, and the instantaneous disappearance through suggestion of each bout of <term>ulnar neuritis</term> <note>Inflammation of the ulnar nerve, which runs from the neck to the hand</note>, clearly indicate that all these troubles were not due to a serious and diffuse lesion of the cerebro-spinal axis, as the symptoms might have led one to suppose.

We believe it is a localized lesion, perhaps located near the spinal origin of the left ulnar nerve; could it be some benign tumor that remains latent and harmless, like certain brain tumors? From time to time, this local lesion would become the site of *dynamic radiations* within the cerebro-spinal axis; depending on how far these radiations extend, they would give rise to either ulnar neuritis alone, or shooting pains with paralysis and <term>anesthesia</term> <note>Loss of physical sensation or numbness</note> of the left lower limb, or paraplegia, or paralysis of all four limbs, or finally, brain-related disturbances: <term>cephalalgia</term> <note>Headache</note>, tearing of the eyes, facial tingling, and <term>apoplectiform</term> <note>Stroke-like</note> attacks. Similarly, a brain tumor that remains silent for a long time can occasionally cause stroke-like or <term>epileptiform</term> <note>Seizure-like</note> attacks with varying degrees of paralysis. These "remote phenomena," so frequent in nerve pathology, must impose a certain caution on the <term>topographic diagnosis</term> <note>The process of pinpointing the exact physical location of a disease or injury</note> of the lesion.

We have seen how suggestion intervenes usefully and dissipates troubles that are not dictated by an irremediable material alteration of the corresponding organic elements. We also see how suggestion contributes, in these cases, to rectifying and confirming the diagnosis by separating, so to speak, what is simply *dynamic* <note>Functional or psychological in origin</note> from what is *organic* <note>Relating to physical, structural damage to organs or tissues</note>.

<summary>The author concludes that the patient's symptoms were likely "dynamic radiations" from a small, local lesion rather than widespread physical damage, as evidenced by their disappearance through suggestion. This highlights the use of hypnosis as a diagnostic tool to distinguish between functional and organic disorders.</summary>

One may wonder if the <term>traumatic epilepsy</term> <note>seizures resulting from a physical head injury or trauma</note> in this patient, without the suggestion, would have become persistent. In these cases of long-standing epilepsy assimilated, so to speak, by the nervous system, a cure is most often impossible.

I have tried hypnotic suggestion in some cases of <term>idiopathic epilepsy</term> <note>epilepsy that arises spontaneously or from an unknown cause, rather than from a specific injury</note> which was already long-standing, and I have not succeeded in decreasing the number and frequency of the fits in a very obvious way. In two cases, I believed I had momentary results; the attacks seemed to become rarer; but despite the continuation of the suggestion, the result was not confirmed.

# ORGANIC HEMIANESTHESIA

Admitted to the ward on July 5, suffering since the previous day from a flaccid left-side <term>hemiplegia</term> <note>paralysis affecting one side of the body</note> with left <term>hemianesthesia</term> <note>a total loss of sensation on one side of the body</note>; the attack had been preceded by <term>prodromes</term> <note>early symptoms indicating the onset of a disease</note>. It is a case of an <term>embolism</term> <note>a blockage in an artery, often caused by a blood clot</note> of the <term>thalamostriate artery</term> <note>original: "artère opto-striée"; a vessel supplying blood to the deep structures of the brain</note>, with an area of <term>softening</term> <note>in 19th-century medicine, "ramollissement" referred to the breakdown of brain tissue following a lack of blood supply, or a stroke</note> in the internal white capsule or its vicinity. The hemianesthesia is complete in the upper limb; on the torso, face, and upper limb, it is a <term>hemianalgesia</term> <note>an inability to feel pain on one side of the body</note>.

I will not dwell on the details of the observation, as they are unnecessary for our subject.

On July 11, the analgesia and anesthesia remained complete on the upper limb, as did the abolition of the <term>muscular sense</term> <note>the ability to perceive the position and movement of one's limbs, now known as proprioception</note>; sensitivity had returned slightly to the lower limb, but remained very dull; the latter can only perform slight movements; some slight movements are also possible in the forearm and hand.

A <term>magnet</term> <note>original: "aimant"; during this era, "metallotherapy"—the application of magnets or metals to the skin—was a popular experimental treatment for nervous disorders</note> is applied to the back of the hand and the wrist; it is left there permanently for 3 days, on July 11, 12, and 13.

The anesthesia and paralysis remain the same.

During the following days, the patient suffered from <term>supra-orbital neuralgia</term> <note>nerve pain located above the eye</note> which was treated with quinine sulfate and which only definitively subsided starting on the 20th. The anesthesia persists as before. The motor paralysis is decreasing; the patient can lift his left arm to a right angle and bend his elbow; he can lift his leg up to a height of 25 centimeters.

On the 22nd, a new application of the magnet is made and left in place.

On the 24th, it was noted that despite the application of the magnet, the anesthesia remained absolute. We continue to apply the magnet, but while **assuring** the patient that the magnet will cause the return of sensation, that he would feel his hand and would be able to recognize its position.

On the 25th, he says he feels his arm better; however, when explored, his sensitivity remains doubtful. The **suggestion** is repeated while he is in a <term>waking state</term> <note>the patient was not hypnotized, but given verbal instructions while fully conscious</note>.

On the 26th, tactile sensitivity exists, but is dull; there is a slight sensitivity to a pinprick; the muscular sense has not returned. The suggestion with the magnet is repeated, without sleep.

On the 28th, tactile sensitivity is very clearly present throughout the limb, as are the sensitivity to pain and the muscular sense (awareness of the position of the limb). Tactile sensitivity has also returned more clearly to the lower limb and the torso. — The magnet is removed, and the obtained result is maintained.

### CASE STUDY V. — *Diffuse rheumatic myelitis <term>myelitis</term> <note>inflammation of the spinal cord, which can cause pain, numbness, and paralysis</note>. — Notable improvement through repeated suggestion; — Stationary state.*

A... (Michel), forty-six years old, a laborer <term>manœuvre</term> <note>a manual laborer or unskilled worker</note>, came to the hospital on February 24, 1883.

Two months ago the patient, who had been in good health until then, felt a bruising pain in his left forearm along with a persistent numbness. For two months, at the slightest movement—when he wants to grab an object, for example—he is seized by a temporary cramp that forces his fingers into extension <note>straightening or stretching out</note>, causing him to drop the object; he can almost no longer dress himself because of these cramps.

For the past 15 days, the right hand has been affected, but much less so. One day, about a month ago, the patient while walking suddenly felt a bruising pain in both feet; he could no longer flex his legs, which were stiff, and, trying to continue on his way, he fell on the sidewalk. Having gotten back up, he took about a hundred steps and fell once more. After a moment of rest, he was able to continue his journey and returned home, though with great difficulty. In the following days, he walked with much difficulty and became very fatigued by walking. Often, neighbors were forced to help him climb back up to his room on the second floor.

As for previous illnesses: seven or eight years ago, he had pains in his kidneys, sometimes also in one or the other shoulder; since then, he has been subject to rheumatic pains, but has always been able to continue his work. He says he has been a little short of breath for two or three years but continues, nevertheless, to carry heavy loads.

No history of syphilis or alcoholism.

The following was observed on February 25: strong constitution; full, bounding, and regular pulse; slight aortic insufficiency <term>aortic insufficiency</term> <note>a condition where the heart's aortic valve does not close tightly, allowing blood to flow backward</note> without enlargement of the heart; a soft diastolic murmur at the base. Respiration is clear without any rattling sounds <term>râles</term> <note>abnormal clicking or rattling sounds heard in the lungs during an exam</note>.

The patient rises from his bed with difficulty and walks with effort, his legs spread wide, moving slowly and taking small steps.

# TEMPORARY EFFECTS IN CERTAIN TYPES OF MYELITIS <note>inflammation of the spinal cord</note>

In several patients suffering from <term>spasmodic tabes</term> <note>a historical term for spastic spinal paralysis, characterized by muscle stiffness and weakness</note> or multiple sclerosis with <term>rigid paralysis</term> <note>spasticity where muscles stay continuously contracted</note>, I have been able, through suggestion, to diminish the exaggeration of tendon reflexes and the <term>contracture</term> <note>permanent shortening of a muscle or joint</note> for a more or less long period; but I have never succeeded in forever stopping the evolution of the disease; I am setting aside cases of <term>myelitis</term> <note>inflammation of the spinal cord</note> that are curable or capable of stopping spontaneously, like the one in the previous observation. I hypnotize him on October 9; he reaches the second degree <note>a mid-level state of hypnotic depth</note>. I suggest the disappearance of the trembling and the stiffness.

Upon waking, the hand does not tremble at all; the patient carries a full glass to his mouth without spilling a drop; he walks better and faster; the exaggeration of tendon reflexes persists, but to a lesser degree.

10. — The improvement is maintained. D... walked better yesterday. He still uses his hand without trembling; <term>dynamometric force</term> <note>a measurement of physical grip strength</note> 28 to 32. — New hypnotic suggestion. Upon waking, he walks, still with stiff and swaying legs, but less so than before the suggestive treatment.

11. — He says he no longer has vertigo; he no longer trembles and walks well, though still with a little stiffness. — Suggestion.

On the 13th, the improvement is maintained; there is no more dizziness or trembling. He easily lifts a chair with his hand by grasping it by the backrest.

I place him in <term>somnambulism</term> <note>in this context, a deep state of hypnosis where the patient is highly responsive but will not remember the session</note>; the sleep is deep, with amnesia. Upon waking, he feels stronger and can lift the chair with his hand by grasping it by one leg. The tendon reflexes have greatly diminished.

On the 14th, the patient works in the ward and helps with the service <note>assisting with hospital chores or errands</note>.

19. — Continued to do well. Says he had some headaches yesterday and the day before, and at times a visual disturbance. Looking at objects in front of him, he sees them as large and blurred; this trouble is fleeting, lasting only about five minutes; he only had it once yesterday, twice the day before. — He walks well, but says he still trembles a little in the legs; exaggerated tendon reflexes are no longer produced. At times still, he says, since the day before yesterday, the hand starts trembling again, and he spills the contents of the glass.

# MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS. TEMPORARY IMPROVEMENT

<margin>16</margin>
<meta>catchword: SUGGESTION.</meta>

The <term>dynamometer</term> <note>a device for measuring the strength of a hand-grip</note> gives 48 on the right; 18 on the left. — Hypnotic suggestion.

On the 23rd, [the patient] has been doing well since the 19th; has had no more headaches or visual disturbances; has no more tremors, and exaggerated <term>tendon reflexes</term> <note>involuntary muscle contractions triggered by a stimulus, such as a reflex hammer</note> are no longer observed; speech is still slow.

On the 24th, D... is doing well. A certain stiffness is still observed in the left leg; he cannot lift it to a certain height, nor stand on the left foot alone. Still a slight exaggeration of the tendon reflexes. — New hypnotic suggestion. *Upon waking, he can lift the left leg almost to the same height as the right and stand on the left foot alone for several seconds.*

We cease the suggestion. The improvement is maintained. D... is sufficiently recovered to serve as a hospital orderly. For more than six months, I see him daily, trotting about actively, carrying the patients' food from the kitchen to the ward; he no longer trembles and walks properly.

Then, after this time, the stiffness and tremors gradually return; he is admitted as a patient into the service of one of my colleagues; and suggestion is no longer attempted.

For several months, he has been in the chronic illness ward (Saint-Julien hospice), where I saw him on April 15: the symptoms of <term>multiple sclerosis</term> <note>original: "sclérose en plaque," a disease where the immune system eats away at the protective covering of nerves</note> are clearly pronounced; tremors in the hands, stiffness in the lower limbs, considerable exaggeration of the tendon reflexes, very slow, monotonous, and <term>staccato speech</term> <note>original: "parole... scandée," a rhythmic, syllable-by-syllable speech pattern typical of this condition</note>, etc.

# CASE STUDY

On December 25, while in bed, he felt his entire left hand go numb with a sensation of <term>pins and needles</term> <note>original: "fourmillements," a prickling sensation like ants crawling on the skin</note>, as if he had been sleeping on it; these prickling sensations persisted all day; at six o'clock in the evening, they gradually moved up to the shoulder, then spread from top to bottom along the armpit down to the hip.

The following morning, his neck was stiff; he had the sensation of a "bar" across the left half of the nape of his neck.

These prickling sensations lasted for three days, accompanied by a complete loss of sensation in the entire left upper limb and <term>paresis</term> <note>muscular weakness caused by nerve damage, less severe than full paralysis</note>. After three days, the prickling disappeared, and after five to six days, sensation was totally restored.

During the following days, he experienced a continuous, light tremor that persisted even at rest, lasting until March. Then, "crises" or attacks occurred, characterized by numbness in the hand, moving up the arm and down the left side of the chest; the forearm was contracted in <term>flexion</term> <note>bent inward</note>, the hand in <term>pronation</term> <note>turned palm-down</note>, and the digits flexed, accompanied by sharp pains and a sensation of constriction and suffocation in the <term>precordial region</term> <note>the area of the chest directly over the heart</note>. These cramps lasted about five minutes and were followed by a feeling of utter exhaustion. — He has had four crises in total since March; the last crisis took place twelve days ago. In the intervals between, the arm functions well, except for five or six times a day when he feels numbness in parts of the upper limb—hand, forearm, or arm—lasting about five to six minutes each time. — Since the end of April, he has also been seized two or three times a day by tremors in the left upper limb accompanied by prickling sensations.

He is a married man, hardworking, with no history of alcoholism or <term>venereal diseases</term> <note>a common medical inquiry at the time, as syphilis was a frequent cause of neurological disorders</note>. His original constitution is good; he is very anemic. His temperature is normal. We observe <term>dullness</term> <note>a flat sound during a physical exam, indicating fluid rather than air in the lungs</note> with an absence of breath sounds and thoracic vibrations throughout the side that is not constricted: the <term>pleural effusion</term> <note>a buildup of fluid between the tissues that line the lungs and the chest</note> appears to persist in a passive state.

The heart sounds are normal; there is no pain when pressure is applied to the chest or the <term>brachial plexus</term> <note>the network of nerves sending signals from the spinal cord to the shoulder, arm, and hand</note>. — *Appetite is good, digestion normal. — Diagnosis: a lesion of unknown nature located on the path or the roots of the brachial plexus, causing dynamic radiations?* <note>The physician is questioning if the symptoms are caused by nerve signals "radiating" from a specific injury or blockage</note>

## HYSTERIC AFFECTIONS

**Case Study VIII.** — *Hystero-epilepsy in a young man. Sensory and perceptual hemianesthesia, remarkable effects on the restoration of visual functions obtained through intermittent magnetization and hypnotic suggestion. Does magnetization possess only a suggestive power?*

Mr. Spillmann presented a patient suffering from <term>hystero-epilepsy</term> <note>a historical diagnosis for a condition combining symptoms of hysteria and epilepsy</note> to the Medical Society on February 28, 1883. The case involves an eighteen-year-old man who has seventeen brothers and sisters who have never shown any nervous symptoms; his mother is <term>neuropathic</term> <note>a historical term for someone with a chronic functional nervous disorder</note>.

As a child, he already exhibited symptoms of <term>somnambulism</term> <note>sleepwalking</note>, getting up at night and wandering through the village, from where he had to be brought back home. Three years ago, L... contracted syphilis and presented <term>syphilids</term> <note>original: "syphilides"; skin eruptions caused by syphilis</note> on the scalp, skin, and mucous membranes, etc. He entered the relief house on November 4, 1882. Of below-average intelligence, he can barely read or write. The penis is inflamed and swollen and has two deep ulcers on the sheath the size of a one-franc coin. Very pronounced congenital <term>phimosis</term> <note>a condition where the foreskin cannot be retracted over the glans</note>. A yellowish, foul-smelling purulent matter flows through the opening of the foreskin. <term>Hydrargyric treatment</term> <note>original: "Traitement hydrargyrique"; a medical treatment using mercury, commonly used for syphilis at the time</note>.

Mercury rubs and potassium iodide remain without results. # EFFECTIVENESS OF SIMULATED MAGNETIZATION

...almost normal, except in its outer and lower-outer portions. Color perception was normal. Two days later, March 17, the patient had maintained this enormous visual field on the right; on the left, visual acuity and color perception were completely normal, except for red and blue; the visual field had lost nothing since the last session.

It was then that Messrs. Bernheim and Charpentier <note>Hippolyte Bernheim and Augustin Charpentier were leading figures of the "Nancy School" of psychiatry, which argued that many "hypnotic" phenomena were actually the result of suggestion rather than physical forces.</note> had the idea to see what effect the unconscious suggestion—which would inevitably accompany a sham magnetization—would have on the patient. The coil <note>An electromagnetic induction coil, used at the time to apply magnetic fields to the body.</note> was applied to the left temple as before, but no current was passed through it. The coil was left in place for thirty-five minutes, and at the end of this time, the visual field of the left eye had acquired the same extent as that of the right eye—an extent greater than what is ordinarily considered normal; it had gained 7 degrees on the inside, 25 degrees on the outside, and 20 degrees at the outer and lower edge. The perception of pain <note>original: "perception des douleurs." In this clinical context, the doctors were testing the return of physical sensation to areas that had previously been "numb" or anesthetic due to hysteria.</note> was normal. (See the perimeter chart of March 17.)

*Thus, simulated magnetization had acted upon the sensitivity of the visual apparatus with the same intensity as real magnetization and hypnotic suggestion.*

From this interesting observation, one can see how much suggestion is associated—unknown to the patient and often to the physician—with many therapeutic manipulations. It is an element that must be taken into account before ruling on the value of certain medications.

# TRANSFER OF ANESTHESIA AFTER SUGGESTION

March 27, 1883. On Good Friday, she suffered a <term>luxation</term> <note>original: "luxation"; a dislocation</note> of the shoulder, which was reduced. The following day, she suffered a <term>crise nerveuse</term> <note>original: "crise nerveuse"; a "nervous crisis" or hysterical fit, common in 19th-century clinical descriptions</note> and has apparently been prone to them ever since.

28. — *<term>Hypnotic suggestion</term> (<term>somnambulisme</term> <note>a state of deep hypnosis or "sleepwalking" induced by the doctor</note>) restores sensitivity in the limb. Good night.*

29. — *The shoulder is still painful. The anesthesia, which had returned to the limb, is removed again by suggestion. The pain persists; it resists a second hypnotization.*

A first hypnotization makes the pain disappear, but the anesthesia remains; a second session makes the hemianesthesia disappear, leaving only the shoulder pain.

On the 30th, sensitivity remains on the right side, but the left hand and forearm are anesthetized; on the same side, there is a decrease in hearing; a total loss of smell and taste; and a decrease in vision (reduced to one-third). Sensitivity remains in the lower limbs. Simple suggestion, combined with the application of <term>diachylon</term> <note>a type of adhesive medical plaster</note> on the left hand, produces no change. *Hypnotic suggestion restores sensitivity on the left side in the forearm and the senses; but at the same time as this sensitivity is restored, it is observed that a <term>transfer</term> (not suggested) has occurred; there is now complete right sensory-sensorial anesthesia.* After a new suggestion, the right side becomes sensitive again, except for the forearm.

In the evening, at half-past five, the following is observed: on the right, anesthesia of the face, the upper limb, the chest, and the back down to the 10th dorsal vertebra, along with sensory anesthesia; sensitivity remains in the lower limbs and the abdomen. On the left, anesthesia of the face and the upper limb; the shoulder and breast remain painful, while sensitivity remains in the abdomen and lower limbs. The left eye sees unclearly and can read at a distance of 30 centimeters (<term>acuité visuelle</term> <note>visual acuity</note> of 1/3); there is also anesthesia of taste and smell.

### SENSORY ANESTHESIA MODIFIED BY THE MAGNET

She clearly distinguishes the colors blue, red, and green with both eyes.

The patient has eaten little for four days. Heart sounds are clear. Respiration is normal.

A magnet was applied on November 30 to the left temple, with the negative pole at the bottom facing the outer corner of the eye; another was placed on the inner side of the arm. <note>In the late 19th century, "metallotherapy"—the application of magnets or metals to the body—was a common experimental treatment for hysterical paralysis and sensory loss, popularized by doctors like Jean-Martin Charcot.</note>

**December 1.** — During the night, the painful spot on the breast disappeared. She slept well, felt a twitching of the eyelids and a sensation of heat in the head, then fell back asleep. The paralysis and the <term>sensory-perceptual anesthesia</term> <note>loss of the "special" senses like sight, hearing, and smell, as opposed to just skin touch</note> remain the same.

**2.** — Same state this morning. Intense <term>cephalgia</term> <note>headache</note> last night.

**3.** — Sight, hearing, and smell seem improved. Persistent pain toward the left shoulder. The patient reports tugging in the stomach with a sensation of hunger, nausea, and salivation. Touch on the face is only perceived at the outer corner of the mouth and eye; a pinprick is felt slightly on the forehead and cheek. The limbs remain anesthetized. Pressure is slightly felt. The paralysis persists; movements forced upon the arm <note>physically moving the patient's arm for her</note> are painful. During the night, she had nausea and hot flashes.

*The magnet was applied for three days to the temple; the visual field has expanded notably to the left. Here are the diameters taken this morning with the perimeter:* <note>A perimeter is a clinical instrument used to map a patient's field of vision to see how far their peripheral vision extends.</note>

Left eye: Diameter, 40; horizontal left, 55; inferior, 55; horizontal right, 45.
Right eye: Diameter, 40; horizontal left, 50; inferior, 55; horizontal right, 52.

The field of color is still narrowed for red and green; for the latter more than for the red.

Thus, the magnet has formally modified the sensory anesthesia. As for the <term>tactile anesthesia</term> <note>loss of the sense of touch on the skin</note>, it has remained the same. No sensation, except under fairly strong pressure; this is only painful at the level of the ovarian region <note>In 19th-century medicine, "ovarian tenderness" was frequently cited as a "trigger zone" for symptoms in female patients diagnosed with hysteria</note>, the shoulder, and the bend of the elbow. The **muscle sense** remains abolished. The <term>hemiplegia</term> <note>paralysis of one side of the body</note> remains total, except for the face.

I put the patient to sleep <note>refers to inducing a hypnotic trance</note>: she easily enters a state of **somnambulism** <note>a deep state of hypnosis where the patient can respond to the doctor</note>. Prolonged suggestion. *Of all the suggestions made, only one succeeded: the return of sensitivity to the hand;* finger movements remain impossible.

# OBSERVATION

In the evening at six o'clock, my chief of clinic, **Mr. Ganzinotty**, puts the patient to sleep again by means of fixation of the right pupil. <note>Fixation of the pupil is a technique used to induce a hypnotic trance by having the patient stare intently at a specific point—in this case, the doctor's eye or a fixed object—until the nervous system tires and the subject enters a sleep-like state.</note> In less than a minute, she is sound asleep; at first, she does not answer the questions put to her. Upon insisting, she answers feebly, almost in a whisper. She remains asleep for half an hour. Mr. Ganzinotty makes a series of repeated suggestions, harped upon, so to speak, to encourage movement in the paralyzed arm. For fifteen minutes, nothing works. But, at one point, *the patient is able, through suggestion, to keep her arm raised above the bed for a few seconds, but it always falls back inert and limp. Finally, after a tedious series of suggestions—perpetually the same—the fingers move; the hand can be raised slowly 10 centimeters above the bed and be moved from the left side toward the <term>umbilicus</term> <note>the navel</note>. The patient confesses her inability to do more; if one tries to make her bring her hand to her mouth, it can only be done by supporting the hand during each effort made by the patient to prevent it from falling; finally, it is brought to the mouth; when it is released, it falls back.* However, the movements persist in the fingers, and the <term>flexion</term> <note>bending</note> of the forearm toward the upper arm is possible. Lifting the entire arm remains impossible, and the patient complains of pain in the outer edge of the biceps.

Upon waking, the patient seems to emerge from a dream and is surprised to find herself in the hospital; then her memory returns, but she says she heard nothing and said nothing; she believes she is waking from a deep sleep.

After a few minutes, she is asked to perform the same movement, and the patient moves her fingers, shifts her hand, and flexes the forearm toward the arm—actions she was incapable of doing before.

However, she says she has pain in her elbow and shoulder; furthermore, there is a state of nausea with a sharp pain in the <term>precordial region</term> <note>the area of the chest directly over the heart</note>.

Mr. Ganzinotty puts her to sleep a second time by having her fixate on his right pupil. Same suggestion: more extensive and precise movements are obtained; the patient can bring her hand all the way to her head. Then, if the suggestion ceases, the arm falls back inert. Upon waking, the same astonishment: the discomfort and pain have disappeared, though a heaviness persists in the left shoulder and arm.

*The patient can perform, while awake, the movements she performed during her sleep. There is therefore a partial recovery.*

### **OBSERVATION XI.** — *Hysterical sensitivo-sensory hemianesthesia. — Restoration of sensitivity after a single session. — Increase in visual acuity and visual field. — Permanent restoration.*

B..., aged seventeen, entered the hospital on *March* 18, 1884. Married, she gave birth on March 30, 1883, to a full-term child who lived for twenty days; the postpartum period was normal. Since the month of September 1883, she has complained of abdominal pain and <term>leucorrhea</term> <note>A thick, whitish or yellowish vaginal discharge, often associated at the time with various "nervous" or uterine complaints.</note>; for a week, she has reported a painful spot at the left <term>scapulum</term> <note>The shoulder blade.</note> and in the <term>precordial region</term> <note>The area of the chest immediately over the heart.</note>; she walks with difficulty, digests poorly, has been constipated for eight days, and has some vomiting. Her last menstrual period occurred on March 10; since the 12th, she has had frontal <term>cephalalgia</term> <note>A medical term for a headache.</note>, shooting pains toward the temples, and a rolling noise in the left ear.

Let us note, among the causes of this nervous state indicated by her, frequent disagreements with her mother-in-law, following which, on the 16th, her husband reportedly threw her out of the marital home.

On the 19th, it is noted: delicate constitution, nervous temperament. Anxious <term>facies</term> <note>The facial expression or appearance of a patient, used as a diagnostic tool.</note>, irritable character, the exit points of the facial nerve are painful upon pressure on both sides. She experienced the hallucinations very well; and, as she adored music, her face brightened. She followed the rhythm with gestures of her hand and foot, and, thanks to this musical diversion, the anxiety—the precursor to a crisis—disappeared. She said to me: "In eight days." — "That is good," I said, "in eight days, it will be next Thursday." — "Yes," she said, "next Thursday." — "Then it is agreed: next Thursday, when I have put you to sleep, upon your waking, you will speak." — "Yes," she said. Upon waking, she remembered nothing.

# CASE STUDY XVI. — *Hysteria-like symptoms. — Sensation of emptiness in the head and ringing in the ears, moral inertia <note>A state of psychological apathy, lack of motivation, or listlessness.</note>. — Almost total, rapid disappearance of these symptoms through hypnotic suggestion.*

## III

### NEUROPATHIC AFFECTIONS
<note>In 19th-century medicine, "neuropathic" referred to functional disorders of the nervous system where no physical lesion was found; today we might call these psychosomatic or functional neurological disorders.</note>

**CASE STUDY XVII.** — *Nervous aphonia <term>aphonia: the total loss of voice</term> for one month. — Cure by simple affirmation.*

Miss B..., a sixteen-year-old girl, a domestic servant, entered my clinical service on March 3, 1885. Small, delicate, and lymphatic <note>A historical medical term for a constitution thought to be pale, sluggish, or prone to swelling and infection.</note>, she has been coughing without expectorating for twenty-five days; for ten days, she has had "stitches" in her side, and a lack of appetite for fifteen days; she has had hoarseness for a month, and the loss of voice has been complete for three weeks. Amenorrhea <term>amenorrhea: the absence of menstrual periods</term> for six months. On examination, we find slight dullness <term>submatité: a muffled sound produced during chest percussion, indicating denser tissue</term> in front at the fourth right intercostal space, and sub-crepitant crackles <term>râles sous-crépitants: bubbling sounds in the lungs often associated with fluid or inflammation</term> starting from the third; in the back, slight dullness on the right, from the sub-spinous fossa to the bottom, with slightly "blowing" expiration in both lung apexes with fine sub-crepitant crackles; otherwise, no fever. *Diagnosis: Slowly progressing pulmonary tuberculosis.*

On the 7th, the condition remains the same; the loss of voice persists completely. There is no cough or expectoration; since the patient has neither difficulty swallowing <term>dysphagia</term> nor laryngeal pain (whether spontaneous or when touched), and no fever—and because the tuberculosis appears stationary—I wonder if the loss of voice is not nervous in origin. I tell the students that nervous aphonia sometimes yields instantly to electrization <note>The medical application of electric current, which the author suspects works through the power of "suggestion" rather than the electricity itself.</note>, which may act simply through its suggestive influence. I send for the induction apparatus. Before using it, I want to try simple suggestion in the waking state: *affirmation*. I say to the patient: "I am going to give you back..."

### *CASE STUDY XIX. — Nervous gastric disorders. Epigastric pain. Anesthesia of the limbs. Rapid disappearance of anesthesia by suggestion; temporary improvement of gastric disorders.*

F. C..., forty-nine years old, a day laborer, single, without children, entered the hospital on April 29, 1884; she had reportedly been ill for three months. The ailment began with strong pains in the epigastrium <term>epigastrium: the upper part of the abdomen, located just below the ribs</term> and in the hypochondria <term>hypochondria: the regions of the upper abdomen on either side of the epigastrium</term>. After meals, she has a sensation of constriction above the navel and in the larynx, which lasts about an hour, along with frequent belching and vomiting; even outside of meals, she feels a burning sensation in the upper abdomen; she has no watery regurgitation; habitual constipation: she has a bowel movement only every three days. For three months, she has had frequent nervous twitches, especially following fits of anger, with tingling in the fingers lasting for two minutes, followed by crying; for two years, she has suffered from dizziness. Neuropathy <term>névropathie: in the 19th century, this referred broadly to functional nervous disorders without a clear physical cause</term>.

The vomiting has ceased since her admission to the hospital, but the other symptoms persist. We note only a slight bulging with tenderness in the epigastric region; the stomach is not dilated, and the liver is not swollen.

On May 7, we further observe analgesia <term>analgésie: the inability to feel pain</term> along with anesthesia <term>anesthésie: the loss of all physical sensation, including touch</term> of the torso and the upper limbs; the muscle sense <note>original: "sens musculaire"; today known as proprioception, or the ability to sense the position and movement of our limbs</note> is lost. In the lower limbs, sensation exists only on the soles of the feet.

The patient is hypnotized (deep sleep): suggestion is used. During the day, she digests what she eats well and has little burning in the upper abdomen. At night, she sleeps for six hours; she says she has not slept that much in six months.

On the 8th, it is noted that the anesthesia has disappeared; the patient feels when she is touched, but a pinprick, although felt, is not painful; the muscle sense has also returned.

The restoration of sensation is maintained.

The other gastric and mental troubles are favorably influenced by repeated suggestions, but they generally recur after a variable amount of time.

G..., aged fifty-six, a flour dealer, entered the hospital on October 26, 1884, for chronic bronchitis with emphysema and chronic interstitial pneumonia <note>a condition where lung tissue becomes scarred, making breathing difficult</note>, due to the inhalation of flour dust and silica to which he is exposed while sharpening millstones. I will not dwell on the details of his chest condition, which does not concern us here. He has stopped working for a month; as a miller, he was in the habit of waking up at two o'clock in the morning, and since he no longer works, he continues to wake up at that hour and cannot fall back asleep.

It is to correct this insomnia that I am trying hypnotic suggestion. A first attempt on the 28th produced only numbness; a second attempt immediately after put him into a deep sleep without memory upon waking. I suggested to him that he should not wake up during the night.

## CASE STUDY XXXII. — *Disturbances in writing movements following chorea. Cure by a single session of hypnotic suggestion.*

Henri Grosse, sixteen years of age, from Hayange (Alsace-Lorraine), comes with his mother to see me on June 5, 1884. This attack had been preceded for one month by acute articular rheumatism <note>Now commonly known as rheumatic fever, a condition that frequently causes Sydenham's chorea in children.</note>. In February last, he was again seized by chorea; for one month, he suffered very great disordered agitation, limited to the upper limbs. Since the month of March, these movements gradually decreased in intensity and have since disappeared; however, he can no longer write, he has been forced to interrupt his studies, and it is for this reason that he comes to consult me. He has undergone various treatments; during the month of February, he took bromide for three weeks, then chloral syrup <note>A sedative and hypnotic medication used to calm the nervous system.</note> which calmed the agitation. During the month of March, he took antimony tartrate <note>original: "tartre stibié," a potent chemical compound used historically as an emetic and to treat inflammatory conditions.</note>, then arsenic for three weeks. During the months of April and May, ether sprays were conscientiously applied to the spine twice a day. The choreic agitation had ceased, but the hands remained clumsy for tasks that were somewhat delicate; he can neither write nor straighten the knot of his tie.

Currently, June 5, he is a lymphatic <note>In 19th-century medicine, a "lymphatic temperament" described a person who appeared pale, sluggish, or lacking in physical vigor.</note> boy, quite tall, timid, speaking little; his intelligence is nevertheless clear; he eats and sleeps well; no choreic movement is observed, though there are barely perceptible slight twitches in the hand. I suggest to his mother that I put her child to sleep; she consents. The first attempt is not successful: he furrows his brow, blinks his eyelids, and claims he cannot sleep. Knowing that in this deep sleep one sometimes obtains immediate results, I propose to put him to sleep a second time, and I place him back into a somnambulistic state in less than a minute. The duration of this first onset was three months. Cold water showers were the only treatment used.

Between six and seven years old, joint pain.

*Third onset*, at nine and a half years old. — Only the right side was affected; six to seven attacks per day; duration: six weeks. No treatment.

*Fourth onset*, at eleven and a half years old. — Same <term>hemi-choreic</term> form; same duration; still six to seven attacks per day. No treatment.

*Fifth onset*, at twelve and a half years old. — The first attack took place on May 27 and was followed that same day by six very violent attacks. On the 31st, she was subjected to <term>induced sleep</term> <note>A synonym for the hypnotic state.</note>; only one slight attack occurred, which was the last.

On June 9, following a scare, the choreic movements reappeared, though with less intensity.

*Generalized chorea*, when treated right at its onset, seemed more difficult for me to influence. In addition to the observation I am reporting, I have tried it in other cases. In general, it seemed to me that as long as the chorea is general, intense, and "furious," involving the eyes and face along with psychological disturbances, suggestion has no hold. When the disease has entered a period of lesser agitation, hypnotization often succeeds quickly in reducing the intensity of the disordered movements; however, it must be continued for weeks before reaching their complete cessation.

We know how often writer’s cramp is resistant to all forms of medical treatment. A calligraphy teacher from Frankfurt-on-Main, Mr. Wolff, often succeeds through <term>empirical</term> <note>Practical methods based on observation and experience rather than scientific theory.</note> means where physicians have failed.

Mr. Wolff’s method is detailed by Mr. Romain Vigouroux in *The Medical Progress* (1882, no. 3) in the following terms. It can be summarized in two points: gymnastics and massage:

> 1. Gymnastics are both active and passive. Three times a day, patients must perform a series of movements of the upper limbs, successively in all directions. These movements are generally sharp, with the hands sometimes open, sometimes closed. The number of movements in each series and, consequently, the duration of the sessions is increased progressively and varies according to the case.
> 
> Passive movements consist of more or less forced stretching—we might almost say <term>elongation</term> <note>The physical lengthening of the muscle fibers to relieve tension.</note>—of the muscles specifically affected. This is the most delicate part of the treatment, as it is dangerous, according to Mr. Wolff, to exceed a certain point. Furthermore, the patient repeats this maneuver on himself three or four hundred times a day.
> 
> Writing exercises begin as soon as the <term>spasmodic state</term> <note>The condition of having involuntary muscle spasms or contractions.</note> has notably diminished—that is, from the very first days.
> 
> 2. Massage and friction are also practiced very carefully by Mr. Wolff every day. He insists on the importance of what we shall call <term>tapotement</term> <note>original: "tapotement"; a specific massage technique involving rhythmic tapping or percussion of the muscles with the edge of the hand or fingertips.</note> of the muscles.
> 
> The duration of the portion of the treatment conducted under Mr. Wolff’s immediate supervision is about fifteen days. According to him, a treatment that has not produced improvement within four or five sessions should be abandoned.

One might wonder if <term>suggestion</term> <note>The psychological influence exerted by a practitioner over a patient, which was a central theme of the Nancy School of hypnotism at this time.</note> does not play its part...

# MR. WOLFF'S METHOD

to claim credit for the cures obtained. Patients come to a specialist renowned for curing the ailment with which they are afflicted; the specialist affirms the cure; the manipulation performed for half an hour, the massage, the frictions, the passive movements repeated 300 or 400 times a day—all of this concentrates the attention on the curative idea. All of this prompts the brain to perform the act of **inhibition** <note>In 19th-century psychology, "inhibition" referred to the brain's ability to suppress involuntary movements or nervous impulses, such as spasms.</note> necessary for the cessation of the spasm.

When one sees, on the other hand, ignorant **bone-setters** <note>Traditional folk healers who treated musculoskeletal injuries without formal medical training.</note> or crude massagers succeed in quickly curing certain sprains or pains through practices that are in no way reasoned—and sometimes not even rational—is it not also, to a certain extent, the patient himself who, through **auto-suggestion**, achieves or facilitates his own recovery?

### CASE STUDY XXXVI. — *Tetany of the upper limbs. — Bouts of somnambulism with nocturnal nightmares. — Cure of the tetany in two sessions, and of the somnambulism in one session.*

Since childhood, he has had a **double clubfoot (talipes equinovarus)** <note>A congenital deformity where the feet are rotated inward and downward.</note>. Of a delicate, **lymphatic** <note>A 19th-century medical term used to describe a pale, sluggish, or fragile constitution, often associated with a perceived lack of "vital energy."</note> temperament, he has nonetheless not suffered from any serious illnesses. Only once were his legs affected at the same time.

Currently, he reports that since yesterday at four o'clock in the evening, he has felt a cramp in his hands and a pain radiating from the shoulder into the fingers. The last three fingers of both hands are flexed [bent inward]. One can extend them with difficulty, but the flexion recurs immediately. The index finger and thumb remain extended. Other movements are performed well. He can bend his elbows and bring his arms over his head. The arm and forearm are painful to pressure, especially at the level of the biceps. When one presses this muscle, it produces a flexion of the forearm.

### CASE STUDY XXXVIII. — *Nocturnal incontinence of urine cured by suggestion in a single session.*

M..., a thirteen-year-old child, <term>lymphatic</term> <note>A historical medical classification for a temperament thought to be sluggish or pale, often associated with a weak constitution.</note>, rather delicate, is in Nancy, boarding with a teacher. This boy, of rare intelligence, wets the bed two or three times a week; since his childhood, he has not been able to be broken of this habit.

The child comes to see me on October 16. In the ten days preceding this date, the child has urinated in bed four times.

I put him to sleep on October 16; he only reaches the second degree: <term>suggestive catalepsy</term> <note>A state where the patient’s limbs remain in whatever position they are placed by the doctor, yet the patient remains somewhat aware.</note>, with memory upon waking. I suggest to him that he will no longer urinate in bed, that he will no longer be able to urinate while lying down, but only while standing up, in the vertical position.

He comes back to see me again on the 17th, 18th, and 23rd of October; since the first <term>suggestion</term>, he has never again lost his urine.

### CASE STUDY XXXIX. — *Aphonia consecutive to pneumonia cured by energetic affirmation. — Nocturnal incontinence of urine in the process of being cured by suggestion.*

G. C..., fifteen years old, living with her parents, enters the hospital in my clinical service on April 13, 1886, suffering from <term>frank pneumonia</term> <note>An acute form of pneumonia that affects a specific lobe of the lung.</note> of the lower right lobe on the sixth day. This <term>pneumonia</term> reaches its <term>defervescence</term> <note>The period during which a fever subsides and the body temperature returns to normal.</note> on the morning of the 16th, the ninth day.

# URINARY INCONTINENCE CURED BY SUGGESTION

I try hypnotic suggestion on April 17, 18, and 19, without therapeutic result. G. C... easily enters into <term>somnambulism</term> <note>A deep hypnotic state where the patient may act or speak while appearing to be asleep.</note>, but does not carry out hypnotic hallucinations or post-hypnotic suggestions.

On the 21st, after a final unsuccessful hypnotization, I provide the suggestion in the <term>waking state</term> <note>Giving therapeutic instructions while the patient is fully conscious, rather than in a trance.</note>. At first, it is useless: the young patient laughs easily and takes my assertions lightly, without letting herself be impressed. I pretend to get angry; I imperiously command her to speak aloud, to say *a*, *b*; I affirm that she can do it and I enjoin her to do so. She makes an effort and clearly articulates: *a*, *b*, then her name. Her voice, still <term>aphonic</term> <note>original: "aphone"; the medical term for a total loss of voice.</note> without effort, becomes resonant if she makes an effort. During the day, her voice—still hoarse—improves. The next day, it continues to be articulated, and starting from the evening of the 23rd, it has almost returned to what it was before.

That is not all. Since childhood, this young girl has had an infirmity: urinary incontinence. At night, she wets the bed, soaking it; she must be woken up three times during the night to prevent this result. During the day, she cannot go more than an hour and a half without urinating. Furthermore, because of this infirmity, she could not be sent to school; she knows how to neither read nor write. Two years ago, she spent two months in the hospital to be rid of this condition. She was treated without result with cold water compresses applied to the <term>hypogastric region</term> <note>The lower part of the abdomen, just above the pubic bone.</note>.

Until about the 20th, the patient soaked her bed every night. Starting on the 21st, I provide the hypnotic suggestion that she retain her urine, that she can no longer urinate in bed, and that she can go a long time without needing to urinate.

Since that day, she can go three hours without urinating during the day. On the night of the 22nd to the 23rd, she did not wet the bed. But on the night of the 23rd to the 24th, she wet the bed again.

On the 24th, she went the entire day without urinating, and since that moment, she only urinates twice a day.

Continuation of the suggestion. — During the night, she still wets the bed a little, although she gets up three times to urinate.

I am away from Nancy <note>A city in France where a famous school of hypnotic therapy, led by Dr. Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault and Dr. Hippolyte Bernheim, was established.</note> for a few days. The suggestion treatment is stopped. The urinary incontinence remains cured during the day; at night, she still wets the bed, but very little; she is woken up once each night.

Suggestive therapy is resumed on May 6.
