# DYNAMIC PARALYSES

### V

## DYNAMIC PARESIS AND PARALYSES
<note>In this context, "dynamic" refers to functional disorders—symptoms that have no underlying physical or "organic" damage to the nerves or muscles, but are instead psychological or "psychic" in origin. "Paresis" refers to muscular weakness, while "paralysis" refers to a total loss of movement.</note>

**OBSERVATION XL.** — *Numbness with muscular weakness of the left upper limb. — Significant improvement in a single session.*

J... (Joseph), eighteen years old, a locksmith, comes for a consultation on February 25, 1885. Ten to twelve days ago, he felt a numbness in his left hand which has persisted since then and prevents him from working with that hand. He can close it, but with considerable difficulty, and he opens it slowly; he flexes his arm and forearm with a certain stiffness; he reports a sensation like "rubber" in his fingers; he can only pick up a sheet of paper with great difficulty; furthermore, there is no pain, either spontaneous or when pressure is applied; tactile sensitivity is preserved; additionally, near the <term>deltoid</term> <note>The large triangular muscle covering the shoulder joint.</note>, he feels a sensation like a heavy "roll" or padding. — There is a certain discomfort in the left knee; when walking, the movement of flexion is more abrupt and gives his gait a style reminiscent of <term>ataxia</term> <note>A neurological sign consisting of a lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements.</note>.

On the <term>dynamometer</term> <note>A device used to measure the strength of a muscle squeeze, usually a hand grip.</note>, the left hand gives a reading of 15 to 16; the right hand gives 37.

The patient is hypnotized and reaches a deep sleep. *After suggestion and awakening, the dynamometer gives a reading of 22 for the left hand and 32 for the right hand; he picks up a sheet of paper very well with his left hand.*

A new hypnotization is performed immediately after the first, with a new suggestion. Upon awakening, the left hand gives 26 on the dynamometer, the right hand 31. J... now feels only a slight stiffness in the hand; he walks a little better.

He did not return for further consultation.

On April 12, 1884, a woman was admitted for <term>pneumonia</term> <note>An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs.</note> of the lower right lobe, which had been present for nine days and has since undergone <term>defervescence</term> <note>The medical term for the period during which a fever subsides.</note>. Two months ago, she added (nearly a month before her pneumonia), her walking became more difficult; she dragged herself along painfully, and since her pneumonia, she can no longer stand at all. She reports neither tingling nor numbness; her sensitivity is perfect, her tendon reflexes are normal, and her muscles are not <term>atrophied</term> <note>The wasting away or thinning of muscle tissue.</note>. Regarding her medical history, she reported having had quite frequent <term>epileptic</term> attacks during her adult life; she has not had any for two years.

I found no sign of <term>myelitis</term> <note>Inflammation of the spinal cord, which would cause physical nerve damage.</note>, and I believe it is a case of "dynamic weakness," which the patient's impressionability has transformed into *psychic paralysis*.

During that same session on May 8, I hypnotized her and she fell into a deep sleep; I suggested to her that she could walk. Upon waking, she stood upright without support for three seconds, though manifesting a marked tendency to lean backward.

On the 9th, after a second session, she *stood much better and took a few steps*, quite astonished at being able to do so.

On the 10th, after the third session, she *walked at a slow pace*, without falling, and without showing any tendency to lean backward. When she stands, she *spreads her legs to widen her base of support* <note>original: "base de sustentation" — the area beneath a person that includes every point of contact they make with the floor; a wider base provides more stability.</note>.

On the 11th, she *walked all day* without support, something she had been unable to do for more than two months.

I continued to hypnotize her from time to time; she continued to walk well; on the 24th, she *climbed and descended the stairs alone*.

She remains cured.

### CASE STUDY XLII. — *Growing pains and muscular weakening of the lower limbs. — Notable improvement from the first session. — Complete recovery in five sessions.*

S... (Eugène), fifteen and a half years old, a well-built boy with no previous illnesses, has complained for six months of a weakness in his legs. This has been accompanied for the last three weeks by pain in the <term>jarrets</term> <note>The hollows of the knees or the hamstrings at the back of the leg.</note> when he walks, and especially when he climbs stairs; he then feels a sensation like a stab from a penknife in the hollows of the knees, descending into the calves and the <term>rotules</term> <note>The kneecaps (patellae).</note>. When he walks on uneven ground, he constantly missteps; his foot turns inward. He cannot run. He walks like a sailor, swaying [ballottant]; the tenants in his building, seeing him pass, say to him: "One would say you are driving a plow."

He comes to see me on May 30, 1885. I find no <term>lesion</term> <note>A physical injury or structural damage to the tissue.</note>, nor any functional disorder other than the pain in the knees and the difficulty in his gait; his muscular strength is normal. I believe it is a <term>dynamic muscular disorder</term> <note>In 19th-century medicine, a "dynamic" disorder meant a functional problem where the organ itself is healthy, but its operation is disturbed, often by psychological or nervous factors.</note> perhaps linked to growth. The child says he has grown by a head's height in the last six months.

I hypnotize him: he reaches the third degree <note>A classification of the depth of a hypnotic trance; at this level, the subject is highly suggestible but retains their memory of the events upon waking.</note>, and his memory is preserved upon waking. He has almost no pain at all while walking and carries himself much better.

*31. — He continues to improve; he only made two or three missteps while descending a hill; he was able to walk from half-past one until five o'clock without fatigue, whereas previously, he was tired after a fifteen-minute walk; he still has some pain when climbing stairs. — Second session.*

June 3, third session. — June 4, fourth session. He still reports pain when bending the knee and standing back up.

On the 9th, he says he walked yesterday for three hours without any fatigue or pain; he could not have done a quarter of that for two months.

Continuation of the suggestion.

On the 11th, he says he no longer feels anything; no pain when climbing the stairs; he has walked without swaying since the first suggestion.

On the 13th, the last session; he runs, he jumps, no longer missteps, and no longer feels any discomfort.

I continue to see this young man often; the recovery has persisted to this day.

### VII

### VARIOUS PAINS

**OBSERVATION XLVII.** — *<term>Epigastralgia</term> <note>Pain in the upper middle abdomen.</note> removed by a single suggestion.*

M.., forty years old, a switchman at the Rosières railway station, comes for a consultation on May 28, 1884. Of a good constitution but very nervous, though usually in good health, he already came to see me two months ago for epigastric pain which disappeared through hypnotic suggestion.
For the past two days, this pain has returned; it no longer occurs spontaneously, but—especially when he is on night duty—he is seized at intervals by a sharp pain with a feeling of oppression in the <term>epigastrium</term>, lasting fifteen to thirty minutes. It then disappears and gives way to a kidney pain that lasts for the same amount of time. This cycle recurs twice every twenty-four hours. His appetite is maintained and his digestion is quite good. Pressure applied to the epigastric region causes very sharp pain.
Through suggestion, he enters a deep sleep, with no memory upon waking. After waking, he no longer feels anything.
A few months later, he returns with the same pain. It again yields entirely to a hypnotic suggestion.

### CASE STUDY L. — *Tubercular diathesis. Restoration of sleep and disappearance of chest pains by suggestion.*

### **CASE STUDY LI.** — *Hypogastric and left supra-inguinal pain linked to old pelvic peritonitis. They disappear in a few sessions.*

B... (Yvonne), twenty-one years old, a seamstress, entered the service on January 24, 1885. She was discharged toward the end of July, cured; her periods became normal and light again, the last time being on January 1st.

For the past nine days, new pains have appeared above the groin and in the <term>hypogastrium</term> <note>The lowest central region of the abdomen.</note>; the patient has been bedridden for eight days; the pains return especially in the evening and morning for an hour. — Insomnia for the past eight days.

Significant <term>anteflexion</term> <note>A condition where the uterus is tilted or folded forward.</note> of the uterus. — The <term>vaginal vaults</term> <note>Original: "culs-de-sac."</note> are clear. — Profuse, non-fetid <term>leucorrhea</term> <note>A thick, whitish or yellowish vaginal discharge.</note> for three months. — Pain in the kidneys coexisting with the abdominal pains. — No <term>globus</term> <note>Original: "boule," referring to "globus hystericus," the sensation of a lump in the throat often associated with historical diagnoses of hysteria.</note> or other hysterical manifestation. ### CASE STUDY LIV. — *Painful contusion of the deltoid. — Inability to lift the arm. — Almost complete recovery in two sessions.*

Sch..., sixty-three years old, a laborer in Nancy, was carrying <term>planks</term> <note>original: "madriers"; large, heavy pieces of timber used in construction</note> on September 3 at nine o'clock in the morning when he fell on his left shoulder, which struck against a wall.

On September 4, I noted a simple <term>contusion</term> <note>a bruise or injury caused by a blow that does not break the skin</note>. The patient cannot lift his arm, nor move it away from his torso without using his other hand; the pain is located toward the front-inner part of the <term>deltoid</term> <note>the large triangular muscle covering the shoulder joint</note>. I hypnotize him on the spot; he reaches the second degree <note>The "degrees" refer to the depth of the hypnotic trance according to the Nancy School's classification system</note>; I suggest to him the disappearance of the pain and the ability to lift his arm. Upon waking, he raises it to 45° without using his other hand, and up to the top of his head with its help. The pain has greatly diminished.

On September 5, second session, third degree. After the session, he carries his arm to the top of his head and holds it vertically in the air. Before the session, when the arm was lifted, he could not lower it gradually; the arm would drop abruptly. Now, he can hold it in the air. Only a little painful discomfort remains in the deltoid.

## CASE STUDY LVII. — *Pain in the flexor muscles of the forearm dating back two months. — Healing in two sessions.*

### Observation LX. — *Muscular rheumatism with cramps in the limbs; rapid cure by suggestion.*

C... (Jean-Claude), seventy-two years old, a gardener, enters the hospital on November 6, 1883; for four weeks, he has complained of widespread pain throughout his body, especially in the limbs, occurring two or three times a day and lasting up to forty-five minutes; furthermore, two or three times a day, he has cramps in the back of the knee <note>original: "jarret"</note> accompanied by the bending of the knees for several minutes. Frequently exposed to rain, he was thoroughly soaked four weeks ago and has had a cough since that time; some opaque mucous phlegm with foamy fluid; a slight feeling of heaviness <term>oppression</term> <note>difficulty breathing or chest tightness</note> when he walks; he does not suffer from his usual shortness of breath. His appetite has always been good.

He is a well-preserved man of strong constitution; the chest is slightly rounded and resonant; breathing is harsh in the front, with clear exhalation; breathing is harsh and rough in the upper back on the left side, and a bit "blown" in the area above the shoulder blade <term>supraspinous fossa</term> on the right; some fine crackling sounds <term>sub-crepitant rales</term> <note>clicking or rattling sounds heard in the lungs through a stethoscope, often indicating fluid</note> at the base of the left lung. Heart sounds are normal. (*Early-stage age-related emphysema, bronchitis, age-related hardening of the lung tips.*) The finger joints are slightly deformed (*nodular rheumatism*) and crackle slightly during guided movements. By pressing on the muscles of the buttock and the left thigh, one identifies pain and involuntary muscle contractions <term>contractures</term> (*muscular rheumatism*). Left for several days without treatment, his condition remains the same; he has cramps every day; on the 7th, three attacks of cramps in the legs and wrists; on the 8th, four cramps in both arms.

On the 11th, it was noted: the patient complains of pain in the Achilles tendon and in the inner part of the thighs; he frequently has cramps that occur simultaneously or alternately in all limbs, accompanied by a sensation of "pins and needles" <term>formication</term>, with the fingers and knees being contracted in a half-bent position.

Starting from the 12th, the patient is hypnotized every day (*deep sleep*) with suggestion. *Since the first session, he has had no more cramps; the widespread pains are diminishing; they no longer exist when the patient is at rest, though they still manifest when the patient walks.*

# CASE STUDY LXI. — *Rheumatic ileo-lumbar neuralgia.* — *Rapid improvement in one session. Gradual total recovery in eighteen days.*

T... (Marie), a day laborer, fifty-five years old, enters the hospital on November 27, 1884; she is a widow and mother of twelve children, all of whom died, like their father, of chest disease <note>original: "de la poitrine"; in the 19th century, this usually referred to pulmonary tuberculosis</note>.

A few days ago, this woman, who is usually in good health, was doing laundry with her lower back leaning against the stone. Suddenly, she had to stop her work because of a pain located in the right side, radiating toward the front of the hip bone <term>anterior iliac spine</term>. She had to return home and was seized by chills. The pain was so sharp that she could not climb back into her bed. This lumbar pain has persisted since then, with painful radiations, sometimes into both legs. Otherwise in good health, she has a good appetite.

On the 29th, the following is noted: good constitution; absence of fever <term>apyrexia</term>; a fluid-filled swelling in front of the left kneecap <term>prepatellar hygroma</term> <note>commonly known as "housemaid's knee," caused by prolonged kneeling</note>. Excessively sharp pain at the level of the lumbar vertebral region, below the right rib cage margin and at the origin of the right sciatic nerve. The pain is less intense on the left side. These pains often radiate to the lower right part of the abdomen and into the limbs. (*Rheumatic ileo-lumbar neuralgia.*)

*Hypnotization.* — The patient falls into somnambulism <note>a deep state of hypnotic trance where the patient can often talk or move while appearing to be asleep</note>; during the sleep, she has an active spontaneous dream; she talks about washing a floor. I dispel this dream and affirm the disappearance of the pains. Upon waking, she remains deeply drowsy and falls back asleep spontaneously until three o'clock in the afternoon (having been asleep since eleven o'clock in the morning).

On the 30th, she feels much better and slept well during the night. The lumbar region is almost no longer painful. Only the sacral region <note>the triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> is still painful when pressure is applied to the midline; there have been no more radiations of pain. The patient can turn over in her bed, which she was unable to do before.

On December 1st, she still had a very sharp pain when pressure was applied to the sacrum; but the pain remains localized to that region; the lower back, the rib margin, and the origin of the sciatic nerve are no longer painful; no more radiations. *Suggestion.*

### CASE STUDY LXII. — *Joint pain following inflammation. — Immediate cure by suggestion.*

D... (Louis), twenty-one years old, comes to the consultation on April 2, 1884. On the 16th, we observe exactly the same state as upon his arrival; the same condition of the wrists and insteps. The patient still walks with his left leg spread; he cannot stand on the sole of his foot without supporting himself with his hand.

### **OBSERVATION LXXI. — *Muscular rheumatic pains in the left arm, then in the right leg. — Healed each time in a single hypnotic session.***

Marie X..., aged ten, comes to see me on February 20, 1886. This child, usually in good health and with no previous illnesses, reports a pain in the right arm for the last four to five days. The arm is sensitive to pressure; the child cannot lift it to her head. I put her to sleep by simple closure of the eyelids; I suggest the disappearance of the pain; I perform some frictions <note>therapeutic rubbing or massaging of the skin</note> on the arm. Upon waking, the child has no memory of anything. The pain has almost completely disappeared, and she can easily lift her arm to her head. During the day, all painful sensations vanish without returning.
On April 14, the child returns. Since the previous day at four o'clock in the evening, she has had a pain in the right leg and thigh. Pressure is painful on the front surface of both limbs. She walks while dragging her leg, the knee and the **instep** <term>instep</term> <note>original: "cou de pied"; the arched upper part of the foot between the toes and the ankle</note> being almost stiff.
I place her back into **somnambulism** <term>somnambulism</term> <note>a deep state of hypnotic sleep where the patient can often move or talk while remaining in a trance</note>; I suggest the disappearance of the pain. Upon waking, she has almost no more pain, but still drags her leg, though less so. I put her under a second time and repeat the suggestion; I make her walk during her sleep, leading her along quickly. Upon waking, she walks very well and only drags her leg very slightly; she no longer reports any pain. The father tells me the next day that she returned home skipping and that she is totally cured.

Through these numerous observations, I have tried to demonstrate how vast the field of suggestive psychotherapy is. It is not only in hysteria, in neuroses, or in purely functional nervous diseases that it finds its application. We have seen the results it can produce in organic conditions of the nervous system, in chronic articular rheumatism, in stomach ailments, and so on. I have sought to explain (see observations I and II) the mechanism by which suggestion can act usefully in cases of this kind. 

At first glance, it may seem childish to appeal to the imagination to cure or improve functional disorders linked to cerebral hemorrhage, <term>softening</term> <note>the historical term for a stroke or cerebral infarction</note>, rheumatoid arthritis, or chronic <term>myelitis</term> <note>inflammation of the spinal cord</note>! Many doctors will shrug their shoulders and raise their arms to the heavens to protest against such assertions! Let them reflect and verify before protesting! They will be forced to bow before the evidence of the facts!

I do not claim that suggestion acts directly upon the diseased organ to eliminate vascular congestion, resolve inflammatory <term>exudate</term> <note>fluid that leaks out of blood vessels into nearby tissues due to inflammation</note>, or restore elements of the destroyed or degenerate <term>parenchyma</term> <note>the functional tissue of an organ as distinguished from the connective and supporting tissue</note>.

# MECHANISM OF HEALING BY SUGGESTION

What agent in <term>materia medica</term> <note>the body of collected knowledge about the therapeutic properties of any substance used for healing</note> is capable of sparking this direct healing process? Diseases heal through their natural biological evolution, when they are able to heal. Our ordinary therapeutic methods consist of putting the organism in the best conditions so that a <term>restoration to wholeness</term> <note>original Latin: "restitutio ad integrum"</note> can occur; we suppress pain, we modify function, we put the organ at rest, we calm the fever, we slow the pulse, we induce sleep, we activate secretions and excretions, and in doing so, we allow the healing nature—or to use modern language, we allow the activity of the forces and properties inherent in biological elements—to accomplish its work. The therapeutic agents at our disposal are merely functional medications. Suggestion, too, is a powerful functional medication.

All organs and all functions are commanded by the nervous centers. Each element of the organism has, so to speak, its center of action leading to the brain. Sensitivity, movement, nutrition, secretions, excretions, and the production of body heat are governed or at least influenced by this central organism which presides over the complex mechanism of animal physiology. This central organism can intervene usefully to restore, as far as possible, the activity of disturbed organs and functions.

I say *as far as possible*. Take, for example, a patient in whom a cerebral hemorrhage has destroyed, I suppose, the entire internal <term>white capsule</term> <note>a part of the brain that carries signals between the primary motor cortex and the spinal cord</note>; a descending degeneration has occurred in the <term>pyramidal tract</term> <note>the path the brain uses to send movement commands</note>, and a rigid <term>hemiplegia</term> <note>paralysis on one side of the body</note> has followed. Here, the motor organ that is the <term>indispensable requirement</term> <note>original Latin: "sine quâ non"</note> for the movements of half the body is destroyed. No organic replacement is possible. No medication can restore what is destroyed. Suggestion, no more than other medications, can restore a function whose indispensable organ no longer exists.

# DYNAMISM IN DISEASES

...a few conducting fibers sufficient to transmit the centrifugal influence of the will to the <term>motor cells</term> <note>nerve cells in the brain or spinal cord that send signals to muscles to trigger movement</note>. These fibers are only affected in their function, struck by the shock of proximity, affected <term>virtually</term> <note>meaning the fibers are physically present but functionally dormant or suppressed</note>. Powerless to emerge spontaneously from their torpor, suggestion can act <term>dynamically</term> <note>referring to the energy or "force" of the nervous system rather than its physical structure</note> upon them; the psychic activity brought into play, concentrated toward these fibers, brings them a new stimulus that revives their numbed state. Through this <term>dynamogenic</term> <note>the process of generating or increasing nervous energy</note> excitation, the cerebral impulse manages to clear a path to the motor cells, and the interrupted conductivity is restored, bringing back function.

Now, we have seen what a considerable role dynamism plays in nervous functions. It is known that <term>organic hemianesthesias</term> <note>a loss of sensation on one side of the body caused by physical injury to the brain or nerves</note> persisting stubbornly for years (for four years in one of my own observations) have been cured rapidly by various practices: <term>electrization</term> <note>the application of electric currents for medical treatment</note>, <term>metallotherapy</term> <note>an 19th-century treatment involving the application of certain metals to the skin to restore sensation</note>, <term>magnetotherapy</term> <note>the therapeutic use of magnets</note>, and suggestion. It is known that dynamic, hysterical, and psychic <term>paralyses and contractures</term> <note>prolonged, involuntary muscle contractions or inability to move</note>, after persisting for years and defying all therapy, sometimes give way as if by magic to a violent emotional upheaval. There is nothing exceptional in the living organism; every fact that occurs is capable of recurring, for that fact implies the activation of a physiological mechanism inherent to the organism.

A consideration that must never be lost sight of in therapeutics is this: the functional disorder can survive the cause or the <term>organic lesion</term> <note>physical damage or a wound in an organ or tissue</note> that gave rise to it: this disorder is no longer sustained by the lesion, but "retained," if I may say so, by the nervous system. The latter has a great tendency to preserve certain <term>modalities</term> <note>specific ways in which something happens or is experienced</note> that have been imprinted upon it. A child who has had many convulsions repeats these convulsions under the slightest influence; <term>tics</term> <note>involuntary, repetitive movements</note>, nervous movements, hysterical crises, nervous cough, vomiting, diarrhea, etc., are acts that the nervous centers execute spontaneously...

# SUGGESTION ACTS DYNAMIQUEMENT

...when these acts, having been frequently repeated by the patient, are, so to speak, assimilated by them. Certain pains persist indefinitely, even when the underlying <term>lesion</term> <note>a physical injury or structural change in an organ or tissue</note> no longer exists. Every surgeon has seen, following a contusion for example, a limb remain <term>dynamically</term> <note>meaning the "nerve force" or function is impaired even though the physical structure appears healed</note> affected: the patient continues to suffer and to keep the limb immobilized, even though the bruise seems to have healed. <term>Electrization</term> <note>the medical application of electric currents</note>, <term>hydrotherapy</term> <note>the use of water treatments, such as baths or sprays</note>, massage, <term>moral influence</term> <note>in the 19th century, this referred to psychological or mental influence rather than ethics</note>, and suggestion often intervene usefully to dissipate these surviving troubles.

One readily concedes that in the realm of nervous pathology, psychic influence can have a certain effectiveness; but it is harder to conceive that, outside of this realm, the same influence could achieve any result! "Look," one might say, "at a case of chronic <term>rheumatic arthritis</term> <note>a general historical term for various forms of chronic joint inflammation</note>! The joint is diseased; the articular and periarticular tissues are profoundly altered! Do you claim to suggest to the lesion that it should resolve itself, to the <term>synovial membrane</term> <note>the soft tissue found between the joint capsule and the joint cavity</note> to resume its normal structure, to the destroyed cartilage to reconstitute itself?"

I do not claim that. I observe through experience that <term>suggestive therapeutics</term> <note>the use of verbal suggestion or hypnosis to treat illness</note> is sometimes undeniably useful in diseases of this kind. Many will see and yet deny, blinded by prejudice in the face of the evidence of the facts, because they are steeped in the infallibility of their own judgment, and because they systematically close their eyes to truths that do not fit their preconceived ideas.

No doubt, against a dislocated joint, against a bony or fibrous <term>ankylose</term> <note>stiffness of a joint due to abnormal adhesion and rigidity of the bones</note>, or against old <term>articular fungosities</term> <note>a historical term for inflammatory growths or spongy tumors in the joints, often associated with tuberculosis</note>, suggestion can do nothing. But such is not the case for all chronic rheumatic arthropathies. Here is a man whose joints remain swollen and painful; but the lesion is not incompatible with the functioning of the joint; it is capable of resolving; the cartilages and synovial membranes have not yet undergone an irremediable alteration; it is the immobility of the joint that can partly maintain the lesion; it creates the retraction of the...

# THE DYNAMIC ROLE OF SUGGESTION

...cellular-fibrous articular and peri-articular tissue: it perhaps robs the <term>synovial fluid</term> <note>the clear, thick fluid that lubricates joints</note> of its lubricating qualities; it makes the cartilaginous surfaces uneven, and maintains a passive <term>stasis</term> <note>a slowing or stoppage of the flow of blood or other body fluids</note> in the capillaries; surgeons are well aware of "arthritis from prolonged rest." Suggestion, by calming the pain and giving the patient the possibility of performing the movements necessary for the joint's integrity—thus restoring flexibility to the fibro-serous tissues, lubrication to the synovial fluid, and activity to the capillary circulation—can act effectively to improve and cure the <term>arthropathy</term> <note>any disease or disorder of the joints</note>.

Suggestion attacks the disease through one of its elements, and the suppression of this <term>morbid</term> <note>diseased or unhealthy</note> element can have a positive ripple effect across the entire pathological system, where all elements are mutually dependent on one another. And what else does standard <term>therapeutics</term> <note>the branch of medicine concerned with the treatment of disease</note> do? Do opium, quinine, salicylate, rubs, <term>revulsives</term> <note>treatments intended to divert blood or inflammation from a diseased part to another part of the body, like mustard plasters</note>, <term>blistering agents</term> <note>called 'vésicatoires' in the original French; these were substances used to induce blisters as a form of counter-irritation therapy</note>, massage, or electricity do anything other than attack the disease through one of its elements? Do we have many medications with the property of directly modifying a material <term>lesion</term> <note>a physical injury or structural change in an organ or tissue</note>? It is functional restoration that brings about organic restoration, when such a thing is possible.

I have said enough to indicate the point of view I take to explain the results of suggestive psychotherapy.

I was not familiar with this therapeutic method when I wrote in 1875 in the *Encyclopedic Dictionary*, in the article *Reaction*:

> "Often the <term>moral</term> <note>original: "le moral"; in 19th-century medicine, this referred to a person’s mental or psychological state rather than their ethics</note>—that is to say, the activation of psychic functions—produces healthy reactions. To console a patient, to bolster their shaken courage, to banish the terrifying anxieties that undermine them, is often to react effectively against the disease. At the doctor’s soft and persuasive voice, the patient, restored as if by a healing balm, feels confidence reborn and their malaise dissipate. No doubt organic alterations, once fully established, persist..."

# THE DANGERS OF HYPNOTISM

One more word, before ending this book, regarding *the dangers of hypnotism*.

Is hypnotism itself dangerous for the person subjected to it? Based on my extensive experience, I do not hesitate to affirm that when it is handled well, it does not offer the slightest inconvenience. It does not disturb the functions of organic life in any way; we have seen that respiration and circulation are not influenced in subjects whose minds are at rest. If some individuals, during the first sessions, exhibit certain nervous phenomena—such as muscular twitches, gasping breath, malaise, or an accelerated pulse—or if some <term>hysterics</term> <note>a historical medical term for patients thought to suffer from uncontrollable emotional excesses or physical symptoms without a clear organic cause</note> experience convulsive fits during the procedure, these symptoms (which are <term>auto-suggestive</term> <note>arising from the patient's own thoughts or fears rather than the doctor's actions</note>, so to speak, and due to emotional distress or a feeling of fear) always disappear in subsequent sessions thanks to a calming suggestion that restores peaceful confidence. Once the habit is formed, the subjects fall asleep as peacefully as in natural sleep and wake up the same way, without the slightest discomfort, provided one takes care to suggest the absence of discomfort upon waking.

Never in my already long practice have I seen any inconvenience follow the induced sleep as we perform it; for suggestion is always present as a corrective for any issues that might arise.

There are, however, some points which it is important to know and which I shall point out. Some people, after having been hypnoti-

## EXAGGERATED SUGGESTIBILITY

...hypnotized a certain number of times, retain a disposition where they easily fall asleep spontaneously. Some, barely awake, fall back asleep on their own a few moments after waking, into the same hypnotic sleep. Others fall asleep in this way during the course of the day. This *auto-hypnotizing* <note>the tendency to enter a hypnotic state spontaneously without an external operator</note> tendency can be suppressed by suggestion. It is enough to affirm to the subject during their sleep that once awake, they will be completely awake and will no longer be able to fall back asleep spontaneously during the day, in order to prevent this propensity for spontaneous sleep.

Others become too easily hypnotizable; when they have frequently been put into <term>somnambulism</term> <note>a deep state of hypnosis where the subject can act and speak while appearing to be asleep</note>, the first person to come along can sometimes put them into this state by surprise, through simple occlusion of the eyes. Such hypnotic suggestibility is a real danger! Left at the mercy of anyone, deprived of psychic and moral resistance, certain somnambulists thus become beings who are "taxable and malleable" <note>original: "taillable et malléable." This is a play on a French feudal expression meaning to be entirely at someone's mercy or disposal</note> at the whim of the suggestionists!

Those moralists concerned with human dignity are right to be anxiously preoccupied with such a possibility, so fraught with peril! They would be right to condemn a practice that can strip from man, without any possible resistance on his part, his **free will**, they would be a thousand times right, if the remedy were not right alongside the evil. When we foresee such a disposition in our somnambulists, we take care to affirm to them during their sleep—and this is a rule from which it is good not to deviate:

> "No one will be able to put you to sleep, except for your doctor, to relieve you."

And the subject, docile to the injunction, becomes refractory to any outside suggestion. One day I tried to hypnotize an excellent somnambulist whom I had already put to sleep several times; I could not manage it; I called <term>Mr. Liébeault</term> <note>Ambroise-Auguste Liébeault (1823–1904), a French physician and a founder of the Nancy School of hypnotism</note> to my aid; he put her to sleep in a few seconds. I then asked her why I had not succeeded. She told me that several months earlier <term>Mr. Beaunis</term> <note>Henri-Étienne Beaunis (1830–1921), a French physiologist and psychologist also associated with the Nancy School</note> had suggested to her...

Therefore, the danger of excessive hypnotic suggestibility can be averted by suggestion itself.

### ACTION ON THE BRAIN

A more serious apprehension that naturally arises is this: Do you not fear, it will be asked, that hypnotism—even when handled with caution, for a purely therapeutic purpose, and without induced hallucinations—might eventually cause serious harm to the cerebral faculties? That the brain becomes sluggish, the intelligence depressed, and cerebral activity diminished; that the subject falls into and remains in a state of intellectual torpor.

Experience alone can provide the answer. Now, I have put highly intelligent people to sleep for months and even years, daily, even twice a day; and never have I observed the slightest harm to the faculties of the <term>understanding</term> <note>the capacity for rational thought and comprehension</note>; cerebral initiative persisted just as actively; it even sometimes became more active, because many functional disorders from which patients suffer—such as pain, anxiety, nervous agitation, and insomnia—have a negative impact on psychic activity. To suppress these troubles through suggestion is to set the brain at rest, to release it from impressions that hinder its free functioning, and to safeguard the functional integrity of the organ that generates thought. Hypnotic sleep by itself is beneficial and free of drawbacks, just like natural sleep.

But another order of danger can result from induced hallucinations <note>hallucinations intentionally triggered by the hypnotist during or after a session</note>, and I must state my full thoughts here. Undoubtedly, harmless hallucinations induced at fairly long intervals, whether hypnotic or post-hypnotic, momentarily disturb the mind in the same way as dreams; but balance is quickly restored when the hallucinatory dream has disappeared.

# ABUSE OF HALLUCINATIONS

Is it the same if these hallucinations are frequently suggested to the imagination? Could there not eventually remain some persistent disturbance in the brain? Is it not to be feared that a more or less notable disruption of the intellectual faculties might persist? I would not wish to assert that certain fragile brains, predisposed to **mental illness** <note>original: "aliénation mentale"—a common 19th-century term for insanity or psychiatric disorders</note>, could not receive a serious injury from these ill-timed and clumsy experiments, knowing that any emotion, any violent upheaval can trigger the onset of a madness whose <term>diathetic</term> <note>referring to a "diathesis," or a constitutional predisposition or hereditary tendency toward a particular disease or condition</note> seed, often hereditary, is inherent to the organism. I must only say that, in the many experiments I have conducted, I have never observed any psychic disturbance persisting after the experiments. In one of my patients, whom I have mentioned, M... G..., a very intelligent woman suffering from <term>locomotor ataxia</term> <note>a condition characterized by a loss of coordination in voluntary muscle movements, typically associated with late-stage syphilis</note>, I allowed myself, without forcing her, a few experiments for this purpose, while carefully monitoring her psychic state, ready to stop the experimentation at the slightest worrying sign that might appear. I subjected her, on various occasions for several days in a row, to complex, repeated hallucinations—**hypnotic** and **post-hypnotic**, both short-term and long-term—and from all of this, nothing remained. During the three years she has been in the ward, despite very numerous suggestions in both the **waking state** and sleep, her intelligence has remained just as sharp, and her initiative has not been affected. I hasten to add that this fact should not serve as encouragement; such experimentation is dangerous; experiments involving induced hallucinations must be conducted only with prudence and reserve.

Another real danger is this: certain subjects, after many hypnotizations and many hallucinations induced during sleep, become **suggestible** and liable to hallucinate in the waking state.

Their brain realizes with extreme ease all the concepts deposited within it: every idea becomes an act, every evoked image becomes a reality for them; they no

And once this extreme **hallucinability** <term>the state of being susceptible to suggested hallucinations</term> is produced, once this nervous illness is created, it is not always easy to cure or to lessen through a new suggestive intervention. Undoubtedly, suggestion handled by dishonest or clumsy people is a dangerous practice. The law can and must intervene to suppress such abuses.

Used for a therapeutic purpose, handled with prudence and intelligence, suggestion is nothing but **beneficial**. It is up to the physician to identify the useful effect and apply it to the relief of his patients. When in the presence of a patient, I believe that suggestive therapy has some chance of success, I would consider myself blameworthy, as a physician, if I did not propose it to my client, and if I did not insist on deciding them to submit to it.

# MEDICAL PRECEPTS

...must adhere, in order to safeguard his conscience and professional honor.

1. Never put any subject to sleep without their formal consent or the consent of those who have authority over them.

2. Induce sleep only in the presence of an authorized third party—a parent, husband, father, etc.—who guarantees the protection of both the hypnotist and the hypnotized person. This will prevent any unfortunate suppositions, any subsequent accusations, or any suspicion of an attempt that did not have the relief of the subject as its goal." (Beaunis) <note>Henri-Étienne Beaunis (1830–1921) was a prominent French physiologist and a member of the Nancy School of hypnotism, which emphasized the role of suggestion.</note>.

3. Do not give the hypnotized subject, without their consent, any suggestions other than those necessary for their healing. The physician has no rights other than those conferred upon him by the patient; he must limit himself to **therapeutic suggestion** <term>the use of hypnotic influence specifically to treat medical symptoms or psychological distress</term>. Any other experiment is forbidden to him without the formal consent of the patient, even if it were in the interest of science. Furthermore, the physician must not take advantage of his authority over the patient to elicit this consent if he believes the intended experiment could cause the slightest inconvenience.

It is suggestion applied to therapeutics that, as a physician and clinical professor, I had the duty to study in a special way.

I have the right to affirm, based on numerous facts, that **suggestive therapy** <term>a treatment method where the doctor suggests health improvements to a patient in a relaxed or hypnotic state</term> exists, without meaning to say that this therapy is always applicable or always effective. But it often is. It was not for an idle purpose, nor even for the sole goal of satisfying a vain scientific curiosity, that I began this study nearly five years ago, amidst many obstacles, and that I have pursued it rigorously despite many smirks! <note>The author refers here to the skepticism and ridicule faced by early researchers of hypnotism from the mainstream medical establishment.</note>
